item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox have secured a spot in baseball's postseason, making history by becoming the first team to clinch a playoff berth after being 14 games below .500. As of Sunday (September 20), the Red Sox have achieved an 84-72 record under interim manager Chad Tracy, following a remarkable second-half surge. Their playoff spot was confirmed with the Houston Astros' loss to the Atlanta Braves.
Despite a 5-1 loss to the Tampa Bay Rays, the Red Sox celebrated their postseason berth with a clubhouse party. The team, led by spiritual leader Willson Contreras, has shown resilience throughout the season. Tracy, who took over from Alex Cora on April 26, has been credited with stabilizing the team and fostering a supportive environment.
The Red Sox's journey to the playoffs included a significant turnaround starting with a four-game sweep of the New York Yankees in late June. They went on to achieve a 15-game winning streak, tying a franchise record set in 1946. This impressive run has positioned them as the No. 5 seed, likely facing the Yankees in the AL Wild Card round.
The team overcame early-season challenges, including the dismissal of Cora and several coaches. Chief Baseball Officer Craig Breslow emphasized the importance of decisive action in creating a thriving environment for the players. Looking ahead, the Red Sox aim to continue their momentum into the postseason, with the first game of the Wild Card Series expected to take place at Yankee Stadium on September 29.

item.title: [Yardbarker] Boston Red Sox Announce Major Aroldis Chapman News
item.dc:creator: Jake Rogers

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox will take Monday off after dropping two of three games to the Tampa Bay Rays in Florida, but they return home Tuesday for a three-game series against the Cleveland Guardians with encouraging news on their closer.
Aroldis Chapman has not pitched since Sept. 13 against Kansas City. The 38-year-old left-hander has been dealing with lat tightness that kept him unavailable over the weekend.
The club indicated Chapman should be ready for the final homestand that begins Tuesday at Fenway Park.
Chapman is in the midst of another strong season. He is 3-4 with a 1.95 ERA, 34 saves and 68 strikeouts in 50 2/3 innings across 52 appearances. His WHIP sits at 1.14.He has converted 34 of 36 save chances. His four-seam fastball has averaged 96.9 mph this year.
The Cuban-born reliever reached 401 career saves earlier this season. He also became the all-time strikeout leader among relief pitchers in July.
Boston clinched a wild-card berth Sunday despite a 5-1 loss to the Rays. The Red Sox are 84-72 and sit third in the AL East, 11 1/2 games behind Tampa Bay.
They have gone 52-25 since sitting 32-46 and 15 1/2 games out of first place on June 24. Interim manager Chad Tracy is 74-55 since taking over in late April.
The team holds a four-game lead over the Chicago White Sox for the second wild-card spot with six games remaining.
Garrett Whitlock and Erik Miller handled recent save situations while Chapman was sidelined. Whitlock recorded his fourth save of the year last week.
Chapman is under contract for $13.3 million this season. A $13 million mutual option for 2027 becomes guaranteed if he remains healthy and passes a physical after the season. He has already surpassed the 40-inning threshold attached to that clause.
The Red Sox bullpen has been a strength throughout the year. Chapman’s availability for the Guardians series and the following set against the Chicago Cubs would give the club a clearer picture heading into the postseason.
Boston is projected to face the New York Yankees in a best-of-three Wild Card series beginning Sept. 29 on the road unless the standings shift in the final week.
The Guardians arrive at Fenway after their own late-season push. Cleveland remains in the mix for an AL Wild Card berth.
Chapman first felt the lat tightness last Tuesday. He has reported improvement through the week and was not placed on the injured list.
The Red Sox have been cautious with their veteran closer given the proximity of the playoffs. They have enough of a cushion in the wild-card race that they do not need to rush him back.
Chapman’s last outing was a scoreless ninth inning with three strikeouts against the Royals. He walked two in that appearance.
His 2026 numbers include a 12.08 strikeouts-per-nine-innings rate and just three home runs allowed.
The left-hander was named an All-Star for the ninth time this summer. He also earned All-Star honors in 2025.
Boston’s remaining regular season games are all at Fenway Park. The homestand offers a chance to get Chapman work before the postseason begins.
The clubhouse celebrated the playoff clinch Sunday night in St. Petersburg after the Houston Astros lost to Atlanta, which officially locked in Boston’s berth.
Players and staff gathered for a team photo on the field after the result became official.
The Red Sox now shift focus to finishing the regular season healthy and sharp. Chapman’s expected return is a key piece of that preparation.

item.title: [nesn.com] Red Sox Final-Week Breakdown: Schedule, Playoff Stakes and Biggest Questions | NESN
item.dc:creator: Rodney Knuppel
item.description: The Boston Red Sox are headed back to the postseason, but their work is not finished. Boston enters the final week of the regular season at 84-72 after Sunday’s 5-1 loss to the Tampa Bay Rays. The Red Sox secured their second consecutive postseason appearance when other results around the American League eliminated the remaining path for them to fall out of the playoff field. The final six games will determine how prepared Boston looks when October begins. All six will be played at Fenway Park.
item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox are headed back to the postseason, but their work is not finished. Boston enters the final week of the regular season at 84-72 after Sunday’s 5-1 loss to the Tampa Bay Rays. The Red Sox secured their second consecutive postseason appearance when other results around the American League eliminated the remaining path for them to fall out of the playoff field.
The final six games will determine how prepared Boston looks when October begins. All six will be played at Fenway Park.
The Red Sox host the Cleveland Guardians at 6:45 p.m. ET on Tuesday, 7:10 p.m. Wednesday and 6:45 p.m. Thursday. Boston will conclude the regular season with three games against the Chicago Cubs from Friday through Sunday. Cleveland arrives with its own postseason urgency. The Guardians are attempting to protect their position from the Chicago White Sox, who remain close behind in the standings.
The Cubs enter the week at 87-69 after defeating the Cincinnati Reds 9-1. Pete Crow-Armstrong hit his 45th home run Sunday and has emerged as one of the most dangerous power-speed players in the National League.
Trying To Get Right With The Bats
Boston’s most immediate assignment is restoring its offense. The Red Sox managed only six hits during Sunday’s loss to Tampa Bay. Trevor Story prevented a shutout with a ninth-inning home run, but Boston wasted its best opportunity after loading the bases in the fifth inning.
Roman Anthony struck out to end that threat. Patrick Sandoval allowed five runs, although he recovered from a four-run first inning to complete seven frames. The loss dropped Boston to 84-72.
Chad Tracy must use the final week to balance two priorities.
The Red Sox need enough intensity to sharpen their offense and settle any remaining pitching questions. They also cannot afford to exhaust or injure important players immediately before the postseason.
Bullpen Questions
The bullpen hierarchy is another issue. Close games against Cleveland and Chicago can function as postseason rehearsals, allowing Tracy to test his preferred late-inning combinations before every decision becomes potentially season-ending.
The Red Sox cannot catch Tampa Bay in the American League East, and the New York Yankees remain ahead of Boston in second place. That makes the final six games less about chasing a division championship and more about playoff positioning, health and momentum.
Boston already possesses its October invitation. The final week will determine what kind of team arrives.

item.title: [yardbarker.com] Craig Breslow Reflects On Firing Alex Cora After Red Sox Clinch Postseason Berth
item.dc:creator: Aaliyan Mohammed

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox secured their spot in the postseason thanks to an Atlanta Braves win over the Houston Astros.
Things are going well now, but Red Sox fans remember the 10-17 start that led to Alex Cora and six other coaches being fired. Since then, interim manager Chad Tracy has led the charge in turning things around, but it has not all been him. The players started living up to expectations, and the team has gotten healthy.
At the time, many questioned Craig Breslow's ability to make decisions, with many fans saying Cora was fired as a result of Breslow failing to address the team's biggest flaws in the offseason. However, now it looks like Breslow was right to trust his players.
"I believed in the players that we had,” Breslow said when asked about the move to fire Cora, per The Athletic's Jen McCaffrey. “I felt it was really important that we acted definitively and decisively when we did so that we could create an environment around the players that was supportive, that would allow them to thrive. And they responded. While there may have been some people that questioned what this group was capable of, I think they answered resoundingly.”
One example of Breslow's belief paying off is Caleb Durbin. Durbin was acquired to replace Alex Bregman, and he was a terrible hitter through two months. However, after back-to-back off days in May, he has been on another level. He is looking more like the Rookie of the Year finalist he was for the Milwaukee Brewers last year. He looks like a real player the Red Sox can rely on down the line.
Perhaps what's most impressive about this Red Sox team is that they have turned the season around without arguably their two best pitchers, Garrett Crochet and Roman Anthony. However, Anthony is back, and Crochet could be in the bullpen for October.

item.content:encoded:
Red Sox avanza a playoffs
Roman Anthony: "Nos mantuvimos con vida cuando nadie creía que podríamos. Y aquí estamos"
Boston es el cuarto equipo en clasificar a los playoffs tras haber tenido un récord de 14 o más juegos por debajo de .500 en una temporada en la era de la Serie Mundial, desde 1903
ST. PETERSBURG, Florida.- . "Nos mantuvimos con vida cuando nadie creía que podríamos. Y aquí estamos", dijo Roman Anthony en medio de la celebración de los Medias Rojas de Boston, por su pase a la postemporada.
Mientras los Boston Red Sox celebraban su improbable clasificación a la postemporada en el Tropicana Field, con champán y cerveza a raudales, la música del vestuario parecía la más apropiada.
"Stayin' Alive".
"Creo que eso lo dice todo", declaró el jardinero izquierdo Roman Anthony el domingo, de acuerdo a un reporte de ESPN.
El 24 de junio, los Red Sox tenían un récord de 32-46 y estaban a 15 juegos y medio del liderato de la División Este de la Liga Americana. Desde entonces, han logrado un récord de 52-25 y se clasificarán para los playoffs.
Los Red Sox perdieron 5-1 contra los Tampa Bay Rays en el último partido de su serie, por lo que no pudieron asegurar su pase. Sin embargo, aproximadamente una hora después de que terminara el partido, los Houston Astros perdieron 4-2 contra los Atlanta Braves, lo que permitió a los Red Sox asegurar su lugar como comodín.
Poco después de que se confirmara el resultado del partido Astros-Braves, los jugadores, entrenadores y personal de los Red Sox se reunieron cerca del montículo del Tropicana Field para una foto de equipo.
"Realmente no me importa cómo entramos, lo importante es que entramos", dijo el campocorto Trevor Story.
Los Red Sox son el cuarto equipo en clasificar a los playoffs tras haber tenido un récord de 14 o más juegos por debajo de .500 en una temporada en la era de la Serie Mundial (desde 1903). Dos de los tres casos anteriores llegaron a la Serie Mundial, con los Boston Braves ganándola en 1914.
El manager interino Chad Tracy estuvo al mando durante gran parte de la remontada de este año. Desde su nombramiento el 26 de abril tras el despido de Alex Cora, los Red Sox tienen un récord de 74-55.
"Miren, no estábamos en una buena situación", dijo Tracy. "No estábamos jugando bien. Pero esto demuestra que si uno persevera, pueden suceder cosas buenas. No podría estar más orgulloso de este grupo".
El primera base Willson Contreras dijo que mantuvo la fe, incluso cuando las cosas iban mal, y la recompensa fue dulce.
“Es difícil no emocionarse hasta las lágrimas”, dijo Contreras. “Es un gran logro, pero no quiero que este equipo se detenga aquí. Quiero seguir adelante. Hemos demostrado que se puede estar en racha y superar grandes obstáculos”.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Red Sox Get Garrett Crochet News After Clinching Playoff Berth
item.dc:creator: Keith Watkins
item.description: The Boston Red Sox are in the playoffs for the second straight year. item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox are in the playoffs for the second straight year. The clinch became official Sunday when the Braves beat the Astros, guaranteeing Boston a spot in the Wild Card Series starting on September 29.
The roster is not yet complete. Several key arms are still working their way back from injuries, and the next six games at Fenway Park will determine how the pitching staff looks when October arrives.
One of the biggest names on that list took a step forward this week.
Tracy Provides Update on Crochet
Garrett Crochet is closing in on a significant milestone in his comeback. Interim manager Chad Tracy said the plan is for Crochet to throw a live bullpen session against hitters early next week, with Tuesday as the hopeful target.
"Maybe early next week, a potential IBP dependent on how he feels over the next couple days," Tracy said. "Maybe early next week we'll be able to face some hitters. But yeah, tentative."
Crochet's ramp-up has been deliberate at every stage, and the Red Sox are not going to rush the left-hander into a situation he is not ready for.
Facing live hitters would represent the most significant test of Crochet's rehab to this point. He threw 30 pitches over two simulated innings earlier this month, and Tracy said at the time that everything went well. A live session against hitters is the next level up.
What Crochet Would Mean for October
Crochet's potential availability changes the shape of Boston's postseason pitching plans.
The rotation is lining up with Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suarez as the likely starters for the Wild Card Series. Tolle has posted a 2.44 ERA across his last eight starts. Gray has been one of the best starters in the American League this season, carrying a 2.76 ERA.
Adding Crochet would give Tracy another weapon to deploy, albeit from the bullpen.
Tyron Guerrero returned from the injured list Sunday and looked sharp. Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, and Erik Miller round out a late-inning group that has carried the pitching staff down the stretch. Tanner Houck continues to progress through minor league rehab and remains a potential option.
Final Word for the Red Sox
Garrett Crochet is not back yet. The live bullpen is tentative. The timeline is still dependent on how his body responds day to day.
The Red Sox have been patient with this process, and that patience could pay off at exactly the right time.
Tuesday will tell the story. If Crochet gets through a live session clean, Boston's pitching picture for the postseason gets significantly deeper.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Red Sox Get Garrett Crochet News After Clinching Playoff Berth appeared first on HEAVY.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox lost on Sunday, but an Atlanta Braves win over the Houston Astros kicked off champagne showers inside the visitors' clubhouse in Tampa Bay.
The Red Sox's season seemed like a lost cause when Alex Cora got fired and injuries began to pile up. However, with the aid of a 15-game win streak, the Red Sox put themselves in a position to add at the trade deadline and stayed hot. Interim manager Chad Tracy deserves a ton of credit for getting the team back on track.
"I want to express gratitude for everyone in the room," Tracy said to his players before Sunday's celebration, per The Athletic.
"I'm so grateful for you guys, for our staff, for everybody. You stared impossible in the face. The position we were in, you beat it back and said, 'The hell with that, we're going to the playoffs.' And you did."
The Red Sox are going back to the postseason, and in all likelihood, they will face the New York Yankees in the American League Wild Card Series for the second straight year. Just like last year, the Red Sox are headed back to the Bronx, with another American League East team waiting for them if they win.
If the Yankees lose a single game to the Tampa Bay Rays this week, the Rays will clinch the division and pretty much lock in the Yankees as the No. 4 seed and themselves as the No. 1 seed.
Early in the season, it was hard to imagine the Red Sox making the postseason, let alone having a team that looks capable of winning the American League. However, perception means nothing. They need to get the job done in October to make the turnaround worthwhile.
More MLB: Rays Magic Number: When Is The Earliest They Can Clinch AL East?

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Red Sox Roman Anthony Makes Personal Admission After Playoff Clinch
item.dc:creator: Keith Watkins
item.description: The Boston Red Sox lost to the Rays 5-1 on Sunday afternoon at Tropicana Field. The game itself did not matter. What happened later did. The Braves beat the Astros to eliminate Houston from wild card contention, and the Red Sox' postseason berth became official. Players pulled on celebration gear and goggles, posed for a team photo on the field, and returned to a locker room that erupted in champagne and beer. item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox lost to the Rays 5-1 on Sunday afternoon at Tropicana Field. The game itself did not matter. What happened later did.
The Braves beat the Astros to eliminate Houston from wild card contention, and the Red Sox' postseason berth became official. Players pulled on celebration gear and goggles, posed for a team photo on the field, and returned to a locker room that erupted in champagne and beer.
For one player in particular, the moment carried weight that went beyond the standings.
Anthony Gets His Moment
Roman Anthony was on the roster for last year's Wild Card Series against the Yankees. He never got to play in it. An injury kept him off the field for the biggest games of the season, and he could only watch as Boston's run ended in three games.
This year brought another injury. Anthony missed significant time before fighting his way back in August. When the celebration started Sunday, he was in the middle of it.
"I felt this a little bit last year but obviously being injured, I am so happy to be part of it now," Anthony said. "It's just an amazing feeling. Obviously, we wanted to win, but the way it happened, being together watching that game, it was amazing."
The emotion was real. Anthony has dealt with two straight seasons of injury setbacks during the most important stretches. Getting to celebrate with his teammates, healthy and contributing, meant something different for him than it did for most of the room.
Tolle Reflects on How Far The Red Sox Have Come
Payton Tolle was one of the last players to speak with reporters after the celebration had settled. His perspective captured what the locker room was feeling.
"I think it was just relief," Tolle said. "I think there's also just that feeling of like, 'Man, we've come a long way.' You know, we're going to enjoy this and be proud of it. It was a whole lot of fun."
"Obviously, you want to win, but being in is the most important thing," Tolle added.
The big left-hander has been one of the best stories of Boston's season.
Tracy and Contreras Address the Room
Chad Tracy took in the scene from the side of the room before addressing what his team had accomplished.
"At the beginning, we had a long way to go," Tracy said. "It's like, 'How do we get on track and get things moving in the right direction?' When the end of June hit and things started to go, and we started to see things come together, it became very much on our mind. So I'm just really happy for our guys."
"They stared almost an impossible task right in the face, and they refused to take no for an answer," Tracy said. "They're very battle tested, and I'm super, super proud of them."
Willson Contreras called for silence and delivered a message to his teammates.
"We create a good family here, good chemistry throughout the season," Contreras said. "We just needed time, and the time came for us. And what's the most important thing to me is that everybody never stopped working. Everybody was finding a way to make adjustments and play the game the right way."
"This is what we play for," Contreras said. "This is why we're here."
The room answered with a roar, and the celebration picked back up.
Final Word for the Red Sox
The Red Sox were 32-46 on June 24. They are in the playoffs with six games to spare.
The words from Sunday's locker room told the full story. Relief from Tolle. Pride from Tracy and Contreras. Gratitude from Anthony, who finally gets to experience what he missed a year ago.
This team earned every drop of champagne. What comes next starts September 29.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Red Sox Roman Anthony Makes Personal Admission After Playoff Clinch appeared first on HEAVY.

item.content:encoded:
When the Boston Red Sox lost two out of three games to the Colorado Rockies in late June, it felt like rock bottom in the 2026 season. However, what followed shocked many in baseball.
Two lengthy winning streaks later, one that wrapped around the MLB All-Star break, the Red Sox climbed into an American League wild-card spot and never looked back. In fact, they built such a big lead for the second wild-card spot that they have survived a rough September to lock down a playoff berth.
After a 5-1 loss to the Tampa Bay Rays on Sunday afternoon, Boston watched from the clubhouse as the Atlanta Braves completed a sweep of the Houston Astros, which officially clinched a playoff berth for the Red Sox. As the celebration was happening in the clubhouse, first baseman Willson Contreras had a message for his teammates.
Boston Red Sox First Baseman Willson Contreras Drops Honest Quote After Clinching Playoff Berth
Nearly midway through the season, the Red Sox were 32-46, buried in last place in the AL East and the wild-card standings. Then, all of sudden, a switch went off and they made history. According to Ian Browne of MLB.com, Boston is the first team in history to advance to finish above .500 after losing as many as 46 of their first 78 games, but now they have a postseason berth to go with it.
As far as Willson Contreras goes, the All-Star first baseman didn’t mince words about his teammates and believing in his teammates.
“I did believe in my team,” said Contreras, per Browne. “I did believe in everybody who was here. I never had a doubt that this team would get to the position we are in. At one point, I texted the team and I just said, ‘Keep believing in ourselves.’ I said, ‘Believe.’ That was our main word. And that’s what we believed from Day 1.”
Contreras was acquired from the St. Louis Cardinals in a trade last winter. Some thought he might have been traded at the deadline in August. However, Boston’s winning streak around the All-Star break squashed those thoughts. He has been the leader this season for the Red Sox as the season has gone along.
Contreras missed the Rays series over the weekend. He was hit on the hand by a pitch against the Texas Rangers last week. He remains day-to-day as the postseason inches closer.
Boston Red Sox on Collision Course Against New York Yankees
All signs point to an AL wild-card series between Boston and the New York Yankees. Tampa Bay’s magic number to clinch the AL East is two. They have a four-game series against the Yankees in the Bronx, and one win officially clinches it.
It would be the second straight season the two rivals would meet in the wild-card round in New York. Boston has two series remaining at home before the playoffs. They will host the Cleveland Guardians and Chicago Cubs in a pair of three-game series. Interim manager Chad Tracy will likely use that time for rest and lining up his rotation for the postseason. That didn’t seem possible just three months ago.

item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — Craig Breslow stood in a puddle of beer in his stocking feet on Sunday, watching the team he assembled celebrate having clinched its spot in the postseason.
That’s when he realized he still had his phone in his pocket. The Red Sox chief baseball officer carefully picked his way down the hallway to put it out of harm’s way before he got even more soaked.
“Smart move,” Breslow was told.
“It might be too late,” he said, laughing.
You can always get a new phone. But how often can you enjoy the satisfaction of proving that an entire city, if not an entire industry, was wrong?
Breslow made what still remains the most stunning move of this baseball season when he fired Alex Cora and six of his coaches on April 25 after only 27 games.
He was convinced the team had potential it would not realize under Cora and needed a change.
“I believed in the players that we had, and I felt it was really important that we acted definitively and decisively when we did, so that we could create an environment around the players that was supportive, that would allow them to thrive, and they responded,” he said.
“And, while there may have been some people that questioned what this group was capable of, I think they answered.”
Some people? How about most of us?
It was not a straight line to success. The Sox were 13-16 in the first 29 games under interim manager Chad Tracy, and I wrote in late May that it was time to start rebuilding by getting a jump on the trade deadline.
With Roman Anthony and Garrett Crochet on the injured list, it seemed obvious the Sox weren’t going to contend. There were loud “sell the team” chants at Fenway Park.
Tracy’s record was 22-29 three weeks later, and even the players had started to question what was going on at Fenway Park.
“We’re not good. We’re just not a good team right now. That’s just a fact,” righthander Sonny Gray said after a 3-2 loss against the Blue Jays on June 18.
I wrote the next day that it felt inevitable the Sox would be sellers and could well finish the season with 95 losses. Some executives from other teams believed Breslow could only save his job by turning veterans into prospects.
You know what happened next. The Sox went on a season-saving 32-6 run and are now a threat to make a deep run into October. They are the first team in history to lose 44 of their first 75 games and make the playoffs.
“You stared impossible in the face with the position we were in,” Tracy told his players on Sunday.
Breslow did not see any particular series or moment as a turning point.
“I think the turnaround was the result of incremental change, incremental improvement, changes to the way that we practice, the ways that we trained, the way that we delivered information to our players, the way that we supported our players,” he said.
“So I think when you put all those things together, they compound, and then ultimately the performance on the field by way of wins and losses was the last thing to catch up.”
Breslow spent 12 seasons pitching in the majors and grew a beard with the rest of the wild bunch Red Sox of 2013. He appeared in 10 of the 16 playoff games that season and got three huge outs in the eighth inning of Game 6 in the ALCS.
His job now is giving others that opportunity. But in the end, you’re standing in the same puddle of beer with a big smile.
“The obvious difference is I didn’t have a direct impact on the outcomes of games in this role, whereas I did as a player,” Breslow said. “But I think there’s a different sense of gratification when you’re kind of part of this massive effort to identify players and bring them in and help support the coaching staff.
“It’s very different, and in some ways it’s maybe a couple of layers removed. But it’s certainly as satisfying.”
Breslow has earned that satisfaction. The job’s not over, but he had it right about this team.
Peter Abraham can be reached at peter.abraham@globe.com. Follow him on Bluesky at peteabeglobe.bsky.social.

item.title: [The Boston Globe] The moments that marked the Red Sox’ path back to the postseason: ‘Oh, now it’s our turn’ - The Boston Globe
item.dc:creator: Tim Healey
item.description: In their darkest moments, when they were running out of time, all the Red Sox had was faith. Nearly halfway through the season, at the bottom of a bad American League, in a sport dominated by data and measurables, virtually all available evidence led to a consistent conclusion: The 2026 Red Sox were just not good. item.content:encoded:
In their darkest moments, when they were running out of time, all the Red Sox had was faith.
Nearly halfway through the season, at the bottom of a bad American League, in a sport dominated by data and measurables, virtually all available evidence led to a consistent conclusion: The 2026 Red Sox were just not good. They fired the manager a month in. They lost key players to long-term injuries. They showed little life.
And so they were left with mere belief. Belief in themselves, belief that they could salvage it, belief that how could it possibly stay like this forever?
“We all still had faith in each other,” Garrett Whitlock said. “Human beings still do the thing. All the numbers and data would have counted us out and all that kind of stuff. And the players in this clubhouse were like, hey, we can stick with this.”
Or, at least, that’s what they said.
“We wouldn’t have said it if we didn’t believe it,” Caleb Durbin said.
Improbably, incredibly, here they are. They clinched a spot in the postseason Sunday, allowing aspirations of late October in a season that felt over in June.
The moments that marked their ascent were many, an almost endless series of sliding doors and what ifs, minor-turned-monumental plays. Recently, in a series of interviews, some of these Sox reflected on their favorites.
“The fun thing about a season,” Durbin said, “is that there’s a whole lot of moments you can look back on that tell the story.”
The Schlitt Show
The date: June 25
The playoff odds (via FanGraphs): 10.6 percent
The moment: Caleb Durbin homers off Cam Schlittler
Remember how dire it felt on June 25. In the end, it was the start of the Red Sox’ run.
When Boston had last played at Fenway Park, it got swept by the Blue Jays, including a gut-wrenching finale in which the Sox rallied for a late tie only to lose. Emanating from the stands were loud boos and chants of “sell the team,” sentiments and sounds burned into the players’ psyche.
Just before they returned, the Sox dramatically dropped two of three to the Rockies. Durbin partially dislocated his left pinkie finger sliding head-first into first base. On the way back from Colorado, plane problems delayed their Boston arrival to 5 a.m., about 14 hours before the first pitch of a four-game series against the Yankees.
“And,” Isiah Kiner-Falefa said, “Schlittler.”
On the mound that night was righthander Cam Schlittler, the Walpole native and emerging Yankees ace, who ended the Red Sox’ season last year.
The weekend was ripe for misery. And it was the beginning of everything.
“It’s a very discernible line in the sand: the Yankees series at home,” interim manager Chad Tracy said.
The Red Sox were hitting like they had barely slept the night before, so Schlittler cruised into the fifth inning. But when a Yankees fielding error prolonged the frame, the Sox managed to tie it. Up came Durbin with the go-ahead run on base.
Durbin, back in the lineup a day after popping that pinkie back into place, homered to left field — just high enough and just far enough, off the lip of the Green Monster.
The dirt dog Durbin? Against that team, off that pitcher, after that travel and those losses?
“That was the big defining moment of the year,” Kiner-Falefa said. “Turned the whole attitude of the team around.”
The Red Sox trailed for half of an inning the rest of the series, sweeping all four games.
Still in a huge hole, they were 10 games under .500 at 36-46. But for the first time, they had something tangible to build on, not just blind belief.
“Right there is when it changed,” Tracy said. “Oh my God, that was awesome. But like, was that a blip? That’s what people think.”
The comeback
The date: July 12
The playoff odds: 40.5 percent
The moment: Francisco Lindor’s error leads to ninth consecutive win
Against the Angels, against the White Sox, after an overnight flight delay trying to escape Chicago, despite rolling up to Citi Field just two hours before scheduled first pitch, the Red Sox won eight consecutive games to take them into mid-July.
It was a significant accomplishment, especially considering it took them three months to win more than three in a row.
Unfortunately for the Sox, that is where the win streak was going to end. The Red Sox had one hit heading into the ninth inning against the Mets.
With a runner on first base and one out in the ninth, Romy Gonzalez hit a hard ground ball right at Mets shortstop Francisco Lindor. It was a ready-made double play. The game was over, and so was the streak … until it wasn’t.
“The guy has a Platinum Glove,” Whitlock said.
“Oh, now it’s our turn,” Connor Wong said. “Everything was going wrong for us, and then the one thing kind of went right for us.”
“He makes that play, we lose. And we somehow win that game,” Durbin said. “That was probably our biggest game of the year. Not because of who we beat, but because of the way we won that game.”
Lindor failed to turn the double play. He failed to get even one out. The ball ricocheted off his chest, everybody was safe, Devin Williams lost the strike zone, Durbin walked to load the bases, Andruw Monasterio walked to force in a run, and Jarren Duran singled to bring in the tying run. The Red Sox won in 10 innings.
Opportunity knocked, and the Red Sox kicked the door down. It was the difference between an 8-1 road trip, a solid week-plus with a total dud of a loss heading into the break ... and a stunning 9-0, feeling great going into four days off, with a chance to bring the momentum home.
If the win streak had ended at eight, would the Sox have won the next six after the break? Would they have grabbed such a strong hold on a wild-card spot? Would they have known what it felt like to stage late comebacks — the theme of their summer surge?
“Even that ninth inning, though, we needed five people to do the job, and they all did. That was the first time that happened,” Durbin said. “That kind of sparked the feeling of OK, we’re a team that if we need to get something going, we can.”
Tracy said: “Two weeks ago, we were pretty entrenched as the worst team in the American League. Now, we were holding a spot or were really close. I felt like that was — for the whole group — all right, we have turned this around and we have a legitimate chance now.”
The homecoming
The date: July 17-22
The playoff odds: 50.3 percent to 61 percent
The moment: “There’s so many,” Tracy said, leading to six more wins
Upon returning from the All-Star break, the Red Sox reached the chaotic, fever dream, how-is-this-possible portion of their turnaround.
Every game — four more wins against the Rays, then two against the Orioles — seemed to bring out a more electric version of Fenway Park than the one before.
For the Red Sox, that was the most gratifying. Their lowest low, several players said, wasn’t getting dumped in Denver. It was struggling in Boston and hearing it from the home crowds. They went 17-27 at Fenway in the first half.
How to pick just one moment?
For win No. 10, the first game back from the break, the Red Sox beat Tampa Bay, 10-0. It was resounding.
“That was like an important statement game for us,” Greg Weissert said.
For No. 11, the second game of a doubleheader, the Rays scored two runs in the top of the first and the Red Sox came right back with three in the bottom half. That got them back to .500 and into a tie for a playoff spot.
“Relentlessness,” Trevor Story said.
For No. 12, Wilyer Abreu’s fourth homer in two games was a go-ahead shot off Garrett Cleavinger, capping a four-run rally in the seventh for the Sox’ first lead of the day.
“When you win that many games in a row, there’s usually three or four of them that you’re probably not supposed to win,” Tracy said.
For No. 13, Sonny Gray tossed a quality start in an actual low-stress afternoon.
“It’s hard to remember everything,” Wong said.
For No. 14, Durbin went deep again, in the eighth against Tyler Wells to break a tie. Fourth-string shortstop Tsung-Che Cheng recorded the final out with a leaping catch of a line drive to save two runs.
Even for the Red Sox, the believers, it strained belief.
“It comes off the bat and you’re like, ‘Oh no.’ And [Cheng] out of nowhere snares it,” Tracy said. “Everybody’s fired up in the coach’s room and you fist bump. You shake your head like: ‘Holy [expletive]. We did it again.’ There were plenty of those for sure behind the scenes.”
For No. 15, they scored four runs in the first inning, leaving no doubt and matching the franchise record win streak set in 1946.
Later that day, July 22, the Red Sox lost the second game of a doubleheader. The streak was over — for real this time. The season is not.
That 15-0 run was part of 27-3 and 32-5 stretches, some of the wildest in franchise history.
“It was maybe the beginning of August, I think, when someone was like, ‘Hey, you realize we’re six games up in the wild card, right?’” said Whitlock, not a standings tracker. “Wait, what?”
“That’s a testament to the people that we have,” Durbin said. “As a player, we have talent. We have a lot of talent to do the job. But [after] the start we had, it takes the person to continue to push forward and come out of it the way we did.”
“I never doubted it, our ability to come together at some point and turn this thing around,” interim bench coach José David Flores said. “To be honest with you, it was kind of shocking the way we did it.”
Tim Healey can be reached at timothy.healey@globe.com. Follow him @timbhealey.

item.title: [firebrandal.com] The Red Sox Clinched a Playoff Spot by Losing. Chad Tracy’s Case for Permanent Manager Just Wrote Itself.
item.description: The Red Sox clinched a playoff spot on Sept. 20 by losing, 5-1, to the Rays in Tampa. item.content:encoded:
The Red Sox clinched a playoff spot on Sept. 20 by losing, 5-1, to the Rays in Tampa. Their ticket to October got punched about an hour later anyway, when the Braves beat the Astros three time zones away.
Nobody in that clubhouse watched themselves get in.
Rewind five months. Alex Cora got fired on a Saturday morning in April, with Boston sitting at 10-17. By June 24, the Red Sox were 15.5 games back in the AL East, with playoff odds cratered to 8.4%. That’s about as buried as a team gets in June.
Chad Tracy took over that wreckage on April 26 with zero big-league managing experience. Since then, Boston has gone 74-55 under him, a .573 winning percentage that would put most division leaders to shame. From July 27 through the end of the regular season, they played at a .609 clip, 28-18 down the stretch. They’re the first team in MLB history to lose 46 of their first 78 games and still finish above .500. Not one hot month. The roster Tracy built out of the wreckage. It’s the exact arc Central Maine tracked: a dreadful start, then a red-hot summer.
That’s the case for the permanent job. Not vibes. Receipts.
Beat writer Tyler Milliken called it one of the most improbable summers in baseball history, and he’s not exaggerating. A team that lost its manager in a firing nobody saw coming turned around and finished with the second-best road winning percentage in the American League.
This tweet nails how Saturday actually felt in that clubhouse:
Anticlimactic clinch, but to be on pace to go down as one of the worst Red Sox teams ever, then lock in, ignore the noise, and go on a generational run that led to postseason baseball…that’s both incredibly impressive and very much worth celebrating. See you in the Bronx. pic.twitter.com/ETJ7MEnHsj
— Jared Carrabis (@Jared_Carrabis) September 20, 2026
Anticlimactic, sure. You don’t draw up “clinch while getting shut down by Tampa’s bullpen” as the moment. But in a 162-game season, sometimes the celebration starts because of somebody else’s scoreboard, and you find out standing at your locker.
Plenty of the beat corps agrees on where the conversation goes next.
The Red Sox were 10-17 when Chad Tracy took over. A first time manager with no big league experience. He walked into a clubhouse of players that just lost a well-liked and respected manager.
Things weren’t fixed instantly, but they didn’t need to be. They got there in the end,… pic.twitter.com/etkqeb1PUe
— Gordo (@BOSSportsGordo) September 20, 2026
Gordo’s calling for a Manager of the Year case, and he’s not wrong to. Tracy walked into a room that had just lost a manager players actually liked, and he didn’t need some big culture-reset speech to fix it. He kept writing lineups, put Roman Anthony in the leadoff spot down the stretch, and let a talented roster figure itself out.
None of this happened by accident. firebrandal.com made the case for Tracy back in July, and it’s only gotten stronger since, even with the rotation health questions that never fully disappeared. Mickey Gasper’s hot stretch since his recall was part of the same story, a roster that kept finding useful players in June, July and August while the rest of the sport had already buried them.
Mike Mutnansky put it best: when the Red Sox fired Cora on a Saturday morning in April, nobody thought this team would sniff October. Now they’re one of 12 clubs still alive for a title. They’ll open as the No. 2 wild card, likely on the road against the Yankees, so nobody’s handing them anything in the Bronx.
Doesn’t matter how they get in. Tracy got them here. Give the guy the job.

item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. (AP) — As the Boston Red Sox celebrated an improbable postseason berth at Tropicana Field, with Champagne and beer flowing all around, the clubhouse soundtrack seemed appropriate.
“Stayin’ Alive.’’
“I think that pretty much says it all,’’ left fielder Roman Anthony said Sunday. “We pretty much stayed alive when nobody else thought we could. Now here we are.’’
The Red Sox were 32-46 and 15 1/2 games back in the AL East race on June 24. They have since gone 52-25 and will be in the playoffs.
The Red Sox lost 5-1 to the Tampa Bay Rays in their series finale, so couldn’t take care of things themselves. But about an hour after the game finished, the Houston Astros lost 4-2 to the Atlanta Braves, allowing the Red Sox to secure a wild-card spot.
Shortly after the Astros-Braves result went final, Red Sox players, coaches and staff members gathered near the Tropicana Field mound for a team photograph.
“I really don’t care how we got in, as long as we got in,’’ shortstop Trevor Story said.
Interim manager Chad Tracy was in place for much of the turnaround. Since being appointed on April 26 following the dismissal of Alex Cora, the Red Sox have gone 74-55.
“Look, we were not in a good spot,’’ Tracy said. “We were not playing good ball. But it shows you that if you stick to it, good things can happen. I couldn’t be more proud of this group.’’
First baseman Willson Contreras said he kept the faith, even when things trended downward, and the reward was sweet.
“It’s hard not to have some tears over this,’’ Contreras said. “It’s a great accomplishment, but I don’t want this team to stop here. I want to keep going. We have proven that you can get hot and overcome a lot of big odds.’’
___

item.title: [Boston Herald] ‘Battle-tested’ Red Sox eager to prove they’re ready for more in postseason
item.dc:creator: Gabrielle Starr
item.description: As the clinch celebration played out in the Tropicana Field visitors’ clubhouse early Sunday evening, the incompleteness of the moment was not lost on the revelling Boston Red Sox. The achievement was dampened, and not only in the literal sense by the champagne with which the Red Sox doused each other and the room. That they had lost the series to the Tampa Bay Rays barely an hour earlier and instead had their ticket punched via an Atlanta Braves victory over the Houston Astros. The Red Sox are
item.content:encoded:
As the clinch celebration played out in the Tropicana Field visitors’ clubhouse early Sunday evening, the incompleteness of the moment was not lost on the revelling Boston Red Sox.
The achievement was dampened, and not only in the literal sense by the champagne with which the Red Sox doused each other and the room. That they had lost the series to the Tampa Bay Rays barely an hour earlier and instead had their ticket punched via an Atlanta Braves victory over the Houston Astros. The Red Sox are 9-9 this month, struggling offensively, without on several injured stars, and are their first postseason round will almost certainly be a rematch of last year’s best-of-three Wild Card series at Yankee Stadium, where they fell to their rivals 2-1.
In other words, there is much work to be done. The Red Sox know it, and they are eager to prove they did not come this far to only go this far.
“This has been a turbulent season,” Red Sox chief baseball officer Craig Breslow told reporters. “This is certainly an accomplishment, but it’s not the primary objective here.”
But neither the recent struggles nor the battles ahead should diminish the magnitude of the overall achievement of getting to this point.
The Red Sox lost American League Cy Young runner-up Garrett Crochet to a shoulder injury in mid-April, and he has yet to return.
They fired manager Alex Cora and several coaches in the middle of a late-April road series in Baltimore, and promoted Triple-A Worcester skipper Chad Tracy and several others from their minor league coaching ranks.
Injuries sidelined star outfielder Roman Anthony and veteran shortstop Trevor Story from early May until the very end of August.
The Red Sox owned their worst home record to start a season since 1932, and were 15 1/2 games out of first in the American League East in June.
On June 24, they fell to 14 games under .500. On Sunday, they became the fourth team in Major League Baseball history to go from as many as 14 games under .500 to the postseason in the same season.
“We needed time, and the time came for us,” veteran first baseman Willson Contreras told his teammates in the clubhouse. “I’m very proud of you all.”
“It’s 162 for a reason,” echoed third baseman Caleb Durbin.
“Obviously, getting where we want to go, but ultimately, what we had to overcome to get here makes it all the more sweet,” Tracy said. “We had a long way to go, and they never stopped, and they didn’t take no for an answer.”
This year looked lost, and the Red Sox managed to save it. They maintained an unshakeable belief in themselves, and it has already taken them to places most of the baseball world doubted it could go.
“Belief, belief, belief,” Contreras told reporters. “That was my main word, and that’s what I did from Day 1.”
The Red Sox are not a perfect team. But they certainly have the grit and gumption to go further than expected, as evidenced by the fact that they have already done so by reaching this point.
“We know how it felt when we left New York at the end of the year,” Story said. “You know how it made me feel. So that stayed with me.”
“They came together, and they found a way to get it done, and they had a long way to go to do it,” Tracy said. “They’re very battle-tested, and I’m super, super proud of them.”
“We don’t care where we play,” Tracy said. “You go back to July, and most people didn’t think we’d even be standing here. So it doesn’t matter where we play.”
“We’re in,” Tracy continued. “You got a ticket to the dance, and now you got to go take care of it there.”
“We’re in, baby,” Story said. “Let’s go.”
“Now, this is the moment,” right-fielder Wilyer Abreu said, “that we (were) waiting for.”

item.content:encoded:
April 23: Payton Tolle didn’t make the team out of camp, but was recalled and proved he was ready to stay, allowing one run while striking out 11 against the Yankees
April 25-26: Hours after a 17-1 win in Baltimore, Alex Cora was fired due to his team’s slow start and Chad Tracy, named interim manager, led the team to a 5-3 win in debut the next day
June 25: Airplane issues forced the team to land in Boston at 5 a.m. with a game against the Yankees that night. Caleb Durbin’s clutch homer started the team’s dramatic surge back from 14 games under .500
July 12: The Sox rallied back in the ninth to cap their first 9-0 road trip since 1977. A nine-game winning streak was a nice way to go into All-Star break
July 18: A late-game, go-ahead homer by Wilyer Abreu electrified Fenway and led the Sox to a dramatic comeback win over the Rays to stretch the winning streak to 12 games
July 22: WIth a 6-3 win in Game 1 of a doubleheader against Baltimore, the Red Sox tie a franchise record set by the ‘46 team with a 15-game winning streak
Aug. 2: Hot as hot gets already, the Red Sox opened even more eyes when they completed a three-game sweep of the Dodgers with an 8-4 win on Sunday Night Baseball
Aug. 6: The game that defined a 27-3 stretch that ended two days later, the Red Sox scored in the ninth, 10th, 11th and 12th to finally beat the White Sox, 12-11
Sept. 13: Payton Tolle overpowered the Royals with an immaculate first inning, going almost exclusively with fastballs. And the grin on his face before the ninth pitch said it all

item.title: [The Boston Globe] Red Sox appear to be getting rotation in line for Wild Card Series - The Boston Globe
item.dc:creator: Peter Abraham
item.description: ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — The Red Sox will start Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suarez in the series against the Guardians that starts Tuesday at Fenway Park. That would conceivably line them up for the Wild Card Series that starts on Sept. 29 with six days rest each. “Don’t read into that yet,” interim manager Chad Tracy said Sunday before a 5-1 loss against the Rays. “We can line that up still however we want.” True. item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — The Red Sox will start Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suarez in the series against the Guardians that starts Tuesday at Fenway Park.
That would conceivably line them up for the Wild Card Series that starts on Sept. 29 with six days rest each.
“Don’t read into that yet,” interim manager Chad Tracy said Sunday before a 5-1 loss against the Rays. “We can line that up still however we want.”
True. But Tolle has a 2.44 ERA in his last eight starts. He also has faced the Yankees twice this season and allowed one run on four hits over 13 innings with three walks and 18 strikeouts.
Gray allowed three runs on nine hits over 13⅔ innings in two starts against the Yankees. He struck out 12 and walked three.
Guerrero returns
Righthanded reliever Tyron Guerrero returned from a 19-day stint on the injured list with shoulder inflammation. Righthanded reliever Wyatt Olds was optioned to Triple-A Worcester.
Guerrero pitched a perfect eighth inning, striking out two.
“Felt good to be out there,” Guerrero said. “If I get a few more games I’ll be fine [for the postseason].”
Guerrero, 35, was called up in May for his first major league stint since 2019. He emerged as a reliable late-inning option, posting a 3.18 ERA over 39 games.
“He’s obviously a very important piece to this puzzle in our bullpen,” Tracy said.
Olds deserved a better fate. The 27-year-old has a 1.20 ERA and 1.20 WHIP in 13 games since making his major league debut on Aug. 17.
“Very tough. He’s thrown the ball great. He’s got big stuff,” Tracy said. “We had to make a roster decision.”
Contreras doing better
Willson Contreras took some swings in the batting cage to test his bruised right hand and came through fine. He said he hopes to be able to do more on Tuesday. “Step in the right direction,” Tracy said … There was no update on Garrett Crochet, who has yet to face hitters. That could come in the next few days … Tanner Houck had a 3.38 ERA over eight innings in four minor league games. Tracy suggested he would face hitters in a simulated game early this week. “Figuring out the next steps at home — and want to figure that out — but no plans for the next outing,” Tracy said. Could Houck be activated? “It’s possible,” Tracy said. “At this point, it’s going to depend very much on where’s the roster at, what are the needs, and then go from there.”… Rays shortstop Taylor Walls showed his baseball acumen in the first inning. With Roman Anthony on first and one out, he allowed Adley Rutschman’s popup to drop. Walls picked up the ball and flipped to second to get the force on Anthony. That left the Sox with a slower runner on first. It ultimately didn’t matter as Trevor Story struck out … Worcester, as Double-A Portland also did last weekend, had its final game rained out. The WooSox finished 76-67. Kutter Crawford was at Polar Park, and the plan was to have him start what would have been a bullpen game. Crawford has not appeared in a major league game since Sept. 28, 2024. He missed the 2025 season because of an injured right knee. He injured his right wrist in August of that season doing yard work at his home in Florida. Crawford pitched three innings in a rehab game for Worcester on April 11 but had a setback and wasn’t cleared for a game until Sunday. “He got to a point where he wanted to go out there and throw one,” Tracy said.
Peter Abraham can be reached at peter.abraham@globe.com. Follow him on Bluesky at peteabeglobe.bsky.social.

item.title: [mlb.com] Red Sox clinch postseason spot that once seemed improbable
item.dc:creator: Ian Browne
item.description: Not long after, the Braves beat the Astros, officially punching Boston’s ticket to the playoffs as one of the AL’s three Wild Card teams. It’s a postseason appearance few saw coming when the Sox started the season 32-46. Not only are they the first team in history to advance to finish above .500 after losing as many as 32 of their first 78 games, but now they have a postseason berth to go with it. Currently sitting as the No. 5 seed, the Red Sox are most likely to open their playoff run with a b
item.content:encoded:
Not long after, the Braves beat the Astros, officially punching Boston’s ticket to the playoffs as one of the AL’s three Wild Card teams.
It’s a postseason appearance few saw coming when the Sox started the season 32-46. Not only are they the first team in history to advance to finish above .500 after losing as many as 32 of their first 78 games, but now they have a postseason berth to go with it.
Currently sitting as the No. 5 seed, the Red Sox are most likely to open their playoff run with a best-of-three Wild Card Series at Yankee Stadium, starting on Sept. 29. It would be a rematch from last year, when the Yankees won in three games after the Sox had taken the opener behind a brilliant performance by Garrett Crochet.
In a bit of baseball poetry, a home run swing from Mike Yastrzemski, the grandson of Red Sox legend Carl, gave the Braves a lead they would not relinquish and helped officially push Boston into the postseason.
“When you work as hard as we have worked, it was almost July [before we got going], and to fight as hard as we did, to put ourselves in the position we did, I don’t think you care much how it gets done,” said interim manager Chad Tracy, who took over after the dismissal of Alex Cora on April 25. “You just want to see your ticket get punched.”
For several weeks, the Red Sox never stopped punching. The road back to contention started with a four-game sweep of the Yankees at Fenway from June 25-28.
It continued on July 3, when the Sox began what would become a winning streak of 15 games, tying the franchise record set by the 1946 pennant winners of Ted Williams, Bobby Doerr, Dom DiMaggio and Johnny Pesky.
And even after that streak was snapped, the Sox shortly thereafter ripped off another nine-game winning streak, giving them the best 30-game stretch in team history. Including the Yankees sweep that started it all, Boston was 32-5 from June 25-Aug. 7.
Just when the rabid fanbase known as Red Sox Nation thought they were losing their summer, Boston pulled off one of the most remarkable turnarounds in history, and got the first reward for that on Sunday.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Red Sox's Curtis Mead Quietly Inching Closer to Playoff Return
item.dc:creator: Jackson Roberts; Unknown
item.description: Curtis Mead has arguably been the most frustrating non-factor for the Boston Red Sox this season, because he never got his chance to make an impact. In his very first game after being acquired in a trade with the Washington Nationals, Mead fractured his left wrist on a high-and-tight fastball against the Athletics. item.content:encoded:
Curtis Mead has arguably been the most frustrating non-factor for the Boston Red Sox this season, because he never got his chance to make an impact.
In his very first game after being acquired in a trade with the Washington Nationals, Mead fractured his left wrist on a high-and-tight fastball against the Athletics. He quickly found himself in an uphill battle to return to action before the Red Sox's season ended at some point in the playoffs, but he's started making some progress.
According to a Saturday MLB.com injury update, Mead has begun hitting off a tee, which slipped under the radar amid a slough of injury news about Willson Contreras, Garrett Crochet, and others. Good news, to be sure, but far from a guarantee he makes it back for a game this year.
Mead's return not imminent, but progress made
Interim manager Chad Tracy said earlier this week that the tee work was beginning on Wednesday, per Boston Sports Gordo on X. That means we're a few days late to this particular story, so apologies to our readers — but not much slips by us, so it was a particularly quiet announcement.
Mead's breakout season (.851 OPS, 17 home runs in 88 games) was halted at the worst possible time. The Red Sox were looking to add an impact bat at the trade deadline, and Mead's absence has been nearly as awkward as Adley Rutschman's struggles.
Would Mead be the slam-dunk starter at second base even if he came back fully healthy this week? That's another real issue to consider, since Nick Sogard has done a nice job over the last month-plus. Perhaps Mead would at least be in the lineup against left-handed pitchers over the struggling Andruw Monasterio and/or Isiah Kiner-Falefa.
The Red Sox will have interesting decisions to make at the fringes of the roster for the first couple of rounds of the playoffs, no matter what. If Mead re-enters the picture, we could see someone who feels like they earned their spot get the axe, but that's the cost of doing business in a year when the American League could be up for grabs.
Jackson Roberts is a former Division III All-Region DH who now writes and talks about sports for a living. A Bay Area native and a graduate of Swarthmore College and the Newhouse School at Syracuse University, Jackson makes his home in North Jersey. He grew up rooting for the Red Sox, Patriots, and Warriors, and he recently added the Devils to his sports fandom mosaic. item.title: [Yardbarker] Boston Red Sox Announce Jarren Duran Move on Sunday
item.dc:creator: Simeon Kotto
item.description: The Boston Red Sox and Tampa Bay Rays head into Sunday’s series finale at Fenway Park with the three-game set knotted at one win apiece after Saturday’s 2-1 Rays victory. Left-hander Patrick Sandoval takes the mound for Boston against Tampa Bay right-hander Griffin Jax, a matchup that carries extra weight with the regular season winding down and playoff positioning still in flux. item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox and Tampa Bay Rays head into Sunday’s series finale at Fenway Park with the three-game set knotted at one win apiece after Saturday’s 2-1 Rays victory.
Left-hander Patrick Sandoval takes the mound for Boston against Tampa Bay right-hander Griffin Jax, a matchup that carries extra weight with the regular season winding down and playoff positioning still in flux.
Interim manager Chad Tracy has kept the bulk of his starting nine intact, but he has made a modest yet noticeable adjustment involving outfielder Jarren Duran, via Underdog MLB.
After sitting out the series opener and batting eighth on Saturday, Duran will slide up one spot into the seventh hole. He will hit in front of Isaiah Kiner-Falefa and Nate Eaton while remaining in center field, the position he has occupied since injuries to Ceddanne Rafaela and Eli White opened the job.
The rest of the order features Roman Anthony in left, Mickey Gasper at designated hitter, Adley Rutschman behind the plate, Trevor Story at shortstop, Nick Sogard at first, and Cooper Durbin at third.
The move comes during a difficult individual season for Duran. Entering Sunday he is hitting .206 in 144 games, with 65 runs, 110 hits, 20 home runs and 69 RBIs. His slugging percentage sits at .364 and his OPS at .626.
Speculation about a possible trade lingered for weeks before the August 4 deadline, yet Duran remained in a Red Sox uniform and has continued to receive regular playing time as the club pushes toward October.
Boston sits at 84-71 with seven games left and occupies what currently looks like the second American League Wild Card spot. Should the standings hold, the Red Sox would open the postseason on the road in a best-of-three Wild Card series against the New York Yankees.
Every remaining game, including Sunday’s finale against a familiar division rival, therefore carries playoff implications.
Tracy’s decision to bump Duran up in the order is a small tactical shift rather than a wholesale overhaul, but it signals a willingness to tinker as the club tries to generate more consistent offense down the stretch.
Whether the extra spot in the lineup produces results remains to be seen.
Duran’s season-long struggles have been well documented, yet he has shown flashes of the power and speed that once made him a fixture in the middle of Boston’s order.
A productive afternoon against Jax and the Rays would give the Red Sox a series victory and a bit of momentum heading into the final week.
With the calendar now late September and the postseason picture still taking shape, even incremental lineup changes can feel significant.

item.description: X-rays on Willson Contreras’s hand were negative, but don’t take that to mean everything is sunshine, rainbows, and Swiss cheese. Contreras’s hand still shows visible bruising and he cannot grip a bat. He hopes to take some initial swings today. “Hand’s still really sore. Woke up feeling a little better,” he said. “I can squeeze a little better than [Friday], but it’s going to take a few days… I’m going to do everything in my power to get back on the field before the playoffs.” (Peter Abraham, B
item.content:encoded:
X-rays on Willson Contreras’s hand were negative, but don’t take that to mean everything is sunshine, rainbows, and Swiss cheese. Contreras’s hand still shows visible bruising and he cannot grip a bat. He hopes to take some initial swings today. “Hand’s still really sore. Woke up feeling a little better,” he said. “I can squeeze a little better than [Friday], but it’s going to take a few days… I’m going to do everything in my power to get back on the field before the playoffs.” (Peter Abraham, Boston Globe)
Contreras won’t be on the field for a few days, but he’s still in the clubhouse. That wasn’t the case for Roman Anthony, who was sent to Fort Myers during his rehab, where he worked hard to stay connected to the team. “Just staying in touch with them and seeing what they were doing, I think it’s just the relationship we have,” Anthony said. “As a group, we’re all so close. For me, obviously, Fort Myers wasn’t the most ideal situation, but that’s part of it, and I had a good group of guys down there, and up here.” (Tara Sullivan, Boston Globe)
But now that he’s back in the big leagues, it’s time for Roman to start producing more consistently. He did some extra hitting work before this series against the Rays began and the team is confident he’s going to really get going. “I mean, you see what he can do. It’s the game of baseball, there’s ebbs and flows,” said Chad Tracy. “He came off the rehab, and for like five games, he looked fantastic. Then he went through some stuff, and now he’s starting to look good again. When he’s going well, you see the impact he can make.” (Jen McCaffrey, The Athletic)
Garrett Crochet isn’t with the time right now, but he’s still trying to get back with them. He donned his full uniform yesterday at Polar Park in Worcester and threw 20 pitches, topping out at 92 MPH. The Sox hope he can throw to live hitters at Fenway later this week. Tanner Houck, meanwhile, threw 3.1 innings for the WooSox in his final rehab appearance. (Ian Browne, MLB.com)
A healthy Crochet and Houck could make for a formidable bridge to the back of the bullpen. And after yesterday’s outstanding start, Brayan Bello has also shown that he’s ready to be a part of the postseason action. “For me, it’s just showing the team that I’m ready for these kind of games,” Bello said. “Also, them giving me the opportunity to pitch today was a good step for that. And I thank them for giving me the confidence and the opportunity to start again.” (Rob Bradford, WEEI)
If Crochet and Houck do make it back to the roster, hopefully their transition will be as seamless as Trevor Story’s has been. “The point of getting the surgery was to come back and try to be the player that I know I can be,” he said, “and it’s starting to show.” (Hayden Bird, Boston.com)

The Boston Red Sox lost 2-1 against the Tampa Bay Rays on Saturday to even the series at one game apiece entering Sunday’s finale.
On the mound for the Red Sox will be left-hander Patrick Sandoval, while the Rays will send out righty Griffin Jax.
Ahead of the matchup, Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy didn’t make many major changes to his starting lineup but made a few tweaks, including one involving outfielder Jarren Duran.
Red Sox Announce Duran Change
After not playing in the series opener and batting eighth on Saturday, Tracy is moving Duran up one spot in the batting order to the seven-hole, where he’ll hit in front of Isaiah Kiner-Falefa and Nate Eaton.
Duran will once again start in center field, where he’s continued to play since injuries to Ceddanne Rafaela and Eli White.
Here’s the full Red Sox lineup:
Via Underdog MLB: “Red Sox 9/20 R. Anthony LF M. Gasper DH A. Rutschman C T. Story SS N. Sogard 1B C. Durbin 3B J. Duran CF I. Kiner-Falefa 2B N. Eaton RF P. Sandoval SP.”

M. Gasper DH
A. Rutschman C
T. Story SS
N. Sogard 1B
C. Durbin 3B
J. Duran CF
I. Kiner-Falefa 2B
N. Eaton RF
P. Sandoval SP
— Underdog MLB (@UnderdogMLB) September 20, 2026
Duran’s 2026 Season
It’s been a challenging year for Duran. And he didn’t even know if he’d remain in a Red Sox uniform beyond the Aug. 4 trade deadline after his name surfaced as a possible trade candidate for weeks.
Yet, he’s still in Boston, and entering Sunday afternoon, he’s hitting .206 across 144 games with 65 runs, 110 hits, 20 home runs, and 69 RBIs while slugging .364 with a .626 OPS.
Looking at the Red Sox
Boston holds an 84-71 overall record with just seven games remaining in the regular season. They’re currently in position to likely be the second Wild Card team in the AL.
If the current standings hold, the Red Sox would travel to the Bronx for a best-of-three series against the New York Yankees in Round 1.

item.title: [Audacy] Brayan Bello has suddenly become a potential key postseason piece
item.dc:creator: Rob Bradford
item.description: ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. - There was no celebration, but there was a revelation. item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. - There was no celebration, but there was a revelation.
The Red Sox couldn't close the deal in securing a postseason berth, succumbing to a Rays 2-1 walk-off win at Tropicana Field on Saturday. But an interesting development emerged along the way. Brayan Bello is suddenly a potential huge part of the postseason solution.
The almost out-of-nowhere conversation about Bello's importance was given an enormous boost by one of the pitcher's best outings of his career. Not only did Bello hold the Rays to just one run over eight innings, but he also struck out 11 and walked no one.
Why was this even more impressive than simply the end-of-day box score? Because Bello managed all those punchouts, along with 17 whiffs, against a Rays team that has struck out fewer times than any club in baseball. No starting pitcher had managed double-digit strikeouts against Tampa Bay, with Toronto's Dylan Cease coming the closest with nine.
Bello matches his career high with 11 strikeouts! pic.twitter.com/NA2a2pDcAy
— Red Sox (@RedSox) September 19, 2026
The dominance was just what the doctor ordered for Bello and the Red Sox, even if starting a postseason game isn't in the righty's immediate future.
While there has been no announcement, it appears the Red Sox are lining up their wild-card rotation with Payton Tolle to pitch Game 1 against the Yankees, followed by Sonny Gray and then Ranger Suarez if Game 3 is needed in the best-of-three series. But that doesn't mean Bello can't have an impact on outcomes from late September into October.
Bello's fastball routinely sat at 97 mph, almost two mph above his season-average velocity. It was a fastball that got nine whiffs, with the Rays coming away with just four hard-hit balls all day.
"That was exceptional," Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy said. "By far and away, his best outing of the year, as good as I've seen him, so, I don't know what else to say, he was awesome. Really awesome."
Bello's appearance allowed for thoughts on what might be in store for his effectiveness out of the bullpen in high-leverage situations come Sept. 29. It has been well-documented what he can do as a reliever, posting a 1.98 ERA in 15 games out of the bullpen this season. But now we're not just talking about bulk roles or giving the Red Sox some length.
This version of Bello can absolutely be a late-inning, high-leverage weapon.
For instance, while we aren't sure of Aaron Judge's health heading into the postseason, if the Yankees' slugger does play, this might not be a bad reminder to put in your statistical back pocket: Judge is just 2-for-21 with eight strikeouts against Bello.
While some naysayers might point to the less-than-inspiring appearances Bello has turned in at Yankee Stadium as of late, including maybe his worst relief outing of the season at the end of August when he allowed four runs over 4 1/3 innings, or the 2 1/3-inning start in Game 2 of last season's wild card round. But before those two, the pitcher had been absolutely nails in the Bronx, totaling a 1.44 ERA in five starts.
Assuming their health is OK, the Red Sox will have Aroldis Chapman and Garrett Whitlock at the ready to help close out games. But with a week to go in the regular season, there is some uncertainty regarding the late-inning options. Saturday, Bello sure seemed like he was ready to help with that.
“For me, it's just showing the team that I'm ready for these kind of games,” Bello said. “Also, them giving me the opportunity to pitch today was a good step for that. And I thank them for giving me the confidence and the opportunity to start again.”

item.title: [Boston Sports Journal] Red Sox denied playoff clincher as Rays walk off Garrett Whitlock, 2-1

item.content:encoded:
The Red Sox were one swing away from punching their ticket to October. Instead, they’ll have to wait at least one more day.
Richie Palacios dumped a walk-off single into right field off Garrett Whitlock in the bottom of the ninth inning Saturday, lifting the Rays to a 2-1 win over the Red Sox at Tropicana Field and preventing Boston from clinching a postseason berth.
The Rays pieced together three singles against Whitlock in the ninth after the teams entered the inning tied at 1. Boston had opportunities to push across the go-ahead run in the later innings but couldn’t capitalize, wasting an outstanding performance from Brayan Bello.
Bello turned in arguably his most impressive start of the season, allowing just one run on five hits over eight innings while striking out 11 to match his career high.
“That was exceptional,” Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters following the game. “By far and away his best outing of the year. As good as I’ve seen him. So, I don’t know what else to say. He was awesome, really awesome.”
It marked the second consecutive scoreless start for Bello, but Saturday’s outing was far more dominant than his previous one. Against the Angels at Fenway Park, Bello navigated almost constant traffic, allowing four hits and two walks while needing 103 pitches to complete five innings.
Bello needed just 55 pitches to complete his first five innings and kept the Rays off balance throughout the afternoon. He allowed only one run, a Jonathan Aranda’s solo homer leading off the fourth, and gave the Red Sox exactly what they needed with two of their most important late-inning relievers unavailable.
“I just felt confident attacking the zone,” Bello told reporters via team translator.
Bello isn’t expected to start in the Wild Card Series, but his recent performances have provided a reminder of the value he could offer in October. After an uneven season that eventually resulted in a move to the bullpen, he has reestablished himself as someone Tracy can trust in a meaningful spot.
Aranda’s homer was notable for another reason. It was the first home run Bello had allowed since July 12, the final game before the All-Star break, snapping a homerless stretch of roughly 42 innings. Much of that work came in relief, often following an opener, but going more than two months without surrendering a homer remains an impressive run.
“For me, it’s just showing the team that I’m ready for this kind of games,” Bello added.
For the second straight game, Roman Anthony provided Boston with some early offense.
After leading off Friday’s victory with a 438-foot homer, Anthony delivered again in the third inning Saturday. Caleb Durbin opened the inning with a double before Anthony sliced an RBI double into left-center to give Boston a 1-0 lead.
The productive at-bats are an encouraging development for Anthony after his recent slump. With the postseason just over a week away, the rookie is beginning to show signs of heating up at the right time.
Durbin may be coming out of a slump of his own.
After collecting two hits in Friday’s series opener, Durbin added two more Saturday, both sharply hit doubles. His offensive turnaround earlier this season coincided with Boston’s surge up the standings, and another hot stretch would add length to the lineup and provide another productive right-handed bat heading into October.
