item.title: [The Boston Globe] How Red Sox teammates kept Roman Anthony connected during his long injury rehab - The Boston Globe
item.dc:creator: Tara Sullivan
item.description: ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — He’s back, and continuing to rediscover his baseball groove. But Roman Anthony is never going to sugarcoat how difficult it was to be away. It wasn’t simply being forced out of the Red Sox lineup, though the nearly four-month stretch he spent rehabbing a torn ligament in his right hand did feel interminable. It was doing so much of that work at the team facility in Fort Myers, Fla. Being out of the locker room; that really hurt. Good thing he had some friends on the inside
item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — He’s back, and continuing to rediscover his baseball groove. But Roman Anthony is never going to sugarcoat how difficult it was to be away. It wasn’t simply being forced out of the Red Sox lineup, though the nearly four-month stretch he spent rehabbing a torn ligament in his right hand did feel interminable. It was doing so much of that work at the team facility in Fort Myers, Fla.
Being out of the locker room; that really hurt.
Good thing he had some friends on the inside, keeping him in the loop.
Though the Red Sox were denied a chance to clinch a playoff berth Saturday after losing, 2-1, on Richie Palacios’s walk-off hit, Anthony’s two-out double in the third inning drove in Boston’s only run. Add that to his memorable Friday night performance, when a 438-foot leadoff home run and three RBI keyed the series-opening win, and his presence in these tense, playoff-like games against the first-place Rays has been unmistakable. For a team hoping to make a dent in the postseason, that’s promising.
Yet as the 22-year-old shared in a pregame conversation at his locker, sometimes it’s good to look back, too. Remembering the tough times makes the good times all the sweeter. And remembering the way his teammates helped him through his injury-imposed exile fills him with gratitude. Sometimes, it was a quick text or call to check in on his progress or mental state.
Other times, it was a FaceTime call from the room where it was happening, bringing him directly into the postgame victory music and celebrations.
But always, be it Nick Sogard, Jarren Duran, or someone else making the call, in this combination of modern technology, empathy and good old-fashioned kindness, they let him know: He was still one of them.
It kept him afloat.
“Just staying in touch with them and seeing what they were doing, I think it’s just the relationship we have,” Anthony said. “As a group, we’re all so close. For me, obviously, Fort Myers wasn’t the most ideal situation, but that’s part of it, and I had a good group of guys down there, and up here.”
When the final story of this 2026 season is told, the wildly unexpected resurrection from the bottom of the American League barrel to an (all-but-certain-but-not-yet-official) playoff berth will be the headline. The retelling will look back on the shocking April 25 firing of longtime manager Alex Cora and just about all of his staff, replaced by Chad Tracy and a handful of his Triple-A Worcester crew. It will look back on a stunning 41-14 run from June 25 to Aug. 28 that included a 21-4 record in July, and it will see how the bonds forged inside the locker room helped make it happen. Bonds that extended not just to those on the inside, but those working hard to return and do their part.
“I think just anytime that you haven’t seen a friend in a while, that’s a thing to do,” said Sogard, “more of like a friendship thing, like, oh, I haven’t talked to Roman in a while, so you know, a text here and there. Maybe we’re just in this every day, and we think, oh, Roman would have done this today, I’ll call him real quick. Stuff like that. He’s just a good friend to me and to a lot of us, so just keeping up with our buddy.”
The conversation around sending Anthony to Fort Myers took some odd turns, becoming talk radio fodder that perhaps Anthony was enjoying an overzealous night life or suffering a lack of discipline. Anthony has refuted all of it, and Tracy again on Saturday pointed to the same reasons the organization has always cited, a cramped and crowded Fenway locker room overflowing with rehabbing players, and a chance for Anthony to get away from the daily media scrutiny that comes with being in Boston. The interim manager, whose relationship with Anthony goes back to Worcester, also recalled his own regular check-ins with one of the franchise’s foundational players of the future.
“If you’re going through that for your very first time ever, being sent down to Florida by yourself, and you’ve never gone through that, I just wanted to make sure there was nothing swimming around his brain, like, you know, did they want me out of there?” Tracy said. “No. We just want you to go and get healthy and get you back here.”
For Sogard, hearing that Anthony had brought up the constant contact underscored how much it was needed.
“I was on the IL for a little over a month this year. It felt like five months,” he said. “It’s not easy to deal with, and there was a lot said about him during that time, and we know how much he wanted to be here and play and how much he cares. So yeah, just keeping up with our guy.”
Now it’s Anthony’s time to surge ahead. An eye on a playoff berth that was taken away by injury last season, when he had to watch from afar as the Sox lost the deciding Game 3 of the Wild Card series against the Yankees.
“That one stung,” he said. “Watching that, watching those games, obviously you just sit there and you kind of hit yourself over the head thinking, what if I could be there right now? All the different things I could have done.”
Now he’s back, atop the batting order, his bat heating up, a playoff series fast approaching, looking at a second chance. Much as it hurt to be away, thanks to a little help from his friends, it felt like he never left.
Tara Sullivan is a Globe columnist. She can be reached at tara.sullivan@globe.com. Follow her @Globe_Tara.

item.content:encoded:
Crochet, Houck making good progress toward return for Red Sox
This browser does not support the video element.
ST. PETERSBURG -- While the Red Sox were engaged in a tough battle with the Rays on Saturday, losing 2-1, two of their rehabbing pitchers took steps forward.
Garrett Crochet, the lefty ace who is trying to make it back in time to serve as reliever in the postseason, threw another two-inning side session on Saturday, this one at Polar Park in Worcester, Mass.
If Crochet doesn’t have any ill effects coming out of that session, the Red Sox are hopeful they can have him face hitters at Fenway Park early next week, and perhaps multiple times in the team’s final homestand leading up to the postseason.
“I think it just depends on how he feels coming out of it, how much volume we give him,” said Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy. “So it's hard to say. I know it's not a great answer, but it's just really how it is. How does he feel after each step? So when he does that, how does he feel? And then determine from there. Do we give him more hitters or do we want to put him in a game? It’s hard to say until you know how he feels.”
Meanwhile, righty Tanner Houck made his final rehab appearance for Triple-A Worcester, allowing two hits and two runs (one earned) over 3 1/3 innings. Houck walked none and struck out two as he continued to make progress in his return from Tommy John surgery.
As is the case with Crochet, Houck doesn’t have time to build back up as a starter, but he could be a bullpen option for the Sox in October.
Perhaps Houck could make an appearance or two during the season-ending homestand against the Guardians and Cubs, which starts Tuesday.

item.title: [Boston Herald] Red Sox waste dazzling performance by Brayan Bello, get walked off by Rays

item.content:encoded:
Someone only tuning into their first Red Sox game of the season Saturday might not understand the significance of Brayan Bello’s dominant performance against the hosting Tampa Bay Rays.
Particularly as it will be forever marred by a Rays’ 2-1 walk-off victory that keeps Boston’s postseason ticket dangling out of reach for at least another night.
But before that frustrating ending, there was Bello’s hard-earned triumph. It has been a tumultuous year for the homegrown right-hander, who lost his spot in the Red Sox starting rotation at the beginning of May, and pitched his way into a Triple-A demotion the first week of June. Bello dominated in a bulk-relief role from his mid-July recall through early September before the Red Sox gave him another chance to start.
Making his second start of the month on Saturday, Bello turned in not only his best game of the season, but one of the best of his five-year career. He owned his team’s first-place division rivals for eight innings of one-run ball. He yielded just five hits, issued no walks and matched his career-high 11 strikeouts.
“That was exceptional,” Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters postgame. “By far and away his best outing of the year. As good as I’ve seen him. So, I don’t know what else to say. He was awesome, really awesome.”
Bello’s reward was a no-decision, as the Red Sox lineup went 1 for 11 with runners in scoring position, then lost on Rays second baseman Richie Palacios’ walk-off RBI single in the bottom of the ninth.
Palacios’ game-winning hit came moments after a base-running gamble by Red Sox third baseman Caleb Durbin that proved calamitous. A glimmer of hope flared when Durbin collected his second double of the day, off Bryan Baker with one out in the top of the ninth. But he was then caught trying to steal third, which proved costly almost instantaneously when Jarren Duran tripled on the very next pitch. Isiah Kiner-Falefa’s inning-ending groundout sent the tie game to the bottom of the ninth.
“I’m OK with it,” Tracy said of Durbin’s attempt to steal. “It’s one-to-one game the whole way, and close play.”
“Hindsight is 20/20,” Tracy continued. “It’s easy in baseball. He gets thrown out, and then Duran has a triple. But you don’t have the privilege of hindsight. So (Durbin) was working hard out there, seeing if he can get the bag, and they got him.”
“I thought I had a window, and probably wasn’t a big enough window,” Durbin told reporters. “I those situations, too, you want to be sure about it. So obviously on me. Not really any excuse other than I gotta be more sure.”
Roman Anthony gave the Red Sox an early lead for the second straight game, doubling off Rays starter Freddy Peralta with two outs in the third. Anthony’s third RBI base hit of the series scored Durbin, who led off the frame with his first double.
But that was all the Red Sox wrote. The home team peppered the middle innings with costly mistakes, but the visitors never took advantage.
Rays centerfielder Cedric Mullins reached safely on a bunt single and advanced to second on a throwing error by Durbin to begin the bottom of the third, but Boston’s third baseman immediately atoned for the miscue by completing a caught-stealing relay with catcher Adley Rutschman and shortstop Trevor Story.
Tampa Bay ran out of ABS challenges by the fourth inning. Shortstop Jorge Mateo burned one on a called Strike 3 from Bello (1.2” Edge Distance) for the second out of the bottom of the third. Peralta lost his team’s remaining bid trying to overturn a Ball 4 with a 2.8” Edge Distance, which put right-fielder Wilyer Abreu on with one out in the fourth.
The worm turned in the bottom of the fourth. Boston’s squandering of a one-out opportunity with Abreu and Nick Sogard (single) on first and second in the top of the inning proved costly immediately when Jonathan Aranda led off the bottom with a first-pitch, game-tying home run.
An undeterred Bello held fast to the knot inning after inning, and looked effortless doing so. Whereas Peralta exited after 5 2/3 innings that required 97 pitches (59 for strikes), Bello needed 55 pitches to complete the first five frames, and his count sat at 68 at the end of the sixth.
When the Rays finally threatened in the bottom of the seventh, the Sox starter was the picture of poise. Unruffled by the back-to-back singles by Liam Hicks and Chandler Simpson, Bello retired the next three men in order. The game became his longest of the season as a starter or reliever when he recorded the first out of the seventh, and when he returned to the dugout after finishing the eighth inning, it marked his deepest outing since his complete game on July 8, 2025.
With closer Aroldis Chapman still unavailable due to lat tightness, it fell to righty Garrett Whitlock to pitch the game to extra innings. Whitlock was one strike away from stranding slugger Junior Caminero and Simpson when Palacios sent his 1-2 sinker to right field, where it plunked down in front of Abreu.
The loss means Sunday is the earliest the Red Sox can punch their ticket to October. The current playoff picture has the Red Sox and Yankees meeting in a rematch of last year’s best-of-three Wild Card series at Yankee Stadium. If Boston gets beyond that, they could see Tampa Bay again.
Saturday’s intensity felt like a preview to the Red Sox. Durbin hopes they can turn the experience into an advantage.
“That was a hell of a baseball game,” Tracy said. “I don’t have really anything negative to say about that game, other than it was really well-played on both sides by both teams. Big moments, and people rose the occasion. It was just a heck of a baseball game, and they were able to beat us.”
“Even yesterday and tomorrow, like they got a little bit of a playoff feel,” Durbin said. “I feel like last year (with the Milwaukee Brewers), first couple playoff games … adrenaline’s way higher. So to get that feel before playoffs even start is super important, because it usually takes a couple games to really settle in. So if we could settle in by Game 1 or 2, that’ll be big for us.”

item.title: [The Boston Globe] Willson Contreras hopes to get back into Red Sox lineup before the regular season ends - The Boston Globe
item.dc:creator: Peter Abraham
item.description: ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — Willson Contreras stood at his locker Saturday afternoon and showed reporters the spot where a pitch hit his right hand in Texas on Thursday. It was on the knuckles between his pinky finger and ring finger, and there was still swelling and a yellow bruise. Contreras could flex his hand but can’t yet grip a bat well enough to hit. item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — Willson Contreras stood at his locker Saturday afternoon and showed reporters the spot where a pitch hit his right hand in Texas on Thursday.
It was on the knuckles between his pinky finger and ring finger, and there was still swelling and a yellow bruise. Contreras could flex his hand but can’t yet grip a bat well enough to hit.
If you didn’t know Contreras was a baseball player, you’d think he was a boxer based on his battered hands.
“When I got hit, I felt my hand going numb. I thought it was bad because that’s a sign of a fracture,” he said. “That’s why I came off the game.”
Contreras is hopeful of getting in a few games before the start of the postseason.
“Hand’s still really sore. Woke up feeling a little better,” he said. “I can squeeze a little better than [Friday], but it’s gonna take a few days.”
The initial X-rays were negative, and any further scans will wait until after the swelling goes down, but Contreras is confident there isn’t a fracture based on his experience.
“I can squeeze a lot better. I’ve had fractures before, and when I have fractures, I couldn’t squeeze,” he said.
Contreras is hoping he can take some swings on Sunday. But because the injury is to his top hand, he has to make sure he can absorb the impact of making contact.
“I’m going to take it day-to-day. Of course I want to come back and play with the guys and be there for them,” he said. “It’s a part of baseball.”
Contreras said he might try using a guard over his batting glove to protect his hand.
The Sox play the Rays on Sunday afternoon and are off on Monday. Contreras could possibly return on Tuesday against the Guardians.
“I’m going to do everything in my power to get back on the field before the playoffs,” he said.
Contreras has been hit 24 times this season, tied for third-most in the majors, and 47 times over last two seasons. It’s largely because he stands close to the plate. But Contreras suggested on Thursday that Sox pitchers should retaliate on his behalf.
“I see, and completely feel and understand Willson’s frustration,” interim manager Chad Tracy said. “He’s been hit close to 50 times the last couple of years so he’s frustrated. Whether he’s referring to the umpires doing something or the pitchers, it’s irrelevant.”
Tracy acknowledged that Contreras crowds the plate. “But there’s a lot of guys that are close to the plate that don’t get hit as much as he does,” he said.
Rafaela progressing
Ceddanne Rafaela, who has been on the injured list since Sept. 3 with a strained right quadriceps, worked out at Worcester on Saturday and faced live pitching for the first time since the injury.
“I felt comfortable,” he said. “My body is rested, and I feel ready to go.”
The last hurdle is to sprint at 100 percent effort, something he will try on Sunday. Rafaela hopes to play against the Guardians on Tuesday.
Crochet could face hitters
Tracy said the goal set for Garrett Crochet would be to face hitters early in the week. That would likely be at Fenway Park before a game. Whether one such session would be enough to merit inclusion on the postseason roster isn’t certain. “Hard to say. I know that’s not a great answer, but it just really is,” Tracy said. … Righthanded reliever Tyron Guerrero could be activated off the injured list as soon as Sunday. He has been out since Sept. 1 with a sore shoulder.
Globe staff writer Alex Speier contributed to this report from Worcester.
Peter Abraham can be reached at peter.abraham@globe.com. Follow him on Bluesky at peteabeglobe.bsky.social.

item.title: [Boston Herald] Red Sox get promising Willson Contreras injury update as postseason nears
item.dc:creator: Gabrielle Starr
item.description: On the verge of clinching a postseason berth for the second straight year, the Boston Red Sox have reason to be cautiously optimistic about the health of one of their best hitters. Though still “pretty sore” from taking a pitch to the right hand on Sept. 17, Willson Contreras no longer believes he suffered a fracture, because he woke up feeling better and had improved range of motion and grip. “I’m not concerned about having a fracture, just because I can squeeze a lot better today,” the All-Sta
item.content:encoded:
On the verge of clinching a postseason berth for the second straight year, the Boston Red Sox have reason to be cautiously optimistic about the health of one of their best hitters.
Though still “pretty sore” from taking a pitch to the right hand on Sept. 17, Willson Contreras no longer believes he suffered a fracture, because he woke up feeling better and had improved range of motion and grip.
“I’m not concerned about having a fracture, just because I can squeeze a lot better today,” the All-Star first baseman told reporters before the team’s Saturday afternoon game at the Tampa Bay Rays’ Tropicana Field. “I had a fracture in my right hand in 2024 by hit-by-pitch, and I couldn’t squeeze at all.”
“But it’s going to take days,” Contreras cautioned.
Contreras’ 24th hit-by-pitch of the season, a 92.3 mph sinker from Rangers’ Jakob Junis to his knuckle in the eighth inning, was a moment of extreme panic for him and the team. Contreras initially went to take his base, but was evidently in severe pain and interim manager Chad Tracy and athletic trainer Dave Herrera quickly removed him from the game.
Though initial imaging was negative, Contreras and Tracy both acknowledged the swelling could be obscurative, with the former telling reporters postgame, “It felt like a fracture.”
“When I got hit, I felt my hand going numb, and I thought it was bad, because that’s a sign of a fracture,” Contreras said on Saturday. “And it was like, tingling for like five minutes.”
Contreras will try to grip a bat on Sunday, and if so, try to do some cage work. He is champing at the bit to get back in games before the postseason begins. He has soared to new heights in his 11th big-league season and first with the Red Sox, putting up career-best marks in his .905 OPS, 59 walks, 81 RBI, and 27 home runs (129 games).
“I’m dying to go out and play with the guys and be there for them,” Contreras said. “It’s part of baseball; I’ll do everything in my power to get back on the field.”
“You don’t want to get to the playoffs without playing any games,” he said. “I want to do everything in my power to get back on the field before the playoffs. If it happens, it happens. If it doesn’t happen, we’ll see what happens.”
Contreras is one of several injured stars the Red Sox are eager to have back as they careen toward October baseball. Gold Glove centerfielder Ceddanne Rafaela last played Sept. 2 before going on the injured list with a right quad strain. Though it’s unlikely Rafaela will get into a Triple-A Worcester game before their season ends on Sunday, interim manager Chad Tracy described him as “moving quickly in the right direction,” and said the goal is for him to get “live BP-type at-bats of some kind, plus the Trajekt (pitching machine).”
All-Star closer Aroldis Chapman is not on the IL, but remains day-to-day due to the lat tightness he felt during a workout before Tuesday’s game in Texas. Though unavailable for this weekend’s series in Tampa, he told reporters there (through a team translator), “I’m not worried at all. … I feel very good. I was going to go out and throw, but the team wants to take it slow, and they want me to take my time.” Chapman plans to get back in games during the team’s final homestand, which begins Tuesday versus the Cleveland Guardians.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox dropped Nick Sogard in the lineup in the second game of a three-game series against the Tampa Bay Rays.
Boston is coming off a 4-2 win over the Rays in the series opener, in a game where Sogard went 0-for-5 while hitting second.
The Red Sox are 84-70.
Boston Red Sox Drop Nick Sogard
Ahead of the second game of the series, Boston dropped Sogard in the lineup after his 0-for-5 night.
Sogard is playing first base as Willson Contreras remains out. Yet, his spot in the order is different, as he is now hitting fifth.
The Red Sox lineup on Saturday against the Rays is as follows:
- R. Anthony LF
- M. Gasper DH
- A. Rutschman C
- W. Abreu RF
- N. Sogard 1B
- T. Story SS
- C. Durbin 3B
- J. Duran CF
- I. Kiner-Falefa 2B
Sogard has struggled at the plate as of late, as he's now been dropped to fifth in the order. He's hitting .255 with 5 home runs and 19 RBIs. However, in his last 7 games, he's hitting .167 with 1 home run and 3 RBIs, while striking out 5 times.
First pitch on Saturday is set for 4:10 p.m. ET.
Boston Right Now
Boston is firmly in the second Wild Card spot in the American League.
The Red Sox are closing in on a playoff berth, and it could happen on Saturday depending on some outcomes.
"I think everybody does, for sure," said interim manager Chad Tracy. "We came out and looked really good offensively in the first part of that game, and there was a lot of energy in the dugout. And I think guys feel it. We're not done yet, but I definitely think they sniff it, and we're wanting to get there for sure."
Although Boston is likely to make the postseason, the Red Sox haven't clinched, so they aren't talking about anything yet.
"When we clinch, I want to be able to [celebrate]," said Ranger Suarez. "But mathematically, we're not there yet, so I'm not thinking about that yet."
Boston will likely face the New York Yankees in the Wild Card round for the second straight year.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Boston Red Sox Drop Nick Sogard During Rays Series appeared first on HEAVY.

item.content:encoded:
Red Sox ace Crochet throws side session at Polar Park before WooSox game
WORCESTER — Garrett Crochet threw a baseball at Polar Park Saturday.
Four hours before the WooSox hosted the Durham Bulls (Tampa Bay Rays AAA club), the Red Sox star left-handed pitcher threw a side session as he continues his rehab from a left shoulder injury.
Crochet, dressed in a full white Red Sox uniform, tossed roughly 20 pitches and sat in the 91 to 92 mph range.
“He looks great,” WooSox pitching coach Dan DeLucia said. “It was pretty much what we expected. Like, that was the expectation, go out there and kind of make it an in-between side start. No, actually probably a tick above what I think the expectations were, but for the most part, as expected the fine-tuning things, getting on the mound again.
“(We had) one of the coaches stand in (in the batter’s box) and he still just needs to fine-tune things, and that takes some time, but the outputs look pretty good. Like, how the body’s moving and all that looks pretty good.”
Crochet (3-3, 6.30 ERA with 37 strikeouts in 30 IP) last pitched for the Red Sox on April 25 in a game against the Baltimore Orioles. He was placed on the 15-day injured list four days later (retroactive to April 26) and transferred to the 60-day IL on June 5.
While meeting with media members in St. Petersburg, Fla. Friday, Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy wasn’t clear on the next steps for Crochet moving forward as the Red Sox wrap up their regular season a week from Sunday.
Crochet is attempting to come back to help Boston out of the bullpen for their likely upcoming playoff series against the New York Yankees.
“It’s hard to say. If everything goes well Saturday, then you kind of determine what that looks like at the beginning part of next week,” said Tracy, according to Sean McAdam of MassLive. “I’d say we’re at a point where these next five days are going to be pretty telling. How does the side go and what can we do with him at the start of next week? That will give us a better idea.”
With fellow Red Sox pitcher Tanner Houck scheduled to pitch for Triple-A Worcester later in the day in a rehab assignment, both Crochet and Houck — and starting center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela, who hit living pitching at Polar Park pregame Saturday as he continues his recovery from a right quadriceps strain — present possible reinforcements for the Red Sox as they look to make a run in the playoffs.

item.dc:creator: Matías Persuh

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox have been one of the major storylines in the AL East right up until the final stretch of the season. Behind the Tampa Bay Rays and New York Yankees, the team managed by interim manager Chad Tracy needs a series of results to secure a Wild Card berth and keep its postseason hopes alive.
Beating the Rays on the road at Tropicana Field is a must. On top of that, the Red Sox need either the Texas Rangers or the Houston Astros to lose their game in order to finally punch their ticket to the postseason.
Both the Rangers and the Astros will play at home in the evening. Texas will host the Toronto Blue Jays at Globe Life Field, while Jose Espada’s team will welcome the Atlanta Braves to Daikin Park.
Boston wants to return to the World Series
The Boston Red Sox are itching to make a serious Fall Classic run, aiming to bring the Commissioner’s Trophy back to Fenway for the first time since their dominant 2018 championship. Sitting at an impressive 84-70 record late into the campaign, the club has completely revitalized its season under manager Chad Tracy, who took the helm and turned things around after a rough start.
Chad Tracy of the Boston Red Sox.
With the squad clicking at the right time and buying into Tracy’s energetic leadership, Boston looks ready to cause standard postseason chaos and prove they belong back on baseball’s biggest stage.
More chances to clinch a postseason spot
If the Red Sox can’t lock up their Wild Card spot today against Tampa Bay, they still have plenty of chances left on the schedule to seal the deal. They’ll wrap up their road trip at Tropicana Field on Sunday against the Rays before returning home for a critical six-game homestand to close out the regular season.
BoSox will host a three-game series against the Cleveland Guardians mid-week, followed by a final three-game Interleague matchup against the Chicago Cubs at Fenway Park from September 25-27. With those remaining games right in front of their home crowd, the Red Sox hold their postseason destiny firmly in their own hands.

item.content:encoded:
Quedó a un pelotazo de igualar el récord para venezolanos en una temporada.
El carabobeño Willson Contreras, de los Medias Rojas de Boston, se vio obligado a salir del encuentro del jueves contra los Rangers de Texas debido a un bolazo en la mano derecha, durante el octavo inning, en la victoria de su club 4-3.
Leer También: MLB: ´El Abusador´ Ronald Acuña jr. clave en la clasificación de los Bravos de Atlanta
Su compatriota Wilyer Abreu negoció un boleto para iniciar el episodio antes de que Contreras fuera golpeado por un sinker de 92.3 millas por hora (mph) de Jakob Junis.
El toletero de 34 años de edad, quien disputa su undécima campaña en las Grandes Ligas, cayó al suelo del dolor antes de pararse otra vez y dirigirse a la primera base, donde Abreu lo atendió brevemente. El mánager interino de los patirrojos, Chad Tracy, y los preparadores físicos entraron al terreno, y Willson Contreras salió del encuentro poco después.
Esta campaña el ahora inicialista lleva 24 pelotazos para igualar su tope personal del certamen de 2022.
El récord de número pelotazos para venezolanos en una temporada es de 25. Lo comparten el caraqueño Andrés Galarraga (1998) y el larense Andrés Giménez (2022).
Andrés Galarraga es el líder en pelotazos recibidos en la historia entre los criollos tras ser golpeado 178 veces en 19 temporadas y 2.257 partidos. A Willson Contreras le han pegado 153 pelotazos en 1.207 juegos.
Contreras ha alcanzado marcas personales en jonrones (27), impulsadas (81) y OPS+ (155) en su primera temporada con los Medias Rojas. Lleva 199 cuadrangulares por vida en MLB.
Las radiografías realizadas el jueves a la mano lesionada del carabobeño descartaron cualquier fractura.
Willson Contreras batea para promedio este año de .276 en 129 careos. El nativo de Puerto Cabello marcha líder jonronero e impulsor de Boston.

Con información de Líder

item.dc:creator: Scott Roche

item.content:encoded:
When the Boston Red Sox lost Roman Anthony to an injury in early May, little did anyone know what was about to happen. He would miss the next four months. However, while he was out, the Red Sox went on multiple winning streaks and are now closing in on a postseason berth.
Since coming back, Anthony has been slotted back into the top of the lineup by interim manager Chad Tracy. On Friday night against the Tampa Bay Rays, Anthony showed what he means to the top of the lineup.
Roman Anthony Leads Boston Red Sox To Win Over Tampa Bay Rays
Coming off a 4-3 win over the Texas Rangers, Anthony led off the game with a solo home run. In the second inning, he had a two-run single for a 3-1 lead in what turned into a 4-2 Boston victory. The win moved the Red Sox on the cusp of a postseason berth. They can clinch it as early as Saturday night.
After Anthony’s 2-for-5 night with three of Boston’s four RBIs, Tracy didn’t beat around the bush about what his young outfielder means to his club. Despite his struggles, Tracy has not moved Anthony lower in the lineup.
“You see what he can do,” Tracy said, per Peter Abraham of the Boston Globe. “It’s the game of baseball. There are ebbs and flows . . . When he’s going well, you can see the impact he makes.”
Anthony returned in late August, but his September has been a struggle. He is slashing .214/.335/.374 with four home runs and nine runs driven in this month. For Anthony, it’s all about getting ready for postseason baseball. That’s what Friday night’s game felt like.
“Obviously that’s a great team over there,” Anthony said, per Abraham. “It kind of felt like a playoff game and getting into that mode.”
Roman Anthony Credits Hitting Coach for Turning Things Around
After missing four months, it’s not easy to come back and hit MLB pitching. It doesn’t matter how many rehab assignments someone makes in the minors. Anthony has stayed the course and kept working with hitting coach John Soteropulos.
“He’s amazing. He’s somebody who knows my swing so well. We have been together since I came into this org, really, all throughout the Minor Leagues. Having somebody here, somebody who knows my swing and when to talk, nobody knows me better than John,” said Anthony, per Ian Browne of MLB.com. “I give so much credit to him in helping me out and getting into the video room and the cage and making sure everything is where we want it to be.”
Over their last 10 games, Boston is 5-5 thanks to wins over the Rangers and Rays. In 10 days, they will begin the American League wild-card series on the road, most likely in the Bronx against the New York Yankees. If Tampa Bay falters over the next week, New York could sneak up and win the division, which would send Boston to Tampa Bay for the wild-card series.
Regardless of who the Red Sox play, Roman Anthony is heating up, and that could be good news for the Red Sox and bad news for the rest of the playoff field.

item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — When Roman Anthony returned to the Boston Red Sox three weeks ago after nearly four months on the injury list with a torn right finger ligament, it initially looked as if he had barely missed any time.
Through his first five games after he was activated Aug. 30 in New York, Anthony recorded four games with multiple hits, going 10-for-22 with two homers, two doubles and a triple. His methodical rehab, missing 101 games, paid dividends with a bat that was ready to perform.
Advertisement
But then, as so often happens in baseball, he fell out of rhythm at the plate, collecting just seven hits, including just one extra-base hit, in his next 56 plate appearances.
That’s why he found himself in an early batting practice session Friday afternoon with hitting coach John Soteropulos, tinkering in the cage with a few mechanical adjustments.
The work clicked.
Oh baby, Roman! pic.twitter.com/aP7bBEgZX0
— Red Sox (@RedSox) September 18, 2026
Three pitches into the game, Anthony clubbed a solo homer for a lead, and in the second inning, he smacked a bases-loaded single to drive in two more runs as the Red Sox beat the Tampa Bay Rays 4-2, snapping the Rays’ six-game win streak. The win inched the Red Sox closer to clinching a playoff berth. A Red Sox win Saturday, coupled with a Texas Rangers loss, would punch Boston’s ticket to the playoffs.
“We came out and looked really good offensively in the first part of that game, and there was a lot of energy in the dugout,” interim manager Chad Tracy said. “I think guys feel it. We’re not done yet, but I definitely think they sniff it, and we’re wanting to get there for sure.”
With eight games left in the regular season, getting Anthony’s bat hot again, particularly as Willson Contreras remains day to day with a deeply bruised right hand, will be imperative for the Red Sox lineup in the postseason.
“He will,” Tracy said confidently about Anthony’s bat regaining momentum. “I mean, you see what he can do. It’s the game of baseball, there’s ebbs and flows. He came off the rehab, and for like five games, he looked fantastic. Then he went through some stuff, and now he’s starting to look good again. When he’s going well, you see the impact he can make.”
Before Soteropulos was elevated to lead hitting coach this season after an overhaul of the coaching staff, he was the minor-league hitting coordinator and worked closely with Anthony. That relationship has helped.
Advertisement
“Me and John have been working on some things, really since I have been back,” Anthony said. “He’s amazing. He’s somebody who knows my swing so well. We have been together since I came into this org, all throughout the minor leagues. Having somebody here, somebody who knows my swing and when to talk and when to tinker. Nobody knows me better than John.
“It’s such a constant game of adjustments and looking over a span of my last few at-bats, it obviously was not where I wanted to be. I was hitting the ball on the ground, to the right side, so I was trying to get away from that. Hitting early on the field with John and with Trevor (Story) definitely helped.”
Anthony’s first-inning homer came off the bat at an estimated 107.7 mph with an estimated distance of 438 feet, marking the longest homer of his career.
But to him, the two-run single was just as important. In a rough series in Texas, the Red Sox had gone just 1-for-18 with runners in scoring position. His goal was to alleviate some pressure on the offense by simply making contact.
“That’s my job, to do everything I can to put the ball in play and find ways on base,” he said. “That’s how I have had a lot of success in the past as a leadoff hitter. So over these last games, just keep putting an emphasis on being the best leadoff hitter I can be. See as many pitches I can and try and get on base. It was a huge way to start the game. This game is all about momentum, so any time you can get something like that going, it’s huge.”
The two-run single gave the Red Sox the lead back after the Rays tied the score off Ranger Suarez in the bottom of the first. Jahmai Jones made it 4-1 in the third with his sixth homer of the year.
The insurance gave the Red Sox a cushion as Suarez was uncharacteristically spotty with command, walking a career-high five batters.
Advertisement
Still, he navigated traffic in each of the first four innings and allowed just the one run on three hits in 5 2/3 innings. Reliever Wyatt Olds wiggled out of a jam in the sixth after Suarez exited, walking two batters to load the bases, then falling behind pinch hitter Jake Fraley 3-1. Olds came back to strike out Fraley.
The Red Sox faced more trouble in the ninth, with reliever Erik Miller still searching for his command. Closer Aroldis Chapman remains day to day with lat tightness, and Tracy turned to Miller for the ninth with Garrett Whitlock having a heavy load of late.
Miller allowed a run in the ninth on an infield single, a wild pitch, a walk and a groundout. He loaded the bases after a strikeout got away on a wild pitch, but escaped the jam with a groundout to close it out.
Clinching their postseason spot with a week left in the regular season would allow the Red Sox to breathe and reset some players before the postseason. But they’re not there yet. Saturday awaits.
“It just kind of felt like a playoff game,” Anthony said. “Getting into that mode is huge from an at-bat standpoint and from a big-game standpoint of constantly being the next man up.”

item.title: [CBS Sports] Red Sox look to stay hot vs. Rays behind surging Payton Tolle
item.dc:creator: FLM

item.content:encoded:
Boston Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy knows his team has figured out the Tampa Bay Rays pretty well this season.
That said, the Red Sox (84-70) still can learn more about the Rays (93-60) when the teams meet Saturday afternoon in St. Petersburg, Fla.
"At this point with (the Rays), we've played them enough already," Tracy said. "We have a pretty good understanding of them, (and) they have a pretty good understanding of us. But you could always pick up more stuff."
In Friday's series opener, the Red Sox scored four runs over the first three innings and won 4-2 to snap Tampa Bay's six-game winning streak and improve to 6-5 this season vs. the Rays.
Boston currently holds the second wild-card position in the American League but is dealing with several injuries.
"We have guys beat up that aren't here, and the hope is we get people healthy, and the roster could look even different a week from now than it does right now," Tracy said.
Boston's Willson Contreras is day-to-day after getting hit on the hand, while closer Aroldis Chapman (lat tightness) has been unavailable the past two contests.
Right-hander Tanner Houck (Tommy John surgery in 2025) and lefty Garrett Crochet (left shoulder inflammation) have advanced in their rehab assignments.
Boston left-hander Payton Tolle (9-6, 3.02 ERA) is expected to make his 26th start on Saturday and will try to record his sixth consecutive win.
Tolle is 1-0 with an 0.75 ERA over 12 innings in his last two starts, allowing one run on eight hits while striking out 19 with a walk. He is 0-2 with a 4.50 ERA in two starts and one relief outing against Tampa Bay, which already has clinched a playoff berth.
Whatever Rays pitching coach Kyle Snyder and the rest of the staff have done with trade-deadline acquisition Freddy Peralta certainly has been a success.
Acquired by the club from the New York Mets for three prospects on Aug. 2, Peralta (9-11, 4.67 ERA) -- a right-hander who will start for the Rays on Saturday -- arrived from the Big Apple as a lesser version of what he was during his two All-Star seasons with the Milwaukee Brewers.
He was 5-9 with a 4.99 ERA with the Mets, but the work was immediately put in by the Rays to adjust Peralta to where he was when he was a 17-game winner with a sub-3.00 ERA last season.
"For some reason, when I got here, when I sat here with Kyle and (bullpen coach Jorge Moncada) and (manager Kevin Cash), they told me, like, 'You're gonna do what you want to do here, and we are going to help you to do it,'" Peralta said.
"And we know what you need to do to make those adjustments. We just put everything on the table. I just followed all the instructions, and it's what I am right now."
With the Rays, Peralta is 4-2 with a 3.86 ERA in eight starts, but his past four outings have been gems. He has pitched 23 innings and has allowed just two runs on 10 hits, with 17 strikeouts, four walks and an 0.78 ERA in that span.
"Fastball Freddy," who is using his changeup much more with the Rays, is 0-2 with a 5.40 ERA in three career starts against Boston.
Peralta allowed two runs on three hits in 4 1/3 innings in a 4-0 loss at Boston on July 11 while with the Mets.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Red Sox Lose Speedster for 2026, Enter Braiden Ward?
item.dc:creator: Patrick McAvoy; Unknown
item.description: The biggest story of the 2026 Major League Baseball trade deadline was the Boston Red Sox's addition of Adley Rutschman from the Baltimore Orioles. While this is the case, he wasn't Boston's only impactful addition. Boston went out and acquired speedy outfielder Eli White from the Atlanta Braves in exchange for right-handed pitcher Tyler Uberstine. The deal for White was certainly quieter than the Rutschman deal, to say the least. White is a 32-year-old speedster who gets on base, can steal base
item.content:encoded:
The biggest story of the 2026 Major League Baseball trade deadline was the Boston Red Sox's addition of Adley Rutschman from the Baltimore Orioles. While this is the case, he wasn't Boston's only impactful addition.
Boston went out and acquired speedy outfielder Eli White from the Atlanta Braves in exchange for right-handed pitcher Tyler Uberstine. The deal for White was certainly quieter than the Rutschman deal, to say the least. White is a 32-year-old speedster who gets on base, can steal bases and plays good defense. He's a good guy to have on a playoff roster, but unfortunately he is "likely" done for the season now with a torn ligament in his foot in his foot, per WEEI's Rob Bradford.
"No news on Contreras. No new scans. See how grip strength improves. Also, Eli White has a tear in the ligament in his foot and is likely out for the season. Crochet will throw another side session tomorrow with up-downs," Bradford wrote.
With White now likely done for the season, this only adds fuel to the idea that someone like Braiden Ward should be considered for a promotion to the big league club before all is said and done on the 2026 season.
The Red Sox A Decision To Make
White may not be a big-name player, but this news isn't great for Boston. White played in 27 games in Boston after the trade and slashed .276/.300/.379 with a .679 OPS, one home run, 12 RBIs, three doubles and 10 runs scored. Overall, White was a 1.4-WAR player this season, the highest mark of his career, in 96 total games with Boston and Atlanta.
Ward was a Spring Training standout for Boston and stole 19 bases. He was sent down to Triple-A Worcester when the regular season kicked off and he has spent the entire season there. Ward has played in 108 games and is slashing .251/.364/.372 with a .736 OPS, six home runs, 33 RBIs and most importantly, 61 stolen bases.
We made the case for Boston to give Ward a look back on Sep. 13. On Sep. 16, Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy was asked about Ward and insinuated that the idea to promote the speedster would at least be considered. With the bad news for White, now should be the time to give Ward a look. He has game-changing speed and could be used simply as a pinch runner in the playoffs. White likely would've been in a similar role if he didn't get hurt. Now, the Red Sox should turn to Ward.
Patrick McAvoy's experiences include local and national sports coverage at the New England Sports Network with a focus on baseball and basketball. Outside of journalism, Patrick received an MBA at Brandeis University. For all business/marketing inquiries regarding Boston Red Sox On SI, please reach out to Scott Neville: scott@moreviewsmedia.com

item.title: [Boston.com] Red Sox’ Willson Contreras has ominous comments after latest HBP
item.dc:creator: Kaley Brown
item.description: The ever-fiery Willson Contreras had some on-brand quotes after his latest hit-by-pitch. The Red Sox first baseman got drilled on the right hand by a pitch from Texas Rangers right-handed pitcher Jakob Junis in the eighth inning on Thursday night. He was in visible pain and immediately exited the game. After the game, he said he thought his hand was fractured upon being struck, but he appears to have avoided serious injury. His X-rays came back negative. Also postgame, Contreras expressed immens
item.content:encoded:
The ever-fiery Willson Contreras had some on-brand quotes after his latest hit-by-pitch.
The Red Sox first baseman got drilled on the right hand by a pitch from Texas Rangers right-handed pitcher Jakob Junis in the eighth inning on Thursday night. He was in visible pain and immediately exited the game.
After the game, he said he thought his hand was fractured upon being struck, but he appears to have avoided serious injury. His X-rays came back negative.
Also postgame, Contreras expressed immense discontent with the fact that he’s been hit by pitches on 24 separate occasions this season. The total ties a career high (2022 with the Chicago Cubs) and continues a trend he’s experienced his entire MLB career. Only two players have been hit more this year (Cardinals’ Ivan Herrera, 29; White Sox’ Sam Antonacci, 27).
“I feel like … ” Contreras said, pausing for seven seconds, “I want to say something I can’t say. Let’s leave it at that (via The Boston Globe’s Tim Healey).”
Contreras, attempting to elaborate without getting into specifics, added:
“If nobody does anything about it, I’m going to keep getting hit. That’s the way I see it. That’s it.”
The 34-year-old, who has been Boston’s best hitter during its memorable season, came off the injured list last weekend after recovering from a hamstring strain. He expressed frustration about not knowing when he’ll return to the diamond again.
“It’s really frustrating because I just came back from the IL, and this might take days,” Contreras said. “I mean, sore bones in the hands — might take two days, might take a week, might take 10 days.”
Contreras is known as a right-handed batter who crowds the plate, which leads to more HBPs. He pushed back on that notion, though, saying other hitters do the same thing but get drilled less often.
“A lot of people might say that I hit on top of the plate, but I’m seeing a lot of players hit on top of the plate. They don’t get hit like me,” Contreras said.
The Venezuelan has been hit 146 times since 2018, which leads MLB.
Interim manager Chad Tracy offered an injury update on Contreras before Friday’s game against the Rays in Tampa.
“(He’s) sore. Obviously sore with some swelling,” Tracy told reporters. “Nothing new other than just, over the next couple of days, they’ll work on treatment, on getting the swelling out. See if he can get grip strength back, and then we’ll go from there. Just day to day.”
Tracy didn’t write off Contreras returning to the lineup this weekend.
“Never want to rule it out,” he said. “You get the swelling out of there and he could turn a corner really quickly. Just hard to say.”

item.title: [The Boston Globe] Ranger Suarez may not have been at his best, but the Red Sox lefthander still showed he had enough fight - The Boston Globe
item.dc:creator: Tara Sullivan
item.description: ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — A year ago, as the Red Sox crept toward the end of the regular season, the pitching choices for their looming Wild Card Series in New York were limited. Beyond ace Garrett Crochet, who dominated the Yankees in Game 1, the Red Sox ended up going with the unreliable Brayan Bello in Game 2 and the untested Connelly Early in Game 3. Two losses later, they were packing their bags for the winter. This year, with a replay of that series feeling all but certain to begin a week fro
item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — A year ago, as the Red Sox crept toward the end of the regular season, the pitching choices for their looming Wild Card Series in New York were limited. Beyond ace Garrett Crochet, who dominated the Yankees in Game 1, the Red Sox ended up going with the unreliable Brayan Bello in Game 2 and the untested Connelly Early in Game 3. Two losses later, they were packing their bags for the winter.
This year, with a replay of that series feeling all but certain to begin a week from Tuesday and once again in the Bronx, the pitching plans look nothing like they did back then.
Which is good news for the Red Sox.
Even with Crochet sidelined all season by injury, the pitching rotation has been, in the words of interim manager Chad Tracy, “pivotal” to the drastic midseason turnaround that lifted this team from the depths of the American League standings and into the playoff race.
A trade for Sonny Gray. The continued development of Payton Tolle. And the free agent signing of Ranger Suarez. Three big moves, three likely starters for one more entry in the ongoing Boston/New York postseason clash of baseball titans.
Friday night in Florida, it was Suarez’s turn to prove his readiness. Facing the first-place Rays presented an obvious test, but for Suarez, it also was a chance to build on his two previous starts, in which he allowed only one run in 14 innings. As Tracy pointed out before the game, there is no mystery into what makes a good Suarez outing. Control the tempo, get ahead in the count, and locate pitches. When the lefthander does those three things, he can be pretty hard to beat.
But, as the Rays learned Friday, even if he doesn’t quite do those three things as well as he wants to, he can still find a way to battle through.
So there he was at the end of a decidedly mixed bag of a night, leading the Sox to a 4-2 win, improving his record to 8-4 after giving up just one run in 5⅔ innings. On the upside, he struck out five and consistently got key outs in key moments.
On the downside, he had to labor mightily to get there, walking a career-high five batters, throwing just 56 of his 98 pitches for strikes. He got away with it this time, but come the playoffs, that’s playing with fire, whether against the Yankees or perhaps the Rays again, with Tampa Bay in line to host the wild-card winners.
The Sox chose to take the positive out of the night.
“When I issued those walks, I think that the game was taking me to a place that wasn’t the right one. So I just tried to take a deep breath and slow it down, and I was able to then take it from there,” Suarez said.
He struck out Yandy Díaz to end the second inning, stranding two runners on base. He got out of another jam in the third, a Chandler Simpson hard-hit line out to right and a strikeout of Jonny DeLuca to strand two more runners.
Suarez did it again in the fourth, helping his own cause by starting a nifty inning-ending double play, snaring Taylor Walls’s line drive to the mound and then throwing to first to double off Nick Fortes.
A clean fifth ended on a called third strike to Junior Caminero, but gave way to a messier sixth, with a leadoff walk to Ryan Vilade eventually leading Tracy to pull the plug as Suarez approached 100 pitches. But not before he struck out DeLuca to get the first out.
“He’s a very good competitor and a really good pitcher,” Tracy said, “that even when he’s got traffic, you trust that he’s going to find his way through it. . . . He walked five, but still almost completed six innings. He was very competitive with men on base.”
“I got traffic every single inning because of the walks, but I was able to limit damage today, and that was part of it,” Suarez said. “It was one of those nights that you didn’t have the command, but I was able to turn the page quickly and was able to get outs when I needed.”
Good as the escape act was, it’s all just staging for what comes next, a playoff berth the Red Sox could clinch on Saturday. Suarez was signed in part because of his experience in the postseason, earned across eight seasons with the Phillies. Suarez is 4-1 with a 1.48 ERA in 11 playoff appearances, which includes eight starts. He was the winner of Game 3 of the 2022 World Series, beating the eventual champion Astros with five shutout innings.
The Phillies also called on him to come out of the bullpen in Game 5 of the NLCS, and all he did was earn his first postseason save by getting two outs on two pitches, stranding the winning run and clinching the Series berth.
“When you get to this part of the season, not every outing is going to go perfectly. But he’s been there and done that as far as navigating his way through an outing and finding a way to strand base runners,” Tracy said. “The game’s not going to speed up on him. You know, even if he’s walked some and there’s some people on base, he doesn’t ever look like he speeds up. He just keeps making his pitches.”
Tara Sullivan is a Globe columnist. She can be reached at tara.sullivan@globe.com. Follow her @Globe_Tara.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Red Sox’ Ranger Suarez sets a career high in walks, but navigates tightrope in win
item.dc:creator: Sean McAdam
item.description: ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — It was by no means a textbook display of pitching. There were walks in each of the first four innings, and a career-high five in all. There were deep counts, lots of traffic and 98 pitches required in fewer than six innings. But what counts most is not the strikes or the 1-2-3 innings, but the final score. So a taut 4-2 victory for the Red Sox over the Tampa Bay Rays was, especially at this time of year, reward enough. "I think it was OK," shrugged Suarez afterward. "I had
item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — It was by no means a textbook display of pitching. There were walks in each of the first four innings, and a career-high five in all.
There were deep counts, lots of traffic and 98 pitches required in fewer than six innings.
But what counts most is not the strikes or the 1-2-3 innings, but the final score. So a taut 4-2 victory for the Red Sox over the Tampa Bay Rays was, especially at this time of year, reward enough.
"I think it was OK," shrugged Suarez afterward. "I had traffic every single inning because of the walks, but I was able to limit damage today and that was part of it."
Suarez had difficulty explaining how the walks piled up on him. It wasn't mechanical, and it wasn't the result of nibbling around the strike zone.
"I think it was one of those nights when I didn't have the command," he said. "But I was able to get outs when I needed."
The latter has always been his calling card. In an era when most starters unleash fastballs at 95 mph or better, Suarez thrives by mixing pitches, keeping hitters off balance and inducing soft contact.
On nights when he can't locate with precision, the margin for error slips further. But again, knowing how to get out of trouble is a mound skill in and of itself.
Suarez has used that talent particularly well in the postseason before, which is part of what motivated the Red Sox to offer him $130 million over five years last winter. Suarez isn't about to come unglued in Yankee Stadium in two weeks — or any other time he gets the ball in the postseason. His career ERA of 1.48 in the playoffs virtually guarantees that.
"He was very competitive with men on base," said interim manager Chad Tracy. "He lost some counts, was behind more counts today, but he wa able to really good pitches with people on base."
Even as he labored, Suarez was adding to a September resumé which has him 3-0 with 0.92 ERA in his last three outings while limiting opposing hitters to a .186 batting average.
No one knows exactly how or when Suarez will fit into Boston's postseason rotation. The assumption is that Sonny Gray will pitch Game 1, with either Payton Tolle or Suarez slotted for Game 2, and the remaining choice available for a winner-take-all Game 3.
Of course, the risk there is that a team may never get to its third starter if it doesn't win at least one of the first two games. That's part of the difficult decision the Red Sox will have to make before their wild card round gets underway.
Even with his history of success in October, Suarez isn't thinking too much about the postseason — not yet anyway.
"No, no,'' he said with a chuckle. "When we clinch, I'll be able to do that. But mathematically, we're not there yet, so I'm not thinking about that."
Suarez has one more start in the regular season, which he can treat as both a tuneup for himself and an audition for Game 2 in the best-of-three wild card round.,
"He's a very good competitor, a good pitcher that even when he gets traffic, you trust that he's going to find his way through it. He does that at times this year, so that's never a concern with him."

item.title: [Boston Herald] Roman Anthony’s big game puts Red Sox on precipice of clinching playoff bid
item.dc:creator: Mac Cerullo
item.description: Back in late June when the Red Sox sunk to their lowest depths, the idea that the club might still have a shot at reaching the postseason would have seemed hopelessly optimistic. Yet, here they are with a little over a week left to play in the regular season, and the Red Sox have all but punched their ticket to the playoffs. With their 4-2 win over the Tampa Bay Rays in Friday’s series opener, the Red Sox can now clinch a playoff spot as soon as Saturday. The club’s magic number, which stood at
item.content:encoded:
Back in late June when the Red Sox sunk to their lowest depths, the idea that the club might still have a shot at reaching the postseason would have seemed hopelessly optimistic.
Yet, here they are with a little over a week left to play in the regular season, and the Red Sox have all but punched their ticket to the playoffs.
With their 4-2 win over the Tampa Bay Rays in Friday’s series opener, the Red Sox can now clinch a playoff spot as soon as Saturday. The club’s magic number, which stood at three entering the night, will drop to either one or two depending on the outcome of Friday’s late game between the Rangers and Blue Jays.
A Rangers win would mean the Red Sox could clinch with a win on Saturday, while a Blue Jays win would necessitate a win and a Blue Jays loss.
Following a string of poor offensive performances, Friday got off to a much stronger start at the plate. Roman Anthony put the Red Sox in front with a solo home run to lead off the game, and after the Rays tied it up in the bottom half of the first, Anthony delivered again in the second with a go-ahead two-run single with the bases loaded off Rays starter Ian Seymour, an alumnus of St. John’s High School in Shrewsbury.
Anthony finished 2 for 4 with three RBI, and the Red Sox never looked back.
“Taking that first one is big,” Anthony told NESN’s Jahmai Webster postgame. “Any win you can get against a team like that it’s a great win, so it’s a great day.”
Anthony’s first-inning blast was smoked. Measured at 107.7 mph off the bat and traveling 438 feet, the solo home run to right field narrowly missed landing in Tropicana Field’s ray tank.
His two-run single in the second inning was hit even harder, coming off the bat at 108.7 mph. Anthony came through after Trevor Story and Caleb Durbin led off the inning with singles, Isiah Kiner-Falefa moved them into scoring position with a sacrifice bunt and Nate Eaton walked to load the bases.
It was doubly encouraging given Anthony’s recent struggles at the plate. After a hot start coming off the injured list, the outfielder came into Friday batting just .137 with one extra base hit over his past 12 games.
“I’ve been grinding, but that’s the beauty of this team,” Anthony said. “You’re never down and you’re never out.”
Jahmai Jones capped off the early offense with a solo shot to lead off the top of the third.
Tampa Bay scored its early run in the first after Yandy Diaz drew a leadoff walk, advanced to third on a Jonathan Aranda double and scored on a Junior Caminero groundout. But that was all the damage the Rays could do against Ranger Suarez, who allowed one run over 5 2/3 innings while falling one out short of his third consecutive quality start.
Suarez was uncharacteristically wild, walking five batters, but he limited the damage by allowing just three hits while striking out five.
The walks almost cost the Red Sox in the sixth inning.
Still leading by three, Suarez issued his fifth and final walk to lead off the sixth before recording two quick outs to finish his outing. But Wyatt Olds came on and immediately walked the first two men he faced, loading the bases and bringing the go-ahead run to the plate.
A brief mound visit followed, and Olds dug deep and struck out pinch hitter Jake Fraley to escape the inning unscathed.
“It was a weird game all the way around, we walked nine in total, Ranger walked five but still almost completed six innings and he was very competitive with men on base,” Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters in St. Petersburg. “He lost some counts and behind more counts today, but he was able to make really good pitches with people on base.”
Walks put the Red Sox in one more jam in the bottom of the ninth inning.
With Aroldis Chapman unavailable with a lat issue and Garrett Whitlock having pitched on Thursday, Erik Miller took the mound in the ninth and walked three men. He allowed a run to score on a Victor Mesa Jr. groundout, and the third walk to Caminero brought the winning run to the plate with two outs.
Miller struck out Ryan Vilade, but the ball got away from Connor Wong and the Rays batter reached safely to extend the game and load the bases. But Miller fought back and drew a game-ending groundout from Chandler Simpson, leaving the Rays 0 for 13 with runners in scoring position and 12 men left on base in spite of the nine walks issued by the Red Sox pitching staff.
While Miller has now walked seven batters over his last 3 1/3 innings, Tracy said he felt the left-hander looked much better on Friday despite all of the traffic.
“I thought he was way more competitive,” Tracy said. “Everything was around the zone, stuff was good, he was getting some swing and miss like he usually does so I take a lot of good out of that outing.”
The win marked Boston’s first at Tropicana Field this season, and the club hopes plenty more will follow in the days and weeks to come. The Rays have long been in the driver’s seat for the AL East title, and barring a complete collapse over the final week Tampa Bay should soon lock down the American League’s top seed and a bye to the divisional round.
That means if the Red Sox (84-70) can get past the Yankees in the AL Wild Card Series, they’d be headed right back to St. Petersburg to face the Rays in a rematch of the 2021 ALDS.
But first, the Red Sox hope to pop some bottles in the Tropicana Field visitor’s clubhouse before they fly back to Boston. First pitch on Saturday is scheduled for 4:10 p.m.

item.content:encoded:
Red Sox Insert Jahmai Jones into Lineup Against Rays Lefty
The Boston Red Sox placed designated hitter Jahmai Jones in the third spot in the starting lineup on Friday against Tampa Bay Rays left-hander Ian Seymour at Tropicana Field in St. Petersburg, Florida.
According to MLB.com, Jones sits in the heart of the order between outfielders Roman Anthony and Wilyer Abreu. Shortstop Trevor Story and first baseman Nick Sogard also feature in the top five positions for Boston.
Left-hander Ranger Suárez gets the start on the mound for Boston against Tampa Bay's Seymour. Seymour enters the contest holding a 9-6 record with a 4.27 ERA and 150 strikeouts on the season, according to official team statistics.
Boston manager Chad Tracy opted to stack the right-handed hitting Jones near the top of the batting order due to ongoing injuries and lack of availability among several key players, including Ceddanne Rafaela, Masataka Yoshida, Curtis Mead, and Willson Contreras.
According to MLB Trade Rumors, Boston acquired Jones off waivers on July 14 after the Detroit Tigers designated him for assignment, sending pitching prospect Jojo Ingrassia to Detroit as compensation.
Jones struggled with Detroit this season, batting .137 with a .221 slugging percentage across 105 plate appearances before his release. However, he has turned his season around in Boston, slashing .362/.464/.681 with three home runs and eight RBIs in 56 plate appearances.
Friday marks the 20th time overall this season that Jones has occupied the third spot in a starting lineup, having done so 19 times prior across his stints with Detroit and Boston. In those previous 35 plate appearances in the third spot, he posted a .219 batting average and a .661 OPS.
According to FanGraphs, the platoon splits support Boston's heavy usage of Jones against left-handed pitching. Across 138 plate appearances against lefties this year, Jones has recorded a .223 batting average, a .333 on-base percentage, and a .420 slugging percentage with five home runs, 15 walks, and 14 RBIs.
Conversely, Jones has registered just a .130 average in 23 at-bats against right-handed pitchers, with all five of his home runs this season coming exclusively against left-handers. He previously hit a two-run home run off Seymour during a July 18 matchup at Fenway Park.
Boston enters the three-game series against the American League East-leading Rays with an 83-70 record, holding the second AL Wild Card position and a five-game lead over the Cleveland Guardians. NESN reports Boston's magic number to clinch a postseason berth stands at three with nine games remaining on their schedule.

item.title: [MLB.com] Positive news on Contreras, Chapman tops list of injury updates
item.dc:creator: Ian Browne
item.description: ST. PETERSBURG – As they head into the final 10 days of the regular season, the Red Sox are monitoring a plethora of injuries to key players. Given that the Sox still hold firm possession of the second American League Wild Card spot and could clinch a berth as early as this weekend, the plan will be to operate conservatively in hopes of getting everyone healthy for the games that count the most. item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG – As they head into the final 10 days of the regular season, the Red Sox are monitoring a plethora of injuries to key players.
Given that the Sox still hold firm possession of the second American League Wild Card spot and could clinch a berth as early as this weekend, the plan will be to operate conservatively in hopes of getting everyone healthy for the games that count the most.
Here is an update on where things stand with those key players.
First baseman Willson Contreras
There was a big scare on Thursday night in Texas when the team’s most productive hitter this season was pelted on the top of his right hand with a pitch in the top of the eighth and immediately exited the game. Contreras said that in the moment, it felt like a fracture. Fortunately, X-rays taken at the ballpark were negative.
While interim manager Chad Tracy mentioned the possibility of follow-up imaging, there was none on Friday. Contreras didn’t have his hand taped and spent his share of time in the training room.
Where do things stand?
“Obviously, sore with some swelling,” Tracy said. “So nothing new other than just over the next couple of days, they'll work on treatment, on getting the swelling out, see if he can get grip strength back, and then we'll go from there. So just day to day.”
Could there still be additional scans?
“Not right now. Right now, with the initial one, they're optimistic,” said Tracy. “Just work on the swelling and see how he progresses over the next couple days, and then determine if they feel like they need more. But right now, they're just going to work on that.”
Closer Aroldis Chapman
When Garrett Whitlock closed Thursday’s win in Texas, it was obvious something was up with Chapman. It turns out he has been dealing with lat tightness he sustained while working out prior to Tuesday’s game.
Chapman downplayed the injury on Friday, saying the team is being conservative and that he felt healthy enough to play catch before the opener of the three-game series against the Rays. The Red Sox told him not to.
The lefty fireballer said he won’t pitch this weekend, but he expects to return during the final homestand, which starts on Tuesday.
“I’m not worried at all,” Chapman said. “From the first time I felt it to today, I feel very good. I was going to go out and throw, but the team wants to take it slow, and they want me to take my time.“
It is all about being 100% for the first game of the playoffs on Sept. 29, right?
“Yeah, of course,” said Chapman. “A hundred percent.”
Center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela
Boston’s All-Star center fielder hasn’t played since Sept. 2 due to a right quad strain. It sounds unlikely he’ll be able to play in a rehab game for Triple-A Worcester because that season ends on Sunday. But Tracy is confident with where Rafaela is at.
“I think he got close to 90% of his acceleration yesterday,” said Tracy. “So not ready yet, but he's moving quickly in the right direction, which is good. If he doesn’t play [for Worcester], there is a goal of getting him some live at-bats of some kind. You know, like live BP-type at-bats of some kind, plus the Trajekt. The important thing is that the running piece keeps going in the right direction.”
Left-hander Garrett Crochet
Boston’s ace, who has been out since April 25 due to a left shoulder injury, is still racing against the clock to try to pitch in relief during the postseason. His next step will be on Saturday, when he throws his second up-and-down bullpen session of the week at Fenway Park.
For Crochet to have any shot at pitching at the start of the postseason, he would have to start facing hitters by next week.
“I would say we're to the point where these next five days or so are going to be pretty telling,” said Tracy. “How does the side go, and what can we do with him early next week? And that'll give us a better idea of the answer to that question.”
Right-hander Tanner Houck
The righty will make the fourth and final appearance of his Minor League rehab assignment when he throws roughly 50 pitches for Worcester on Saturday. It’s possible Houck will get a tuneup or two in regular-season action for the Red Sox next week, which could give the club a better gauge if he’s a possibility to pitch in the playoffs. Houck had Tommy John surgery 13 months ago.

item.content:encoded:
RedSoxRoundtable's Zach Coe discusses the latest on a number of key injured Red Sox players. Be sure to join our FREE community over on RedSoxRoundtable.com!
Ahead of the Boston Red Sox series opener at Tropicana Field against the Tampa Bay Rays on Friday, interim manager Chad Tracy met with the media and provided updates on a number of injured Red Sox players.
Here's what you need to know:
All eyes were on the All-Star first baseman after Thursday night's win over the Texas Rangers. Contreras exited the game in the eighth inning after being hit by a pitch on the right-hand. According to MassLive.com's Chris Cotillo, Contreras told reporters after the game that the injury "felt" like a fracture. While initial X-Rays were negative, as the team learned with infielder Curtis Mead, that doesn't mean Contreras was completely out of the woods yet. According to MLB.com's Ian Browne, the team is waiting for swelling in the 34-year-old's hand to subside before testing his grip strength to determine if additional testing is needed.
Contreras is out of the lineup for Friday's series opener.
Crochet threw a 30-pitch up-and-down bullpen session on Tuesday back at Fenway Park, representing the most labor-intensive of the four throwing sessions the 27-year-old has done since restarting a throwing progression Aug. 3. According to WEEI's Rob Bradford, Crochet will throw another side session on Saturday as he continues to work his way back from left shoulder inflammation that has kept him out since April 29.
After turning to Garrett Whitlock to lock down Thursday's win, Tracy told reporters, including Cotillo, that Chapman was unavailable with LAT tightness. According to Bradford, Chapman said the injury popped up ahead of Tuesday's series opener in Texas and that he wasn't concerned about the injury, saying the latest he would return to the mound would be during the team's upcoming home stand, beginning on Tuesday night, if he doesn't make an appearance in Tampa.
Tyron Guerrero
After landing on the injured list on Sept. 1 with right shoulder inflammation. The 35-year-old flamethrower was expected to be activated when he was first eligible, ahead of Wednesday's game in Texas. However, after experiencing lower back tightness, the team delayed his activation. According to Bradford, Guerrero "felt fine" after throwing 20 pitches off the mound on Friday afternoon. However, it still remains unclear when he may be activated.
The 32-year-old outfielder landed on the injured list last Friday with a "right foot ligament injury" after getting it caught in the grates along the center field wall in the Sept. 8 loss to the Los Angeles Angels. As Bradford noted, White has been diagnosed with a ligament tear, likely ending his season.
White's injury seems to open the door for Spring Training standout Braiden Ward to join the Red Sox as a fourth outfielder/pinch runner in the playoffs.
Up next for the Sox
The Red Sox will look to carry the momentum from Thursday's come-from-behind win into the final road series of the year against the Rays. Ranger Suarez (7-4, 3.33 ERA) will get the start for the Red Sox opposite Ian Seymour (9-6, 4.27 ERA) for the Rays. First pitch from Tropicana Field is set for 7:10 p.m. ET.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Willson Contreras Injury Update Hints Red Sox Avoided Serious Issue
item.dc:creator: Patrick McAvoy; Unknown
item.description: The Boston Red Sox will not have Willson Contreras in the lineup on Friday night against the Tampa Bay Rays, but there is hope for the All-Star slugger after an early exit on Thursday night. item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox will not have Willson Contreras in the lineup on Friday night against the Tampa Bay Rays, but there is hope for the All-Star slugger after an early exit on Thursday night.
Contreras had to leave the club's series finale against the Texas Rangers on Thursday night after getting hit by a pitch on his hand. At the time, it was reported that his X-rays came back negative, but there was still some fear. Contreras himself spoke about the injury and said that it felt like a fracture while citing the fact that he previously had one.
Now, of course, it would've been great to see Contreras in Boston's lineup on Friday, but he hasn't been ruled out for the weekend and Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy shared that no new scans are currently planned, as shared on X by MassLive.com's Sean McAdam.
Willson Contreras Update
"Willson Contreras is out of the lineup, giving his hand some time to recover. Chad Tracy wouldn’t rule him out for the weekend, but Sox are being cautious. No new scans planned," McAdam wrote on X.
Again, it would've been great to see Contreras back in the lineup, but there are positives to take away from this update. First and foremost, the fact that more scans aren't currently planned is a sign of confidence from the club. Think back to Curtis Mead, for example. When he got hit on the wrist in his first game as a member of the Red Sox, his X-rays initially came back as negative. Then, the next day, it was shared that he actually had suffered a fractured wrist.
At this point, every time someone gets hit by a pitch on the wrist/hand, it immediately makes fans think about Mead. This process with Contreras is much more positive than it was with Mead. The fact that almost 24 hours later, the club hasn't ruled him out for the weekend and doesn't have more tests planned is a very good sign that he simply is dealing with a bruise, or something of that nature.
Boston needs Contreras if it wants to make a run this season. Things are wide open in the American League, especially in the wake of Aaron Judge being placed on the Injured List for the New York Yankees. Boston, New York and Tampa Bay are the top three contenders in the American League and with New York hurting, the top two contenders should be the Red Sox and the Rays. If Contreras returns over the weekend, Boston is going to be just fine.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox secured a major 4-3 victory over the Texas Rangers on Thursday night in their series finale, avoiding the sweep.
On Friday, they’ll start a weekend series against the American League-best Tampa Bay Rays, and ahead of the opener, Red Sox manager Chad Tracy made a notable lineup decision involving All-Star Willson Contreras after a pitch hit him on the hand Thursday.
Red Sox Announce Contreras Decision
X-rays came back negative after Thursday’s game on Contreras’ hand, fortunately. However, he is not in the starting lineup for the opener against Tampa Bay.
Starting at first base in place of Contreras will be Nick Sogard, who will bat second in the order behind leadoff hitter Roman Anthony.
Stepping into the three and four holes will be designated hitter Jahmai Jones and outfielder Wilyer Abreu.
Here’s the full Red Sox lineup:
Via Underdog MLB: “Red Sox 9/18 R. Anthony LF N. Sogard 1B J. Jones DH W. Abreu RF T. Story SS C. Durbin 3B I. Kiner-Falefa 2B N. Eaton CF C. Wong C R. Suarez SP.”

Contreras’ 2026 Season
In his first year with the Red Sox, Contreras has appeared in 129 games and recorded 68 runs, 123 hits, 27 home runs, and 81 RBIs across 446 at-bats while batting .276 with a .518 slugging percentage and a .905 OPS.
Looking at the Red Sox
Boston enters Friday night with an 83-70 overall record and sits on the verge of clinching a postseason bid. If they clinch, they’ll enter the playoffs as the second Wild Card team.
If the current standings hold, the Red Sox would travel to the Bronx to face the New York Yankees in a best-of-three Wild Card series.

item.title: [BoSox Injection] Aroldis Chapman injury news is the last thing Red Sox’s already-strained bullpen needs
item.dc:creator: Katie Manganelli
