Seeing Garrett Whitlock emerge from the bullpen to close a 4-3 game in the ninth inning only made fears worse. After the game, Boston announced that Chapman was
item.content:encoded:
Boston Red Sox fans were already going through it on Thursday night after Willson Contreras left the series finale against the Texas Rangers early after being hit by a pitch on the hand. Seeing Garrett Whitlock emerge from the bullpen to close a 4-3 game in the ninth inning only made fears worse.
Whitlock is no slouch, as Red Sox fans know, and he got through the ninth frame unscathed, but fans expect to see Aroldis Chapman in moments like that. After the game, Boston announced that Chapman was unavailable due to a lat issue.
Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy said in his September 17 postgame presser that Chapman has been dealing with lat tightness for a couple of days but that he's been improving lately. Boston has classified him as day-to-day and it will routinely check on his recovery progress to gauge his availability.
The best news from Tracy on Chapman is that the team will not place him on the injured list. The Sox's bullpen has been one of their deadliest weapons all season and Chapman with his 1.95 ERA, 34 saves, blistering velocity and unmatched consistency at 38 years old has been a huge part of that success.
Aroldis Chapman injury news is a blow the Red Sox's bullpen can't afford as the playoffs near
Still, having Chapman at anything less than 100 percent is dangerous this late in the season with the playoffs on the horizon. In a tight game, one slip-up in the ninth inning could lead to disaster.
The rest of the Red Sox's bullpen is hardly in its best shape. Justin Slaten's season ended following continued flexor issues and Tyron Guerrero is still on the IL bouncing back from shoulder inflammation. Erik Miller is also dealing with a mechanical issue that has severely impacted his command over his last two outings.
If Chapman's injury is as mild as Tracy is letting on and he doesn't need an IL stint, Boston might be able to avoid disaster. But it also needs Chapman's help to clinch its playoff spot in the first place. The offense is struggling to get out to enough of a lead that it doesn't need Chapman to hold a slim margin in the late innings, but that won't fly in the postseason, especially with an injured closer.
At least the Red Sox expect some relief reinforcements in the coming days. Tanner Houck and Garrett Crochet are working towards returns from long-term injuries in a relief role and they could take some pressure off the 'pen, but neither could fill Chapman's role.

item.content:encoded:
Alec Gamboa, who played for the Lotte Giants in the KBO League last year. He failed to re-sign with Lotte, but a year later he debuted in the major leagues and is aiming to make the postseason roster.
On the 18th (Korean time) at Globe Life Field in Arlington, Texas, in the game against the Texas Rangers, Gamboa came in with one out in the eighth inning and no runners on, recorded 2/3 of an inning, allowed one hit and no runs, and earned a hold. It was his second hold of the season.
That day Gamboa entered the game after Trevor Story hit a go-ahead three-run homer in the top of the eighth to put them up 4-3. Starter Sonny Gray pitched well with 6 1/3 innings, three hits (one home run), three walks, six strikeouts and three runs, and second pitcher Wyatt Alls recorded one inning, one strikeout and no runs.
Gamboa came in to face a left-handed batting lineup of Corey Seager and Josh Young. He gave up a single to the first batter, Seager, to right field. Later, he fell behind Josh Young 3-1 in the count but induced a shortstop grounder with a low 95.6-mph sinker, producing a double play to end the inning.
After recording his first hold in his debut by getting Lee Jung-hoo and others out in the Aug. 22 game against the San Francisco Giants, he recorded his second hold of the season. Gamboa's season performance is excellent. In 19 appearances he pitched 29 2/3 innings with 1 win, 2 holds, 1 save, a 1.21 ERA, a .216 batting average against and a 1.04 WHIP.
That day closer Aroldis Chapman could not take the mound because of trapezius muscle stiffness, and another lefty in the high-leverage group, Eric Miller, had earlier shown instability on the 17th against Texas by allowing three runs on 22 pitches in one inning. As a result, rookie right-hander Wyatt Alls and left-hander Gamboa had to take on the high-leverage roles, and setup man Garrett Whitlock had to assume the closer role. All of them then held the one-run lead.
Acting manager Chad Tracy praised Alls and Gamboa's high-leverage performances, saying, "They were really great. They were inserted suddenly into important situations. At times they had to take the mound with the lead, and they did really well."
Gamboa once again successfully passed a high-leverage test for the high-leverage group. Now the question is whether he can join Boston's postseason journey. Boston has a 83-70 record and sits second in the wild-card standings. They are five games ahead of the third-place Cleveland Guardians, so barring an upset they are all but certain to secure the 5 seed.
Over the Monster, which reports on Boston news, listed Gamboa in the "pitchers who need to prove themselves" spot while predicting the postseason roster. The outlet said, "He is a player who had a pleasantly surprising performance this year. He even made two starts as an opener. In recent weeks the bullpen has had injuries, and combined with his own performance, he has risen to the point of being used in higher-stakes, high-leverage situations."
Closers Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, Eric Miller, Tyrone Guerrero and Garrett Crochet are confirmed. It is likely that one more left-handed reliever will be added and the rest filled with right-handers.
They went on to say, "If Aroldis Chapman, Eric Miller and Garrett Crochet are the confirmed left-handed bullpen pieces, the final left-handed spot could be a competition between Hobani Moran and Gamboa," and added, "If I had to pick the final four now, I would choose Brayan Bello, Tanner Houck, Moran and Gamboa," predicting they would make the postseason roster.
Boston regional outlet MassLive also highlighted the performances of Gamboa and Alls on the 17th, saying, "He seized an unexpected opportunity this year, expanded his standing, and his entry into the postseason roster race—which would have been hard to imagine just a few weeks ago—is worthy of high praise," introducing that Gamboa has performed well enough to be included on the postseason roster.
Gamboa was drafted by the Los Angeles Dodgers in the ninth round, 281st overall, in the 2019 draft. But he couldn't break through the Dodgers' deep minor league system, and last year he joined the KBO League's Lotte Giants as a replacement player and delivered a sensational performance.
He had an especially strong performance, including being named player of the month for June, but fatigue accumulated late in the season and elbow pain caused him to miss several turns in the rotation, preventing a smooth finish. His KBO League stats were 19 games, 108 innings, 7 wins, 8 losses and a 3.58 ERA.
Although Gamboa failed to re-sign with Lotte, he said of going to Lotte, "It was a good opportunity to show myself elsewhere. I wanted to experience a bigger and new environment than Triple-A in the U.S. I believed I would show good pitching there, return to the U.S. and seize another opportunity," and added, "Before going to Korea I had never been abroad. Experiencing another country, seeing how polite the people there are and how much they love baseball, and seeing what style of baseball they play was really fun," saying it was an opportunity that lifted his spirits.
Was failing to re-sign with Lotte a blessing in disguise? After signing a minor league deal with Boston he made an emotional big league debut and now stands on the verge of making the postseason roster. Gamboa is becoming a symbol of a life turnaround.

As it turns out, he is. After c
item.content:encoded:
When the Boston Red Sox lost shortstop Trevor Story to an injury earlier this year, one big question was how they were going to replace him. Interim manager Chad Tracy used a couple of different players who more than held things down until the veteran was going to return.
When Story was eligible to return, Andruw Monasterio found himself as the odd man out at shortstop. However, Story had to prove that he was healthy enough to hold down the job late in the season.
As it turns out, he is. After coming up clutch on Thursday night, Story didn't mince words about the noise that there is outside the locker room about him.
Boston Red Sox Shortstop Trevor Story Drops Honest Quote on Outside Noise
Trailing 3-0 against the Texas Rangers on Thursday night in Arlington, Boston was staring at being swept as the game moved into the late innings. After they plated a run in the top of the seventh on a Roman Anthony fielder's choice.
In the top of the eighth, Story stepped up to the plate with two runners on and one out. Story crushed a curveball from Texas' Jacob Latz for a three-run home run and 4-3 lead. The Red Sox got the final six outs to secure a one-run win. After the game, Story didn't mince words about the outside noise and hearing it.
"I'm not really motivated by outside noise, but you hear it," said Story, per Alex Speier of the Boston Globe. "I try to use it in the way that fits me best. The point of getting the surgery was to come back and try to be the player that I know I can be, and it's starting to show."
Halfway through the month of September, Story is slashing .327/.339/.473 in September with one home run and six RBIs.
"He's been great," Tracy said, per Perla Paredes of MLB.com. "He's got a hit in every game but one. That was a hell of an at-bat against a really good pitcher in a really big spot and a huge swing. Obviously needed a win, but all the credit to him.
"You're one pitch away in a spot like that, where he can change a game, like we saw it numerous times in the second half of last year. So, like I said, it was a massive swing."
Trevor Story Looking To Find Swing Before Playoffs
There are nine games for the Red Sox before the playoffs begin. Boston is likely headed for an American League wild-card series against the New York Yankees. The series for the second straight year will be in the Bronx.
Boston has a three-game series against the first-place Tampa Bay Rays this weekend in Central Florida. They then close out the season with a pair of three-game series at home against the Cleveland Guardians and Chicago Cubs.
Finishing the regular season strong will be key. Boston has struggled in September and is limping into the playoffs. A healthy Story could be key for Boston come postseason baseball.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Boston Red Sox Shortstop Trevor Story Has Blunt Quote After Win Over Texas Rangers appeared first on HEAVY.

item.content:encoded:
ARLINGTON, Texas — Trevor Story, who is from Irving, hit a go-ahead, three-run home run off Jacob Latz in the eighth inning Thursday night. The Boston Red Sox beat the Texas Rangers, 4-3, at Globe Life Field and kept Texas from a three-game sweep.
The Colorado Rockies drafted Story 45th overall in 2011 out of Irving High School, where he hit .488 as a senior. He had committed to LSU.
Boston trailed 3-1 entering the eighth. Story reached down for Latz’s second straight low curveball, an 80.3 mph pitch, and lined it over the wall in left-center field. It was his fourth home run of the season and his first since May 13. The loss dropped Texas one game behind the Houston Astros in the AL West.
The challenges of the year were part of it for Story.
“It meant a lot,” Story said. “Just the challenges of the year and all that, but just trying to be present in the moment to help the team win. And today was a good one, that was fun.”
Trevor Story Has A Hit in 15 Of 16 Games Since Sports Hernia Surgery
Boston placed Story on the 10-day injured list May 16 with a sports hernia that had bothered him since the spring. He had surgery later that month and was transferred to the 60-day IL on June 4. Since returning Aug. 30, Story has a hit in all but one of his 16 games, and he is riding an eight-game hitting streak. He is slashing .327/.339/.473 in September.
Story tries to use the outside noise in a way that fits him.
“It’s tough because I’m not really motivated by outside noise or anything,” Story explained. “But you hear it, and I try to use it in a way that fits me best. Like we said, that was the point of getting the surgery, to come back and try to be the player that I know I can be, and I’m starting to show that.”
Chad Tracy Says Trevor Story Delivered ‘A Massive Swing’
Jakob Junis set up the at-bat by walking Wilyer Abreu and hitting Willson Contreras to open the eighth. Latz then struck out Adley Rutschman. Story had just missed Latz’s fastball a couple of times earlier in the at-bat.
“I was looking for something just to put in play,” Story said. “[Latz has] a good fastball and just missed it a couple times, and I felt good about that. Just trying to get something in the zone and get on top of it, and was able to drive one out.”
Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy said he saw Story change games that way numerous times in the second half of last season.
“He’s been great,” Tracy said. “He’s got a hit in every game but one. That was a hell of an at-bat against a really good pitcher in a really big spot and a huge swing. Obviously needed a win, but all the credit to him.”
“You’re one pitch away in a spot like that, where he can change a game, like we saw it numerous times in the second half of last year,” Tracy continued. “So, like I said, it was a massive swing.”
Boston (83-70) holds the second AL Wild Card spot, five games ahead of the Cleveland Guardians. The Red Sox open a three-game series against the Tampa Bay Rays on Friday and could clinch a postseason berth there.

item.content:encoded:
Aroldis Chapman has not pitched since Sunday, and when he was not used with a one-run lead in the ninth inning on Thursday, interim manager Chad Tracy was asked for an explanation.
Tracy said that Chapman was dealing with lat tightness. With the regular season winding down, that is not something that any Boston Red Sox fan wants to hear.
"We're going to be conservative with (it)," Tracy said postgame, per MLB.com's Perla Paredes. "It's getting better, but we're going to make sure it gets there. That's why he wasn't available tonight."
The good news is that Tracy said it's getting better. The Red Sox have Garrett Whitlock, who is more than capable of closing games, and some more bullpen reinforcements potentially on the way. However, Chapman has been one of the most dominant closers in baseball throughout his career, especially in Boston.
Chapman was the American League Reliever of the Year last year, posting a 1.17 ERA in 67 games. This year, he has a 1.95 ERA in 52 games and has 34 saves. The Red Sox's duo of him and Whitlock figures to be very important in October, but the 38-year-old needs to be healthy for that.
"Obviously, you guys know how diligent he is about his prep and getting in and getting treatment. So we'll just monitor it day to day," Tracy said.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox are getting ready for the postseason, and their starting third baseman has been playing hurt.
Caleb Durbin dislocated his pinky earlier in the year and then reinjured it. However, he has continued to play, swing a good bat, and play elite defense at third base. He received X-rays after the original injury and the reinjury, but he was told there was no fracture and he could play if he could handle the pain.
"It doesn't quite straighten or bend all the way," Durbin told the Boston Globe's Alex Speier.
Durbin started the season off terribly at the plate. However, since May 28, he is slashing .285/.371/.444 with 12 home runs and 28 total extra-base hits. He does not miss games, and has lived up to the reputation he built in Milwaukee.
"There really is kind of a joint understanding (with the team) that we'll get it looked at at the end of the season if we have to, because (whatever the diagnosis is), it's not going to impact my decision to play at all," he said.
Durbin said he is not sure if he will require surgery in the offseason, but for now, he is focused on helping the Red Sox win. The team was essentially headed for a lost season, but Chad Tracy has turned things around. Durbin turning his season around has also played a huge role in that.
More MLB: Red Sox's Willson Contreras Comments On Injury After X-Rays Show No Fracture

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Red Sox’s Willson Contreras in injury scare with Yankees’ wild-card showdown looming

item.description: The Red Sox had a scare on Thursday night when Willson Contreras was hit by a pitch on his right hand in the eighth inning of Boston's 4-3 win over the Rangers. Contreras was struck on a first-pitch sinker from Jakob Junis in the eighth inning. He walked to first base showing clear signs of pain before a trainer came to examine him and he went to the dugout. Just a couple of batters later, Trevor Story hit a go-ahead three-run home run to help the Sox avoid the sweep by Texas. Postgame, interim
item.content:encoded:
The Red Sox had a scare on Thursday night when Willson Contreras was hit by a pitch on his right hand in the eighth inning of Boston's 4-3 win over the Rangers.
Contreras was struck on a first-pitch sinker from Jakob Junis in the eighth inning. He walked to first base showing clear signs of pain before a trainer came to examine him and he went to the dugout. Just a couple of batters later, Trevor Story hit a go-ahead three-run home run to help the Sox avoid the sweep by Texas.
Postgame, interim manager Chad Tracy said Contreras's hand was bruised with a little swelling, but X-rays came back negative. Tracy said the team will "take it day to day" with Contreras.
As the regular season winds down, the Red Sox will have to manage their injuries in their pursuit of a deep October run. They open their weekend series against the red-hot Rays in Tampa on Friday night, possibly without their most consistent hitter.
Contreras said he probably won't play in the series opener.
Contreras told the Boston Globe he originally felt like he had fractured his hand, an injury he's experienced before.
"Sore. Painful. My hand was numb for like five minutes," Contreras said. "That was the reason I came out of the game. I have fractured, before, the same hand. It felt like a fracture. Thankfully, it's not a fracture on the top of the bone."
Contreras also expressed frustration over being frequently hit by pitches during his time in the big leagues. This season, Contreras ranks third in the majors in hit-by-pitches.
"If nobody does anything about it, I'm going to keep getting hit. That's the way I see it. That's it," he explained.
"I mean, sore bones in the hands — might take two days, might take a week, might take ten days. I don't know. We'll see how I feel after taking this plane to Tampa."
Should the Rays come out on top of the AL East, the Red Sox will likely face the Yankees in the AL Wild Card series, one in which they'll need their best hitters at 100% against one of the top pitching staffs in the league.

Obviously, it's not a fun experience, and Contreras is getting kind of tired of it. "A lot of people might say that I hit on top of the plate, but I'm seeing a lot of players hit on top of the
item.content:encoded:
Boston Red Sox first baseman Willson Contreras was hit in the hand by a pitch on Thursday and exited the game early.
Contreras has been hit by a pitch 24 times this year, ranking third in all of baseball. He has been known for getting hit a lot throughout his career, but this year marks a new career best. Obviously, it's not a fun experience, and Contreras is getting kind of tired of it.
"A lot of people might say that I hit on top of the plate, but I'm seeing a lot of players hit on top of the plate. They don't get hit like me," Contreras said after the game, per The Boston Globe's Tim Healey. "It's really frustrating because I just came back from the IL (because of a hamstring strain), and this might take days. I mean, sore bones in the hands — might take two days, might take a week, might take 10 days."
The most frustrating part is that the Red Sox don't have much runway left for him to heal. The regular season is almost over, and the Red Sox will need Contreras in the wild card round.
X-rays were negative for Contreras, according to Chad Tracy, but as fans have seen this year, that does not mean he is in the clear. He will likely get additional imaging done.
"It felt like a fracture," Contreras said. "I'm just frustrated."
More MLB: Dodgers Magic Number: How Close Are Dodgers To Securing Bye After Winning NL West?

item.title: [MassLive.com] Johan Oviedo hopes to ‘have a shot to help the [Red Sox]’ any way he can

item.content:encoded:
WORCESTER -- Johan Oviedo is racing against the clock to get back and help the Red Sox.
Making his first rehab start since hitting the injured list on April 3 with a flexor sprain in his right elbow, Oviedo topped out at 98.5 mph with his sinker and went 2 1/3 innings.
The righty allowed one run on two hits and a walk, striking out four. The three swings and misses he recorded came on his four-seamer.
He was efficient, using 30 pitches to reach the third inning.
“(I was) super excited to get the first one out,” Oviedo said. “I just feel blessed, and hopefully I can continue to get healthy.”
Oviedo averaged just under 96 mph with both his four-seamer and his sinker, but said he wasn’t worried about what the radar was reading.
“Velo has never really been a concern,” Oviedo said. “It’s more about health-wise, how the arm feels. It’s more about making sure that my body moves well. If the body’s moving well, I know the velo will be there. But I mean, it’s always a good sign to see good velo on the radar.”
Oviedo was acquired by the Red Sox in December in a five-player deal that sent Jhostynxon Garcia to the Pirates. He only got to make one appearance before landing on the injured list in April.
“You always have great dreams about playing for a team like (Boston) with a lot of history,” Oviedo said. “You want to fill up your spot, and not being available to help the team from the beginning definitely has been a challenge for me. If I still have a shot to help the team in any way, in the last few weeks of the season or the playoffs, I’m just trying to be ready.”
Primarily a starter throughout his career, it’s possible Oviedo may not have enough time to stretch out as a starter before the Red Sox need him, and he says he’s open to however the team could use him.
“I’m more than open to fill any role, and not finish the season on the IL,” Oviedo said. “It’s definitely not the plan for any pitcher. But all I’m trying to do right now is be healthy and be available for the team if they need me.
Oviedo is no stranger to rehabbing; he missed all of 2024 after undergoing Tommy John surgery but returned to make nine starts with a 3.57 ERA in 2025.
“(There were) definitely a lot of feelings,” Oviedo said about making his first appearance in a game in months. “But as a professional, you’re trying to keep everything under control, put your feelings in balance. In the past, on the first outing, you [might] try to do more than what you can do. So today I was trying to keep it the same, treat it like another live BP in Florida.”
Oviedo is running out of days to pitch in games as he tries to get back to the major-league team, as the WooSox’ season ends on Sunday and the opportunity for in-game rehab outings ends with it. The pitcher said he wasn’t aware of what the plan was going forward and whether he’d be part of the Red Sox’ taxi squad.
With nine games left in the Red Sox’ season, there’s a chance the next time Oviedo is with the team is in the postseason,
“I’ve been on a playoff roster before but never pitched,” Oviedo said. “So it’s definitely one of the dreams that I want to accomplish. If Boston will give me that chance, if the team needs me, hopefully I can be ready for it.”
Notes
- Braiden Ward, who has been a topic of conversation since Red Sox manager Chad Tracy brought up his name as a potential late-season call-up, stole his 60th base of the season on Wednesday. Ward leads the International League in stolen bases and holds the WooSox record in steals. He’s 60-for-69 (87%) on attempts this season.
“Speed kills, and it never slumps,” WooSox manager Iggy Suarez said. “Any time you have speed like that, it can change the game; it can be a pain.”
- Tanner Houck is set to pitch for the WooSox again on Saturday after striking out the side in an inning of work on Tuesday for Worcester.
Performance of the Week
As the season winds down for Worcester, Allan Castro is heating up. The outfielder has bashed five home runs in 15 games this month, including two multi-home-run games over the last week. Castro’s two home runs and four RBI propelled the WooSox to a come-from-behind win on Wednesday.
Castro’s hot streak boosts his season slash line to .251/.325/.387 with 16 doubles, 14 home runs, and a triple.
What’s Next
The 2026 season wraps up over the weekend with three final games against the Durham Bulls. Sunday will feature a pre-game meet-the-team autograph party.
The WooSox aren’t officially eliminated from postseason contention, but need a whole lot to go right for them to clinch over the three teams currently above them in the standings with three games to go.

Got him on the top hand as he turned through on his right hand. So some swelling, and we'll just take it day to day.” Wilyer Ab
item.content:encoded:
ARLINGTON – Red Sox first baseman Willson Contreras exited Thursday’s 4-3 win against the Rangers after being hit by a pitch on his right hand in the eighth inning. X-rays were negative, and Contreras is considered day to day.
“He's got a bruise on his hand and some swelling,” interim manager Chad Tracy said postgame. “So we'll just take it day to day and see how he is. Got him on the top hand as he turned through on his right hand. So some swelling, and we'll just take it day to day.”
Wilyer Abreu worked a six-pitch walk to lead off the frame before Contreras was struck on the hand by a 92.3 mph sinker from Jakob Junis.
Contreras went to the ground in pain before getting back to his feet and making his way toward first base, where Abreu helped steady him. Tracy and a member of the training staff emerged from the dugout, and Contreras left the game shortly after.
“[It’s feeling] sore, painful,” Contreras said. “My hand was numb for like, I'll say five minutes. That was the reason why I came out of the game. I had fractures before in the same hand. It felt like a fracture. Thankfully, it was not a fracture on the top of the bone. … I don’t know, I'm just frustrated.”
The injury scare came just four days after Contreras was activated from the 10-day IL. He had been sidelined since Aug. 31 with a left hamstring strain before returning to Boston’s lineup Sunday against the Royals.
“[Junis] apologized to me. I mean, that was nice of him,” Contreras said. “He was trying to pitch inside like everybody else. A lot of people might say that I hit on top of the plate, but I'm seeing a lot of players [that] hit on top of the plate. They don't get hit like me.
“It's really frustrating because I just came back from [the IL], and this might take days. I mean, sore bones in hands might take two days, might take a week, might take 10 days. I don't know. We'll see how I feel after taking this plane to Tampa.”
The 34-year-old said he was unsure whether he would be able to play Friday as the Red Sox open a three-game series against the Rays.
“If nobody [does] anything about it, I am going to keep getting hit,” Contreras said. “That’s the way I see it. That’s it.”
Contreras has set career highs in home runs (27), RBIs (81) and OPS+ (155 entering Thursday) in his first season with Boston. He hit a two-run homer in Wednesday's loss to the Rangers, the 199th home run of his career.

item.content:encoded:
Red Sox news: Aroldis Chapman dealing with concerning injury with playoffs approaching appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
In signature 2026 Boston Red Sox fashion, they rallied late and completed a comeback from three runs down against the Texas Rangers after they scored three runs in the eighth to take a 4-3 lead they would not relinquish. But even with the Red Sox facing a save situation in the bottom of the ninth, it wasn't closer Aroldis Chapman who came off the bullpen to shut the door on the Rangers.
Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy rolled with Garrett Whitlock in the bottom of the ninth, and Whitlock responded with a save, improving Boston to 83-70 on the season. After the game, Tracy revealed that Chapman wasn't available on the night anyway as the hard-throwing lefty is currently dealing with a "lat issue", as per Tim Healey of the Boston Globe.
Tracy added that the Red Sox are going to be "conservative" with utilizing Chapman off the pen to end the regular season, as keeping him healthy for the postseason is going to be important for this team.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
Chapman last made an appearance for the Red Sox on the 13th of September in a 4-1 win over the Kansas City Royals. While he did allow two walks in that save situation, he made up for it by striking the side, making it look as though he wasn't dealing with any injury.
Nonetheless, the Red Sox, now armed with a seven-game cushion over the AL Wild Card cutoff line, have the luxury anyway to bring Chapman along slowly.
The Red Sox also have other injury matters to deal with. According to Healey, Tracy also said that first baseman Willson Contreras, who recently returned to the lineup (returning on September 13 against the Royals), is dealing with a bruised right hand and is currently day-to-day. The good news for Boston is that his X-rays turned out negative.
With the Red Sox on the cusp of sealing a postseason spot, they can afford to do whatever it takes to keep their core players healthy so that they can trot out their best squad come postseason time.

item.content:encoded:
Chapman day to day as Red Sox monitor lat tightness
This browser does not support the video element.
ARLINGTON -- Red Sox closer Aroldis Chapman was unavailable to pitch in Boston’s 4-3 win over the Rangers on Thursday at Globe Life Field due to lat tightness and is considered day to day.
“We're going to be conservative with [it],” interim manager Chad Tracy said postgame. “It's getting better, but we're going to make sure it gets there. That's why he wasn't available tonight.”
According to Tracy, Chapman has been dealing with the tightness for the last couple of days, so the team will continue to evaluate him.
“Obviously, you guys know how diligent he is about his prep and getting in and getting treatment. So we'll just monitor it day to day,” Tracy said.
On Thursday, Garrett Whitlock came in to close out the game, getting a groundout to first, issuing a walk and inducing a 6-4-3 double play to end it.
“[Whitlock is] great,” Tracy said. “He's reliable. He's done it before. If Chappie's down, he's very reliable in any spot we put him in.”
Through 51 games, Chapman owns a 1.95 ERA and a 1.14 WHIP, with hitters batting .190 against him. His 34 saves are tied for third in the AL and tied for fifth in the Majors. He is MLB’s all-time leader in relief strikeouts with 1,399.
Chapman’s absence Thursday was the latest injury concern for a Red Sox team that has had to rely on its depth throughout the season, with eight pitchers currently on the IL. Despite the injuries, Chapman has been impressed by the way younger players have responded when given opportunities.
This browser does not support the video element.
“They’ve come in because of all the injuries we’ve had, and they’ve been able to do an excellent job,” Chapman said in Spanish on Wednesday. “Now, some players have also returned from their injuries, but because of their youth and the limited playing time they’ve had, they’re doing a very good job with what has been asked of them.
“We always keep playing until the end because you never know what can happen, but [to see that from them] keeps me positive all the time.”

item.title: [MassLive.com] Why was Aroldis Chapman unavailable for Red Sox in win? Chad Tracy explains injury

item.description: ARLINGTON, Texas — When Trevor Story hit his clutch three-run homer to flip a two-run deficit into a one-run lead Thursday against the Rangers, interim manager Chad Tracy didn’t rush to get his two highest-leverage bullpen arms instantly ready. That’s because one of them was unavailable due to a nagging — and previously undisclosed — injury. With Boston suddenly up, 4-3, Tracy used a pair of rookies (righty Wyatt Olds and lefty Alec Gamboa) to pitch the eighth, then turned things over to righty
item.content:encoded:
ARLINGTON, Texas — When Trevor Story hit his clutch three-run homer to flip a two-run deficit into a one-run lead Thursday against the Rangers, interim manager Chad Tracy didn’t rush to get his two highest-leverage bullpen arms instantly ready. That’s because one of them was unavailable due to a nagging — and previously undisclosed — injury.
With Boston suddenly up, 4-3, Tracy used a pair of rookies (righty Wyatt Olds and lefty Alec Gamboa) to pitch the eighth, then turned things over to righty Garrett Whitlock in the ninth. For at least one night, Whitlock took the job of closer Aroldis Chapman, who has a tight lat muscle.
“He’s just dealing with some lat tightness we’re going to be conservative with,” Tracy said. “It’s getting better, but we’ve got to make sure it gets there. That’s why he wasn’t available tonight.”
Tracy said Chapman — who last pitched Saturday against the Royals — has been dealing with the injury for “a couple of days.” Asked if an injured list stint was possible for the All-Star, Tracy said: “We’re not doing that right now.”
“We’re just going to keep monitoring it and see where he’s at each day,” Tracy said. “Obviously, you know how diligent he is about his prep and getting in and getting treatment, so we’re just monitoring day-to-day.”
Chapman, 38, has had another stellar season in Boston, tallying 34 saves to go along with a 1.95 ERA and 68 strikeouts in 50 ⅔ innings over 52 games. He was one of two key Red Sox players with an injury concern Thursday; first baseman Willson Contreras left the game in the eighth inning after being hit on top of his right hand with a pitch.
Olds, who has a 1.23 ERA and 19 strikeouts in his first 12 MLB appearances since debuting last month, relieved Sonny Gray with one out in the seventh inning and the Sox trailing by two. He got two quick outs before Story’s three-run blast put Boston up 4-3. Olds got Ezequiel Duran to pop out to start the eighth before Gamboa entered for the left-on-left matchup against Corey Seager. Seager singled but Gamboa got Josh Jung to ground into an inning-ending double play five pitches later.
“They were awesome,” Tracy said. “Getting thrust into a big spot, going back out anyways, and then all of the sudden you’re going out with a lead. They did an amazing job.”
Whitlock then recorded his fourth save of the year, needing 12 pitches and getting a similar 6-4-3 double play to end the game.
“He’s great,” Tracy said. “He’s reliable. He’s done it before if Chappy’s down.”

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox removed first baseman Willson Contreras from Thursday’s 4-3 win against the Texas Rangers at Globe Life Field in Arlington, Texas, after he was hit in the hand by a 92.3 mph sinker from Jakob Junis in the eighth inning.
Following the game, Red Sox manager Chad Tracy said that Contreras suffered a bruised right hand and is day to day.
From Tim Healy of the Boston Globe on X: Willson Contreras has a bruised right hand, Chad Tracy said. He is day to day. X-rays were negative.
Contreras was asked about the injury after the game.
Boston Red Sox 1B Willson Contreras Makes Statement on Injury Following Win Over Rangers
Via Chris Cotillo on X: Willson Contreras: “Sore. Painful. My hand was numb for like five minutes. That was the reason I came out of the game. I have fractured, before, the same hand. It felt like a fracture. Thankfully, it’s not a fracture on the top of the bone. I’m just frustrated.”
Contreras went 1-for-3 with a single and a strikeout in Thursday’s win.
The Red Sox acquired Contreras from the St. Louis Cardinals over the offseason. He is under contract through 2027 and has a 2028 club option worth $20 million.
Contreras, 34, is having a spectacular first season with Boston, slashing .276/.387/.518 with 27 home runs and 81 RBI over 129 games.
Recapping Boston’s 4-3 Win Over Rangers
Trevor Story hit a three-run home run in the eighth inning as the Red Sox beat the Rangers 4-3 on Thursday.
Sonny Gray allowed three earned runs on three hits and three walks while striking out six over 6 1/3 innings.
Rangers designated hitter Josh Jung hit a solo home run in the first inning, giving Texas a 1-0 lead.
Danny Jansen hit an RBI single in the second inning. Evan Carter followed with an RBI sac bunt, increasing the Rangers’ lead to 3-0.
The Red Sox scored their first run of the game on a throwing error from Nicky Lopez in the second inning. Then Story delivered the big hit in the eighth inning.
The Rangers used seven pitchers in the game. Cody Bradford pitched the most of any of them, hurling 4 1/3 scoreless innings.

item.title: [Boston Herald] Trevor Story’s late home run helps Red Sox flip script on Rangers
item.dc:creator: Mac Cerullo
item.description: This has been a rough stretch for the Red Sox offense, which has effectively turned into a pumpkin after a torrid two months this summer. item.content:encoded:
This has been a rough stretch for the Red Sox offense, which has effectively turned into a pumpkin after a torrid two months this summer. This week in particular the bats have fallen silent, and for much of Thursday night the Red Sox looked like they were headed toward a discouraging series sweep at the worst possible time.
Things took an especially grim turn when Willson Contreras left the game in the eighth inning after being hit in the hand by a pitch, but while the specter of his absence will loom over the club in the days to come, Trevor Story once again proved that you can never count this Red Sox team out.
The veteran shortstop came through with a go-ahead three-run home run in the top of the eighth inning, flipping the script and giving the Red Sox a badly needed 4-3 win to avoid a sweep at the hands of the Texas Rangers.
Story’s shot came with one out against Rangers closer Jacob Latz, completing a three-run comeback and cutting Boston’s magic number to clinch a playoff spot to three with nine games remaining.
“To steal that last one is huge,” Story told NESN’s Jahmai Webster postgame. “It’s momentum we can ride out into Tampa.”
Prior to Story’s home run, Thursday was shaping up to be among the club’s worst losses of the season.
A hallmark of the offense’s struggles early in the year was a lot of empty, uncompetitive at-bats, tons of swing and miss and a general inability to make good contact. Even with the Rangers opting for a bullpen game led by Cody Bradford, whose fastball averages just 88.6 mph, the Red Sox couldn’t square anything up.
The Red Sox only managed two hits through the first five innings, both singles in the fourth inning. That put runners at the corners with two outs, but Jarren Duran grounded out to squander the opportunity.
It was a similar story in the sixth, when Wilyer Abreu singled and Adley Rutschman finally did some damage with a ground-rule double into the left-field gap. Had the ball stayed in play, Abreu probably would have scored, but instead the Red Sox had two men in scoring position for Story, who worked a full count and struck out to end the threat.
The offense did nothing to pick up Sonny Gray, who wasn’t perfect but did everything he could to keep the Red Sox in the game.
The veteran right-hander allowed a solo home run to Josh Jung with two outs in the first, and in the second he walked the first two batters of the inning, both of whom came around to score on an RBI bloop single by Danny Jansen and a run-scoring squeeze bunt by Evan Carter.
Gray settled down afterward and retired 14 of the last 16 batters he faced from the second inning into the seventh. He was charged with three runs over 6 1/3 innings and limited the Rangers to three hits and three walks with six strikeouts.
“I thought he was awesome,” Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy said. “The only blemish was the two walks, we kind of walked ourselves into the part of their lineup where they can play baseball a little bit with bunts and they drop a flare into center and there’s a safety squeeze, outside of that, that was a really, really good effort.”
Even when the Red Sox finally scored in the top of the seventh, they did so without recording a hit. Nate Eaton and Caleb Durbin led off with consecutive walks and Eaton advanced to third after Nick Sogard hit a rocket of a fly out to the center field wall. But with one out and a chance to fight back into the game, Roman Anthony grounded into a run-scoring fielder’s choice to make it 3-1. He advanced to second after the Rangers threw away the double-play attempt, but Mickey Gasper grounded out to end the inning.
Then came the eighth.
Once again the Red Sox got two men on base right away, with Abreu drawing a leadoff walk before Contreras was hit in the right hand by a pitch. He immediately left the game with the trainer and was replaced at first by Isiah Kiner-Falefa, but while the Red Sox worried about their slugger, the Rangers pulled Jakob Junis for their closer Latz, who has been among the most dominant closers in the American League this year.
Latz drew a pop out from Rutschman, but then Story stepped up to the plate and everything changed.
“You see one of our guys keeled over holding his hand and you’re down in the dumps seeing that and moments later the whole dugout erupts,” Tracy said. “We haven’t been doing much offensively for a few days and to get a swing right there and feel like you steal a game, it was enormous. Big emotion swing.”
With the lead in hand, Wyatt Olds and Alec Gamboa pitched a scoreless eighth, and with Aroldis Chapman unavailable, Garrett Whitlock came on for the ninth and locked down the save for the win. Story and Sogard turned inning-ending double plays in both the eighth and the ninth to ensure the Rangers couldn’t mount one last comeback.
“Good teams find a way to win and we’ve been doing that in the second half and that’s kind of who you become,” Story said. “And you feel that momentum, you feel that vibe around the game and we never give up.”
X-rays negative, Chapman day-to-day
The Red Sox got some good news postgame when X-rays on Contreras’ hand came back negative.
“He’s got a bruise on the hand and some swelling,” Tracy said. “So we’ll just take it day to day and see how he is.”
Tracy also confirmed that Chapman has been dealing with some lat tightness for the past few days and they are taking a conservative approach.
“It’s getting better but have to make sure it gets there, that’s why he wasn’t available tonight,” Tracy said, adding that an IL stint isn’t being considered for Chapman right now.

item.title: [Boston Herald] Red Sox slugger leaves game after being hit by pitch in hand
item.dc:creator: Mac Cerullo
item.description: The Red Sox held their breath after seeing one of their best hitters exit Thursday’s game after being hit in the hand by a pitch, but the initial reports on Willson Contreras were encouraging. Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters in Texas following the club’s 4-3 win that X-rays on Contreras’ right hand came back negative and that he’ll be day to day going forward. “We did an X-ray, it’s negative, he’s got a bruise on the hand and some swelling,” Tracy said. “We’ll take it day to da
item.content:encoded:
The Red Sox held their breath after seeing one of their best hitters exit Thursday’s game after being hit in the hand by a pitch, but the initial reports on Willson Contreras were encouraging.
Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters in Texas following the club’s 4-3 win that X-rays on Contreras’ right hand came back negative and that he’ll be day to day going forward.
“We did an X-ray, it’s negative, he’s got a bruise on the hand and some swelling,” Tracy said. “We’ll take it day to day and see how he is.”
Contreras left Thursday’s game after being hit in the right hand by a pitch in the top of the eighth inning. He immediately doubled over in pain and after a brief visit from the trainer walked straight to the dugout. He continued to grimace as he flexed his hand on the bench before departing into the tunnel for further testing.
Isiah Kiner-Falefa took Contreras’ place at first base.
With less than two weeks to play before the postseason the Red Sox cannot afford to be without Contreras. The veteran first baseman has been the club’s best hitter this season, leading the team with 27 home runs to go along with a .276 average and a .905 OPS.
The dour mood quickly turned to elation after Trevor Story put the Red Sox ahead with a three-run home run moments after Contreras was hit. With the win the Red Sox’s magic number is now three with nine games to play, giving the club some badly needed breathing room and potentially the luxury of giving Contreras extra rest if further imaging doesn’t reveal anything worse than a bruise.

item.content:encoded:
ARLINGTON, Texas — Nearly three months after Caleb Durbin first dislocated his left pinkie and more than a month after he reinjured it, the third baseman’s digit remains locked nearly at a right angle.
“It doesn’t quite straighten or bend all the way,” Durbin acknowledged.
Durbin received X-rays after his initial injury against the Rockies on June 24 and the reinjury against the White Sox on Aug. 6. In both instances, there was no fracture and he was told playing was simply a matter of pain tolerance.
And so, there was little question about how he’d proceed. He didn’t seek more information.
“There really is kind of a joint understanding [with the team] that we’ll get it looked at at the end of the season if we have to, because [whatever the diagnosis is], it’s not going to impact my decision to play at all,” he said.
Still, Durbin recognizes fingers shouldn’t look like they could be used to mount a shelf. Might he require offseason surgery?
“I don’t know yet. We’ll find out,” he said. “I hope there’s something we can do about it. But we’ll get there when the time comes.”
For now, Durbin remains a lineup constant. Thursday’s contest against the Rangers marked his 145th game of the season. He continues to deliver Gold Glove-caliber defense (his six outs above average lead AL third basemen) while also pushing the envelope on the field with high-IQ plays, most recently advancing from first to third on an infield single on Wednesday.
“He plays the game that way,” said Sox interim manager Chad Tracy. “It’s what he does.”
Still, it seems the injury is impacting him at the plate. He’s hitting .211/.400/.316 in September — showing fight in his at-bats (thus his standout on-base percentage), but rarely driving the ball. His whiff rate (10 percent of swings) is the lowest for any month this year, but he’s rarely been able to drive the ball. His 48 percent ground ball rate is his highest in any month since May.
But to Durbin, the question of whether or how the injury might be affecting him is secondary. His primary concern is simply whether he is positioned to contribute in any way.
“The pain’s gone down drastically since it happened the second time,” Durbin shrugged. “It’s functional.”
Updates on injured trio
Garrett Crochet, who last threw off a mound on Tuesday, worked out at Polar Park in Worcester on Thursday and will continue to throw on flat ground on Friday before the team decides whether to introduce any higher-intensity activities over the weekend.
Tracy said there’s been no discussion about the lefthander pitching in a rehab game for the WooSox this weekend. He didn’t rule out the possibility Crochet could soon face hitters in a live batting practice session, but made clear that there is no known schedule involving the 27-year-old.
“It all depends on how he’s feeling. … He’s been down so long,” said Tracy. “It is day to day. [Friday he’ll] throw, see how he feels, and then determine what the weekend holds.”
Righthander Tyron Guerrero, whose return from shoulder inflammation was delayed slightly by lower back cramps, had a high-intensity throwing session on flat ground. He’s expected to throw off a mound Friday when the Sox open a three-game series at Tampa Bay, a potential prelude to activation later in the weekend. “The shoulder feels great, the arm feels great,” said Guerrero.
Ceddanne Rafaela is increasing (right quad strain) is increasing his agility work but, at this point, there’s “no discernible timeline yet on game action,” according to Tracy. It hasn’t been determined if Rafaela will join the Sox in Tampa.
Oviedo in Worcester
Righthander Johan Oviedo (right elbow strain), pitching in an official game for the first time since March 30, struck out four batters while sitting at 96 miles per hour and touching 99 with his four-seamer in 2⅓ innings in a rehab appearance for the WooSox. He threw 20 of 30 pitches for strikes … Ranger Suarez will start for the Sox on Friday against the Rays, but the Sox have yet to decide who will start the other two games of the series. Payton Tolle, Patrick Sandoval, and Brayan Bello are all considerations … The Red Sox will send two scouts to New York for next week’s four-game Yankees-Rays series, the start of the team’s in-person advance scouting efforts for the postseason.
Alex Speier can be reached at alex.speier@globe.com. Follow him @alexspeier.

item.title: [Yahoo] How Did Johan Oviedo Fare in First Rehab Appearance?

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox starter is working his way back from a right elbow injury.
Video Transcript
What's up, everyone?
Zach Coe here for Roundtable.
Ahead of Tuesday night's loss to the Rangers, Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters that reliever Justin Slayton's season was over after an orthopedic visit revealed degenerative changes in his flexor mass, which required a PRP injection, effectively ending his season.
So obviously, the Red Sox have one of the best bullpens in baseball, backend of Aroldis Chapman, Justin Slayton, and Tayron Guerrero when he returns from the injured list.
But the loss of Slayton is still a really big one for this Red Sox bullpen, especially in the postseason when managers tend to be more aggressive with the hooks on both starters and relievers.
It was a pretty underwhelming season for Slayton when you look at the final line.
It was a 4.60 ERA in 31 1/3 innings.
But he was prone to a couple blowup starts, and that really inflated his ERA for much of the season.
It'll be interesting to see how Tracy's able to piece together the bullpen in Slayton's absence.
Of course, like I said, you have the backend pretty solidified with Tayron Guerrero handling the seventh, Garrett Whitlock in the eighth to All-Star Aroldis Chapman, who's been one of the best closers in baseball over the last two seasons.
But it's how you get to them that I really have some concerns about, and there are plenty of guys that are available to fill that role, but it's whether or not they'll be able to capitalize on their opportunities.
First one being Greg Weiser.
I wrote about it a little bit earlier, but ever since he was recalled from his brief demotion to Triple-A, he's been incredible for the Red Sox, stepping up as they lost guys like Whitlock to an IL stint, Slayton, who landed on the IL shortly after Whitlock, and most recently Guerrero.
There's also Tanner Houk, who's working his way back from Tommy John surgery he underwent last year.
He's gonna try to make a return in a bullpen capacity for the last week of the season.
And then there's the big wild card of it all in Garrett Crochet, who continues to throw side sessions as he tries to get back in a relief role for the postseason.
He's been on the injured list since April 29th with left shoulder inflammation.
So any of those guys are more than capable of stepping up and filling that role.
It's just gonna be about whether or not they're, one, healthy enough to go out there and throw on a near nightly basis like the team might need them to in the postseason, and two, whether or not they're gonna be productive enough.
Obviously, with Houk, he's coming back from Tommy John surgery, and typically you see guys be a little bit wild with their control when they first come back from Tommy John.
We saw it in Houk's first relea-- We saw it in his first rehab appearance with Portland.
He walked two guys, and a run scored as a result.
But it's been a little bit better, since then in the two appearances following that.
So we'll see if that is something that he can shake.
And then Crochet, he's just We haven't seen him in so long, it's tough to say whether or not he's gonna be as effective as he once was.
And even if he isn't able to get to the 2025 Cy Young runner-up caliber, can he at least give you enough to kind of bridge that gap between the starter and to the backend of your bullpen?
And then there's kind of a wild card in it all, and a bit of a forgotten man in Johan Oviedo, who obviously has electric stuff, but he's made only one appearance in a Red Sox uniform before landing on the IL with right elbow inflammation.
So he's planning on making a rehab appearance with Triple-A Worcester on Thursday night, and then they'll figure out the next steps with him.
But Red Sox have plenty of options to fill that void left behind by Slayton.

item.title: [Boston Herald] Injured Red Sox right-hander takes mound for first time since March

item.content:encoded:
Originally viewed as one of the favorites to start the season in the Opening Day rotation, Red Sox right-hander Johan Oviedo wound up making just one appearance out of the bullpen before going on the shelf with a right elbow strain.
Now after missing nearly the entire season, Oviedo may finally be nearing a return.
Oviedo began a rehab assignment at Triple-A Worcester on Thursday, throwing 2 1/3 innings for the WooSox in his first game action since late March.
The 28-year-old threw 30 pitches, 20 for strikes, while allowing one run on two hits and a walk while striking out four. Oviedo allowed an RBI double with one out in the top of the second before striking out the final three batters he faced.
More encouragingly, Oviedo’s fastball averaged 95.9 mph and topped out at 98.5, a sizable jump from the 92-93 he averaged earlier in the season.
Originally acquired last winter from the Pittsburgh Pirates as part of the Jhostynxon Garcia trade, Oviedo was initially expected to provide rotation depth as a possible high-ceiling power arm. Oviedo had previously missed extensive time due to Tommy John surgery, but finished his last season in Pittsburgh strong with a 3.57 ERA and 42 strikeouts over nine starts down the stretch.
The righty entered spring as one of the favorites for the No. 5 rotation spot, but after some promising early starts began showing signs of wear. The last rotation spot wound up going to Connelly Early, with Oviedo making the team as a reliever, and he made one appearance against the Houston Astros on March 30, allowing four runs over 3 2/3 innings.
Oviedo has been on the injured list ever since, but now he could be a dark horse candidate for the Red Sox playoff roster along with Tanner Houck and Garrett Crochet, who are also working their way back from extended injury absences.
Upcoming starters
Ranger Suarez will start Friday’s series opener against the Tampa Bay Rays, but the Red Sox’s other starters remain to be determined. Payton Tolle would normally be in line to start Saturday but Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters in Texas on Thursday that the club is still deciding how it wants to handle the weekend.
Brayan Bello, who was limited to 19 pitches over 1 2/3 innings on Tuesday, would presumably be a candidate to start one of this weekend’s games.

item.content:encoded:
ARLINGTON, Texas (AP) — Willson Contreras left the Boston's 4-3 win over Texas on Thursday night in the eighth inning after he was hit by a pitch on his right hand.
Red Sox manager Chad Tracy said the first baseman's hand was bruised with some swelling and X-rays were negative.
“We're going to take it day to day,” Tracy said.
Contreras was struck by a first-pitch sinker from Jakob Junis after Wilyer Abreu drew a leadoff walk with the Rangers leading 3-1. Contreras walked to first base in obvious pain, was examined by an athletic trainer and headed to the dugout.
Two batters later, Trevor Story hit a three-run home run off Jacob Latz.
Contreras was 1 for 3 with a single. He was hit by a pitch Wednesday night after hitting a two-run home run in the first inning of Boston's 7-3 loss to the Rangers.

item.dc:creator: Zach Coe

item.content:encoded:
RedSoxRoundtable's Zach Coe discusses the potential relievers who could step up and fill the void left behind by Justin Slaten after it was revealed the right-hander was unlikely to return from the injured list in 2026. Be sure to join our FREE community over on RedSoxRoundtable.com!
After an incredible July that saw the Boston Red Sox go 21-4, ultimately saving their season and propelling them into postseason position, the team has given key contributors time on the injured list to address lingering injuries. Among the players placed on the IL was right-handed reliever Justin Slaten, who was dealing with right elbow soreness.
After initially expecting to miss the minimum of 15 days or somewhere close to it, the 29-year-old continued to experience soreness as he began throwing progressions, leading the team to shut him down each time. On Tuesday, interim manager Chad Tracy announced that Slaten received a PRP injection to treat "degenerative changes in his flexor mass," ending his season.
With Slaten set to miss the remainder of the year, the pressure is on these pitchers to help bridge the gap between the starter and All-Star closer Aroldis Chapman:
Tyron Guerrero
Guerrero was expected to be activated off the injured list ahead of Wednesday night's loss to the Texas Rangers, but tightness in his lower back led the team to delay his activation. Still, though, upon his activation, Guerrero will become one of the primary seventh-inning options for Tracy to turn to.
The 35-year-old flamethrower has been an incredible find for Chief Baseball Officer Craig Breslow, posting a 3.26 ERA in 38.2 innings in 2026. However, he hit a rough patch before landing on the IL, allowing eight earned runs in his last 13.2 innings. Boston will need him to return to the pitcher he was for the first 38.2 innings of his season, when he posted a 2.16 ERA.
After not allowing a single earned run in his first 10 appearances after being dealt to Boston at the trade deadline, the 28-year-old lefty has struggled in his last six outings, allowing five earned runs, including three in a blow-up appearance in Wednesday's loss.
Miller told reporters after the loss that he was working through a mechanical issue that led to the struggles. However, he is the primary left-handed high-leverage arm before Chapman, so the team will need him to get those issues squared away ahead of what's likely to be a Wild Card-round matchup against a New York Yankees lineup that's lefty-heavy.
No single pitcher has stepped up more for the Red Sox as they shuffled Garrett Whitlock, Slaten, and Guerrero on the injured list than Weissert. After a brief demotion to Triple-A Worcester on Aug. 7, Weissert returned to the big leagues on Aug. 13, taking Whitlock's spot on the active roster, and has been lights out ever since. In 10.2 innings since being recalled, the 31-year-old right-hander has allowed only two earned runs on 12 hits, striking out 14 and walking only four.
Weissert figures to be the leader in the clubhouse to take over Slaten's role in the bullpen.
A trio of injured options
The Red Sox have several pitchers looking to return from the injured list before the end of the regular season who could factor into the team's playoff push, including 2025 Cy Young Award runner-up Garrett Crochet, 2024 All-Star Tanner Houck, and Johan Oviedo.
Crochet
The 27-year-old ace has thrown four bullpen sessions since restarting a throwing progression on Aug. 3, with his most recent outing, a 30-pitch up-and-down session on the Fenway Park mound, coming on Tuesday afternoon. While Crochet, if healthy enough to appear in games, will almost certainly be on the postseason roster, he is expected to make multi-inning appearances rather than one-inning spurts like Slaten had been used, making him a valuable weapon but an imperfect replacement.
Houck
The now-30-year-old right-hander is attempting to return to the Boston staff in a "Swiss Army knife" role after undergoing Tommy John surgery in August 2025. Houck has already made three rehab appearances with both Double-A Portland and Triple-A Worcester, allowing two earned runs on one hit, walking four, and striking out seven in 4.2 innings. He is expected to return to Worcester on Saturday for a 40-50 pitch outing before potentially rejoining the Red Sox.
Though what exactly Houck can contribute after being out of major league action since May 2025 remains to be seen.
Oviedo
A bit of a forgotten man in the 2026 Red Sox season is the 28-year-old right-hander, who made only one appearance before landing on the injured list on April 3 with right elbow inflammation. Oviedo will make his first rehab appearance Thursday night with Worcester before deciding on next steps; at this point, the risk likely outweighs the reward of making the postseason roster.
Tracy, Breslow, and the rest of Boston's decision makers will have 10 games to make their final decisions on how exactly the postseason roster will look, and who will replace Slaten's high-leverage innings.
Up next for the Sox
The Red Sox will look to avoid the sweep at the hands of the Texas Rangers in Thursday's series finale from Globe Life Field. Sonny Gray (17-5, 2.76 ERA) gets the start for Boston opposite Tyler Alexander (5-2, 3.38 ERA) for Texas. First pitch is set for 8:05 p.m. ET.

item.title: [NBC Sports Boston] Five biggest issues plaguing Red Sox with postseason looming
item.dc:creator: Justin Leger
item.description: The Boston Red Sox are still sitting comfortably in the second Wild Card spot, but there are several issues they must resolve before they start thinking about playoff baseball. Boston is a mediocre 11-11 over its last 22 games. While that's been good enough to sustain its playoff position, its play hasn't exactly inspired optimism for a deep postseason run. item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox are still sitting comfortably in the second Wild Card spot, but there are several issues they must resolve before they start thinking about playoff baseball.
Boston is a mediocre 11-11 over its last 22 games. While that's been good enough to sustain its playoff position, its play hasn't exactly inspired optimism for a deep postseason run.
Most of the Red Sox' problems can be linked to their underperforming lineup. Key hitters like Roman Anthony, Willson Contreras, Adley Rutschman and Wilyer Abreu have been concerningly inconsistent.
A deeper dive into the numbers suggests the struggling Sox will have their work cut out for them in their presumed Wild Card Series rematch at Yankee Stadium. Here are the club's five biggest areas of concern with 10 games remaining:
Roman Anthony is ice-cold
The Red Sox need Roman Anthony to be one of their best offensive players to have any chance of a deep postseason run. If the former No. 1 prospect continues to play the way he has for most of September, that will be problematic.
Anthony is hitting just .149 (7-for-47) with one home run and a .428 OPS over his last 11 games. He has struck out 18 times in 51 plate appearances.
The 22-year-old's struggles beg the question: should he still be the leadoff hitter in the postseason? Interim manager Chad Tracy will have no choice but to reevaluate Anthony's spot in the lineup if his woes continue. The problem with that is there aren't any exciting alternatives. The leadoff spot has been a glaring issue all season long, regardless of who has been thrust into the role.
Struggling against high velocity
The Red Sox offense has been inconsistent no matter who's on the mound, but it has mostly struggled against pitchers with high velo. Here's how some of Boston's regulars have fared this season against pitches greater than or equal to 97 mph:
- Wilyer Abreu: .170 BA, .623 OPS (237 pitches)
- Jarren Duran: .065 BA, .300 OPS (203 pitches)
- Willson Contreras: .170 BA, .512 OPS (166 pitches)
- Ceddanne Rafaela: .205 BA, .449 OPS (157 pitches)
- Roman Anthony: .091 BA, .440 OPS (58 pitches)
- Adley Rutschman: .077 BA, .451 OPS (57 pitches)
The Red Sox' top performer against high velocity (97 mph and above) has been Caleb Durbin (.364 BA, .912 OPS, 161 pitches).
Being so vulnerable against high velocity will especially be a problem for Boston in its expected Wild Card Series matchup against the New York Yankees. Cy Young frontrunner and likely Game 1 starter Cam Schlittler averages 98 mph with his four-seam fastball, which he uses 44.5 percent of the time. Gerrit Cole averages 96.9 mph with his four-seam, using it 49.3 percent of the time.
Leaving runners stranded
Boston has been below average all season at capitalizing on runners in scoring position. It currently ranks 17th in batting average (.250) and 21st in OPS (.731) with RISP. They're hitting just .212 in such situations through 14 games so far in September.
The Yankees' elite pitching staff probably won't provide the Red Sox with many scoring opportunities in their short series, so it's imperative that they come through when given the chance. Lately, Boston hasn't had anyone in its lineup to feel confident about when they step to the plate with runners on.
Role players regressing
As great as guys like Willson Contreras, Caleb Durbin, and Wilyer Abreu were throughout the Red Sox' incredible midseason turnaround, it was the role players who powered their surge. Mickey Gasper, Jahmai Jones, Nick Sogard, Anthony Seigler, and Andruw Monasterio were instrumental in resurrecting Boston's season.
Gasper has cooled off, though no one expected him to sustain his Barry Bonds-like run. Jahmai Jones is 4 for his last 22 (.182) with nine strikeouts, suddenly making him a playoff roster cut candidate. Sogard is still hitting, but his .758 OPS so far in September suggests regression to the mean. Seigler is hurt. Monasterio posted a .578 OPS in August and is 0-for-11 so far in September, putting him on the playoff roster bubble.
That group deserves immense credit for getting the Red Sox here, but it cannot be counted on to propel the club through the postseason.
Erik Miller experiencing command issues
Boston's bullpen is arguably its biggest strength heading into the postseason. The back end with Garrett Whitlock, Tyron Guerrero, and Aroldis Chapman is elite.
We would've included trade deadline addition Erik Miller in that group last month, when he allowed only one earned run with 20 strikeouts and just three walks across his first 11 appearances with the Red Sox. His performance so far this month, however, has been alarming.
Miller, acquired from the San Francisco Giants in the Marcelo Mayer trade, has allowed four earned runs with six walks and six strikeouts through five appearances (4.1 IP) in September. His command struggles were a question mark upon his joining the club, and it appears that issue has reemerged with less than two weeks until the playoffs.
After Wednesday's poor outing against the Texas Rangers (2 H, 3 ER, 1 BB), Miller attributed his recent struggles to his mechanics. The Red Sox will hope that whatever the problem is, it's a quick fix, because Miller will be counted on to be their most reliable left-handed reliever not named Aroldis Chapman.

item.content:encoded:
Garett Crochet wants to pitch in the postseason without making a single rehab appearance. That’s audacious enough, but how about playing in the postseason, without having ever played in the big leagues at all? That could be the situation Braiden Ward finds himself in. If you need to refresh your memory, Ward was the little speedster who was running wild all over Grapefruit League diamonds this spring. He hasn’t gotten a chance to show whether he can do that in the Majors yet, but Chad Tracy isn’t ruling it out. “Every time he gets on, he’s not afraid,” Tracy said. “That’s the thing. If he gets on base, he’s looking to go. That’s a unique trait. There’s a lot of guys who can run and steal bases and then there’s other guys who are, every single time they get on, almost regardless of the timing.” (Conor Ryan, Boston.com)
But a lack of speed on the base paths isn’t really the Red Sox problem right now as they muddle through a middling September. Strikeouts are. “The Red Sox are swinging and missing too much and not walking enough. This month, they have the eighth-most strikeouts and seventh-fewest walks. That doesn’t play in the postseason. Making contact does.” (Rob Bradford, WEEI)
After he initially returned to the big leagues with a bang, Roman Anthony is one of the Sox hitters who’s struggling to make contact right now. But he doesn’t sound worried. “I’m right where I want to be,” said Anthony. “I came back with enough time to get a good number of plate appearances, and to fail like I am right now and to succeed like I did in the beginning, and then kind of meet in the middle and continue to grind out every single day and get ready for what we want to be a long postseason run. [The playoffs are] what you play for after such a long year … At the end of the day, those few weeks are the only thing that really matters.” (Alex Speier, Boston Globe)
Unfortunately, the other big power threat in the Sox lineup is also struggling to get back up to speed. Willson Contreras homered last night, but he’s still dealing with a nagging hamstring injury. “I ran pretty good there on the ground ball to shortstop, but I need to manage my leg better,” he said. “I know it’s feeling good and it’s feeling alright, but on a hard-hit ball like that, I know I’m going to be out. I was just trying to put pressure on him, see if he made a bad throw or whatever. Next time, I’ll manage better.” (Chris Cotillo, MassLive)
With Anthony and Contreras struggling in different ways, it’s important to remember that this team’s success has been built on depth, not individual star power. “Whether it was an expanded version of the trade that brought Caleb Durbin from Milwaukee to include Monasterio and Seigler, or waiver claims of Cheng and Gasper, or a minor league deal for Guerrero, the season has been a case study in the notion that perceived little moves can have a huge impact.” (Alex Speier, Boston Globe)
Fortunately, the Sox have some depth in the good guy department, too. After the departure of Liam Hendriks, who had been nominated for the Clemente Award seven times throughout his career for his charitable efforts, Garrett Whitlock has stepped in and picked up the baton. (Ian Browne, MLB.com)

item.content:encoded:
Red Sox news: Will Tanner Houck return from injury before MLB playoffs? appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Boston Red Sox could get starting pitcher Tanner Houck prior to the 2026 regular season conclusion, but his postseason availability for the Red Sox remains undecided as the right-hander continues rebuilding his workload following elbow surgery.
MLB.com's official Red Sox injury tracker provided the latest update on his recovery and potential return:
"RHP Tanner Houck Injury: Torn ulnar collateral ligament right elbow/right flexor pronator strain IL date: Feb. 10 (60-day IL) Expected return: Aiming for late regular season Status: Pitched a scoreless inning in his third rehab appearance on Sept. 15 with Triple-A Worcester. Expected to pitch again Sept. 18 trying to reach 45-, 50-pitch range. (Last updated: Sept. 16)"
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
Now in his seventh official MLB campaign, Houck has not pitched in a Major League game since May 12, 2025. His previous rehab attempt ended last July before he underwent a hybrid reconstruction of his right ulnar collateral ligament with flexor tendon repair on August 18, 2025.
The Red Sox are preparing the veteran for a relief role rather than asking him to return to the rotation. The best-case scenario would involve Houck appearing in one or two games during the final week of the regular season before a potential postseason roster decision.
There is still no guarantee that happens. Houck's third rehab appearance came Tuesday with Triple-A Worcester, when he struck out three and walked one during a scoreless inning. He threw 22 pitches, 11 for strikes, and reached 94.2 mph with his fastball.
He also worked out of the bullpen during Boston's 2021 postseason run, making five relief appearances and throwing 10.1 innings, experience that could ease a short-term transition in October.
Houck is expected to pitch Friday and work into the 45- to 50-pitch range. His performance and recovery from that outing will help determine whether a late-season return remains realistic and whether the Red Sox consider him worthy of receiving a spot on the postseason bullpen role.

item.dc:creator: Scott Roche

item.content:encoded:
After a historic run in late June and into July, you knew things would end up evening out for the Boston Red Sox. That appears to be the case in September. With 10 games remaining in the regular season, the Red Sox are five games clear of the third and final American League wild-card spot.
They are destined for a matchup in a couple of weeks in a best-of-three series against the New York Yankees in the Bronx. However, Boston is struggling as the regular season winds down after a 7-3 loss to the Texas Rangers on Wednesday night in Arlington. The Red Sox are 5-5 in their last 10 games. What's going on in September? Interim manager Chad Tracy had a simple answer.
Boston Red Sox Interim Manager Chad Tracy Drops Simple Answer on Team's Struggles
Boston is 0-2 on their final road trip of the regular season and will look to avoid a sweep by Texas on Thursday night. They will be sending ace Sonny Gray to the mound. However, the loss on Wednesday night was another frustrating one, but Tracy had a simple answer for his teams recent struggles.
"Probably the easy answer is: baseball," Tracy said, per Tim Healey of the Boston Globe. "We got some guys going through it, and then you could see one or two big swings in a complete turn the other direction. So we just gotta keep plugging away at it."
First baseman Willson Contreras gave Boston a 2-0 first-inning lead on a two-run home run. However, Texas scored seven of the game's final eight runs. Contreras said that despite the recent stretch, Boston is in the right mind set.
"First-inning homer, it's always good, but it's even better if we win," Contreras said, per Healey. "We battle. We come here with the right mindset. We work hard . . . But sometimes it's baseball. Sometimes, it doesn't matter how hard we work. Sometimes, the results are not gonna come. But you have to build off that. You have to take those types of games personal and get better for tomorrow."
Boston managed just two hits over the last eight innings. Trevor Story and pinch-hitter Nick Sogard had the other two hits. That won't win many regular season games, never mind playoff games.
Boston Red Sox Have Difficult Regular Season Schedule Left
Boston's 10 remaining games are all against teams with something to play for. Texas is tied for the AL West lead with the Houston Astros. The Rays are looking to fend off the Yankees to win the AL East.
Their final two series at home are against the Cleveland Guardians and Chicago Cubs. The Guardians are battling the Chicago White Sox for the AL Central Division. Whoever wins the division will most likely get a wild-card round bye. If they don't, the AL West winner will. As for the Cubs, they are battling the Philadelphia Phillies for home-field advantage in the National League wild-card round.
Going into the playoffs, teams want to be playing their best baseball. That's not the case right now for the Red Sox. However, there is still time to gain momentum going into the postseason.
