item.content:encoded:
ARLINGTON, Texas — The Red Sox didn’t have many big swings Tuesday night against Jacob deGrom and the Rangers, but one from a late-game pinch-hitter nearly flipped the script on the whole night.
Pinch-hitting for Jarren Duran against All-Star closer Jacob Latz in the eighth inning with Boston trailing by two, Andruw Monasterio got a 3-2 fastball just below the zone and smoked it — just foul. Monasterio sent a screaming line drive down the left field line, but it landed in the seats in foul territory, 369 feet away from home plate. If the ball had landed a few feet to its right, the Red Sox would have led 6-4 heading into the ninth.
For a second, the Red Sox dugout (on the third base side) thought Monasterio was a hero.
“It’s hard to tell from the dugout, from our angle,” said interim manager Chad Tracy. “When it came off the bat, it looked like, ‘Is that gonna hit the foul pole?’ But for about halfway on the ball flight, it was like, ‘I think that might hit the foul pole, I think it might be close.’”
Instead, Monasterio’s at-bat continued and Latz blew a 97 mph fastball by him to escape the threat. It was the second bases-loaded escape for the Rangers, who also didn’t allow a run in a similar situation in the fifth. In all, the Red Sox were hitless in four at-bats with runners in scoring position and left nine on base.
“We gave ourselves a couple of opportunities to maybe hit a single and tie the game up,” Tracy said. “We just couldn’t do it tonight.”
The pressure-filled situation marked just Monasterio’s 12th plate appearance in 15 games since Trevor Story and Roman Anthony were both activated from the injured list August 30.
Sandoval struggles
When starter Patrick Sandoval struck out the first four batters of his outing, it looked like he was about to go toe-to-toe with deGrom, the five-time All-Star on the other side. But that illusion quickly collapsed in a brutal second inning in which Sandoval allowed four runs and threw 44 pitches.
Sandoval allowed two separate rallies as the Rangers scored four times with two outs. With two men on after both singled, Elias Díaz opened the scoring with a two-run double to left. Sandoval then walked two batters in a row before Corey Seager plated two runs with a bloop single to left-center.
“Just got to pitch better,” said Sandoval, who has a 4.99 ERA. “Got to do better for this team. Can’t be doing this.”
Sandoval was the victim of some bad luck as Seager’s single left the bat at just 67.2 mph and traveled 212 feet. The ball fell in no man’s land between Story and Anthony and glanced off Story’s glove. Still, Sandoval took the blame.
“Just got to make a better pitch,” Sandoval said. “That’s it.”
Sandoval lasted just 2 ⅔ innings in Boston’s 4-2 loss, allowing four earned runs on four hits while walking two batters. He did have five strikeouts.
Sogard homers again
The only scoring of the night for the Red Sox came in the third when Nick Sogard launched a line-drive two-run shot off deGrom that tucked inside the right field foul pole. Considering Boston had just three hits against deGrom, it was an impressive swing on a slider down and in.
“I’d only gotten one fastball that at-bat and it was kinda up-and-in, so with two strikes, he likes to back-foot it,” Sogard said. “One of the best pitchers in the game. Ton of respect for him. But I had a feeling it was going to be something in. I definitely wasn’t sitting on it. I was a little out in front, but I was able to keep it fair and it got over the wall.”
Sogard waited a while for his first big league homer, going 321 plate appearances before going deep against Arizona on August 19. Including Tuesday, he has now homered five times in his last 99 trips to the plate.
“I feel good,” he said. “Just trying to compete and grind out good at-bats and get your pitches to hit. I’ve been able to drive it a little bit better this year.”
Bullpen strategy keeps options open
When Tracy pulled Sandoval with two outs in the third and Wyatt Langford coming to the plate, he went to righty Brayan Bello, a common piggyback option who has given the Red Sox plenty of long relief appearances and threw 103 pitches in his last outing, a start against the Angels on Labor Day. But Tracy chose to only use Bello for 1 ⅔ innings (and 19 pitches). It was his shortest appearance of the year.
The reason, Tracy said, was to keep the possibility open for Bello to make a longer appearance (potentially a start) later in the week. Boston’s well-rested bullpen cobbled together the rest of the game with Bello (five outs), Alec Gamboa (three), Wyatt Olds (two) and Jovani Morán (six) passing the baton.
“We’re keeping options open,” said Tracy. “Part of the reason we were able to be so aggressive is that so much of the bullpen was at five, six or seven days off. Being able to spread the load a little bit and not overextend anybody, but also keeping options open if there is a start or something. We want to keep that on the table.
“We were able to do that today and piece it together with four guys instead of just having one guy take on the whole load.”

item.title: [Boston Sports Journal] Patrick Sandoval unravels as Red Sox strand chances in 4-2 loss to Rangers
item.dc:creator: Chris Henrique
item.description: One miserable inning was enough to put the Red Sox in a hole. A pair of missed opportunities prevented them from climbing out of it. Patrick Sandoval endured a brutal 44-pitch second inning in which the Rangers scored four times, and the Red Sox repeatedly came up empty with runners on base in a 4-2 loss Tuesday night at Globe Life Field. Boston (82-69) opened its final road trip of the regular season with a loss and fell to 7-6 in September. The Red Sox did, however, move another step closer to
item.content:encoded:
One miserable inning was enough to put the Red Sox in a hole. A pair of missed opportunities prevented them from climbing out of it.
Patrick Sandoval endured a brutal 44-pitch second inning in which the Rangers scored four times, and the Red Sox repeatedly came up empty with runners on base in a 4-2 loss Tuesday night at Globe Life Field.
Boston (82-69) opened its final road trip of the regular season with a loss and fell to 7-6 in September. The Red Sox did, however, move another step closer to securing a postseason berth after Toronto was routed by Detroit, reducing Boston’s magic number to five.
Any potential celebration will have to wait until after the Red Sox leave Texas. Even if Boston wins the final two games of the series, Toronto is off Thursday and would remain mathematically alive entering Friday.
Sandoval’s night began when he struck out the first four Rangers he faced before everything unraveled in a second inning that seemed as though it might never end.
With two outs, Brandon Nimmo and Ezequiel Duran delivered hard-hit singles at 106.3 mph and 105.3 mph, respectively. Elias Díaz followed by pulling a two-run double into left field to give Texas a 2-0 lead.
Sandoval never recovered walking former Sox catcher Danny Jansen and Justin Foscue before Corey Seager dropped a bloop single into shallow left, just beyond the reach of Trevor Story, allowing two more runs to score. By the time Sandoval finally escaped, he had thrown 44 pitches in the inning and Boston trailed 4-0.
Sandoval lasted just 2 2/3 innings and saw his ERA climb to 4.99.
“They drug at bats out on him,” Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters postgame. “It looked like he was going to get out of there with Diaz, that was a long at bat, I think one of those pitches was close and then he hits the double in the corner and it was just a struggle, we just couldn’t get out of the inning.”
The left-hander’s return from injury provided Boston with some needed innings after he was activated July 9, and he delivered several quality outings along the way. But with the postseason approaching, his place on the October roster has become increasingly uncertain.
Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez, Payton Tolle and Jake Bennett are ahead of him in the rotation picture, while Brayan Bello has found success in a bulk role. Garrett Crochet and Tanner Houck are also attempting to return before the postseason.
Patrick Sandoval strikes out the side in the 1st.
Justin Foscue made him throw 9 pitches to start the game. Needed 19 total to finish the inning. pic.twitter.com/qpUpDLA5Rc
Sandoval will have time to try and clean things up, but it’s looking as if the Red Sox are better suited with the lefty as a spectator when they inevitably travel to the Bronx.
Boston’s offense quickly cut the deficit in half against Jacob deGrom.
Nick Sogard jumped on a pitch in the third and sent it down the right-field line for a two-run homer, pulling the Red Sox within 4-2.
Sogard didn’t hit his first major league homer until his 322nd plate appearance Aug. 19. He has now hit five in his last 99 plate appearances, all coming over a 24-game span.
The versatile infielder contributed in other ways, too. Sogard perfectly executed a sacrifice bunt in the fifth to move two runners into scoring position and later made an athletic play to complete a 1-4-3 double play.
But the Red Sox couldn’t capitalize on their opportunities against deGrom. The Texas right-hander held Boston to three hits and struck out eight over five innings while maintaining a fastball around 97 mph.

item.title: [Boston Herald] Patrick Sandoval allows four runs in second, Red Sox lose opener to Rangers
item.dc:creator: Mac Cerullo
item.description: Patrick Sandoval has had a rocky month. Entering Tuesday, the Red Sox left-hander had allowed a 6.12 ERA over his last five starts, but coming out of the gate Sandoval looked like he’d finally figured things out. But after striking out the first four batters he faced, the wheels came off in the bottom of the second. Sandoval allowed four runs over an interminable 44-pitch second inning and ultimately got the hook after recording just eight outs in Boston’s 4-2 loss to the Texas Rangers. Nick Sog
item.content:encoded:
Patrick Sandoval has had a rocky month. Entering Tuesday, the Red Sox left-hander had allowed a 6.12 ERA over his last five starts, but coming out of the gate Sandoval looked like he’d finally figured things out.
But after striking out the first four batters he faced, the wheels came off in the bottom of the second.
Sandoval allowed four runs over an interminable 44-pitch second inning and ultimately got the hook after recording just eight outs in Boston’s 4-2 loss to the Texas Rangers.
Nick Sogard hit a two-run home run to help get the Red Sox back into the game, but the offense otherwise couldn’t get anything going against Jacob deGrom and the Rangers bullpen, squandering bases loaded opportunities in the fifth and eighth innings.
Sandoval started strong by striking out the side in the first inning, but after sending down Jake Burger to start the second everything ground to a screeching halt. The right-hander allowed a pair of singles, served up a two-run double to Elias Diaz, and then walked back-to-back batters to load the bases for five-time All-Star Corey Seager.
It appeared for a moment like Sandoval might minimize the damage when he drew a pop fly to shallow left, but the ball drifted into no-man’s land and Trevor Story couldn’t make the catch, allowing two more runs to score and putting the Rangers up 4-0.
Sandoval ultimately needed 44 pitches to get through the second, blowing up his pitch count and ensuring a long evening for the Red Sox bullpen. He recorded two outs in the third and was lifted for Brayan Bello after allowing four runs over 2 2/3 innings.
“They drug at bats out on him,” Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters in Arlington postgame. “It looked like he was going to get out of there with Diaz, that was a long at bat, I think one of those pitches was close and then he hits the double in the corner and it was just a struggle, we just couldn’t get out of the inning.”
Four runs matches the largest deficit the Red Sox have overcome in a win this season, but the club didn’t need long to cut it in half. After Caleb Durbin reached on a one-out single in the top of the third, Sogard ripped a line drive off deGrom that cleared the right field fence for a two-run home run.
It was the fifth home run of the season for Sogard, all of which have come since Aug. 19. Prior to that the 29-year-old had never hit a homer over his first three seasons as a big leaguer.
That wound up being as close as Boston got.
The Red Sox could have tied the score or taken the lead with one swing in the fifth inning, but despite loading the bases without recording a hit the club couldn’t get a run across. Jarren Duran was hit by a pitch, Durbin reached on catcher’s interference and Mickey Gasper walked to bring up Adley Rutschman with two outs, but the catcher grounded out to short to keep it a 4-2 game.
Boston’s bullpen did its part to keep the Red Sox in the game. Bello tossed 1 2/3 perfect innings, Alec Gamboa threw one scoreless aided in large part by a brilliant double play turned by Sogard to end the fifth, and Wyatt Olds worked his way out of a runners-at-the-corners, two-out jam to escape the sixth. Jovani Moran entered with a man on in the seventh and got three quick outs, setting the table for one last Red Sox push in the eighth.
Jahmai Jones sparked the rally with a leadoff single, Willson Contreras drew a one-out walk, and after Wilyer Abreu grounded out to move the two runners into scoring position Story was intentionally walked to load the bases again.
Rather than have Duran face the left-hander Jacob Latz, Tracy pinch hit Andruw Monasterio, but the move didn’t pay off. Monasterio worked a full count and nearly went deep on a hard hit liner that landed just foul before striking out to leave them loaded again.
Boston went quietly in the top of the ninth, finishing the game 0 for 4 with runners in scoring position while stranding nine men on base.
“We gave ourselves a couple of opportunities to maybe hit a single and tie the game up and we couldn’t do it tonight,” Tracy said.
Magic number still 5
In addition to keeping pace in the AL West race, the Rangers also jumped the Toronto Blue Jays to become the first team below the AL Wild Card cutline. As a result the Red Sox’s magic number remains five despite the Blue Jays’ 10-1 loss earlier in the night.
Boston (82-69) can clinch a playoff berth as early as Friday, and depending on how things play out in the AL Central the Red Sox could lock down the second Wild Card spot as soon as this weekend.
Houck scoreless with WooSox
Tanner Houck (Tommy John surgery rehab) tossed a scoreless inning of relief in his latest rehab appearance with the WooSox on Tuesday. The right-hander entered the game in the seventh inning and allowed one walk, no hits and struck out three over 22 pitches.

item.title: [MLB.com] 4 big questions surround Crochet's possible return, impact down the stretch
item.dc:creator: Ian Browne
item.description: The 2026 season has been, for the most part, an injury-plagued loss for Crochet, who made his first six starts before getting shut down with left shoulder inflammation that regressed when he made his first attempted comeback in late May. But the beauty of all this is that Crochet can wash away the sour taste of missing most of the season by getting back as a reliever in time for the most important games. After that setback at the end of May, it took Crochet three months just to be cleared to thr
item.content:encoded:
The 2026 season has been, for the most part, an injury-plagued loss for Crochet, who made his first six starts before getting shut down with left shoulder inflammation that regressed when he made his first attempted comeback in late May.
But the beauty of all this is that Crochet can wash away the sour taste of missing most of the season by getting back as a reliever in time for the most important games.
After that setback at the end of May, it took Crochet three months just to be cleared to throw off the mound again.
Now that he’s been able to do so three times, and is scheduled for a fourth bullpen session at Fenway Park on Tuesday, there is legitimate hope he can be on the roster when the Red Sox open their postseason on Sept. 29 -- likely at Yankee Stadium.
This time, assuming he makes it back, Crochet will be cast in a much different role, but one that can still be impactful.
Figuring you have questions about how and when Crochet fits in, here are some answers.
Can Crochet make it back before the regular season ends?
It’s not impossible. His next key step after graduating from bullpen sessions will be to face hitters. That could happen as soon as this weekend, depending on what the club decides after Tuesday’s session.
Ideally, when it comes to Crochet’s situation, the Triple-A season would go a little longer. But, alas, it ends on Sunday.
It seems more likely Crochet will throw live batting practice and/or some type of simulated game rather than getting into a Minor League game, perhaps doing so multiple times.
Would this leave time for one tune-up before the regular season ends on Sept. 27? Perhaps, but not necessarily.
Would Crochet be thrown right into the fire of the playoffs?
What if there isn’t time for Crochet to pitch in any type of game setting before the Wild Card Series starts? Would the Red Sox still put him on the roster?
Well, if he’s throwing up to his capabilities, the answer is absolutely yes.
“It's Garrett Crochet,” said Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy. “If Garrett Crochet looks like Garrett Crochet and he's healthy and able to go out there and pitch, and it looks like him? Yeah, that helps any team.”
What would Boston’s bullpen cast look like with Crochet in the mix?
In a word, dominant. Through their first 150 games of the season entering Tuesday, Boston’s bullpen has a 3.11 ERA, best in the Majors. That’s without Crochet.
Now, add Crochet and possibly 2024 Tanner Houck, who is on a Minor League rehab assignment in his return from Tommy John surgery, and Tracy’s relief crew could have a succession of pitchers with nasty stuff.
At 38 years old, lefty Aroldis Chapman continues to be a force. He has one of the best eighth-inning setup men in the game in front of him in righty Garrett Whitlock. Tyron Guerrero, the righty with triple-digit heat, is due back in the next couple of days after missing the last couple of weeks with right shoulder inflammation. Power lefty Erik Miller has been tremendous since he was acquired at the Aug. 3 Trade Deadline.
Brayan Bello, who hasn’t had much success has a starter this season but has been largely stellar in relief, is another weapon. Add Crochet and Houck to those five pitchers and the Sox would have bullpen depth that would be the envy of most teams.
How would the Sox use Crochet?
The beauty of Crochet is that he could work out of a hybrid role, meaning he could be available for whichever part of the game Tracy needs him most.
Keep in mind that Crochet was a relief pitcher not just in college at Tennessee, but also for the White Sox before being converted to a starting role in ‘24. He has experience working in the early, middle and late part of games.
Thinking outside the box, the Sox could even deploy Crochet as an opener if the occasion called for it, given his experience starting games.
“He'd have plenty of comfort opening if you wanted to go that route," Tracy said. "He pitched out of the 'pen. So if you need him to come in the middle innings of a game, a two-inning pocket, I'm sure he'd have comfort doing that, too."

item.content:encoded:
ARLINGTON, Texas — Among a series of minor injury updates offered by Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy on Tuesday came some finality on one key reliever. Righty Justin Slaten, after further assessment by a renowned orthopedist in the Dallas area, won’t return to the Red Sox this year.
Slaten visited Dr. Keith Meister on Monday’s off day and testing on his injured elbow revealed “degenerative changes in the flexor mass,” according to Tracy. Slaten is set for a platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injection that is all but certain to rule out his return in 2026.
“It’s a big loss,” Tracy said, “at least now, with the finality of knowing we can’t have him back.”
Slaten was placed on the injured list with elbow inflammation in mid-August and dealt with recurring discomfort as he tried to resume throwing. As of the weekend, he was completely shut down from his progression. Now, he will receive the injection and rest in hopes of getting the issue fixed for 2027.
“Probably just means a chronic thing over time, but I’m speculating there,” Tracy said. “I just know that the conservative course of action is PRP, then he’s gonna rehab and go from there. Because of that, it’s probably going to cost him the rest of the season.”
Slaten appeared in 36 games for the Red Sox this year, posting a 4.60 ERA as a mid-relief option ahead of setup man Garrett Whitlock and closer Aroldis Chapman. For the third straight season, injuries were a big part of Slaten’s season. In 2024, he missed about six weeks due to elbow inflammation in July and August. Last season, he was out from June 1 to August 28 with a balky shoulder. This year, he suffered an oblique strain in early April and missed 31 games, then hit the IL again for the final six weeks.
Mead takes step forward
For the first time since having his left wrist broken by a wayward pitch in West Sacramento on July 27, Curtis Mead will do some offensive work in Boston on Wednesday. According to Tracy, Mead — who is out of a cast and has been doing defensive and baserunning drills for weeks — will hit lightly off a tee as he begins his swing progression.
“Mead will begin, tomorrow, introducing tee work,” Tracy said. “Obviously, we’ve talked a lot about the defensive stuff, being able to catch throws and he’s been doing that. Tomorrow, he’ll start doing some tee work with a light bat and then just kinda progress from there.”
With just 12 games left in the regular season, Mead is in a race against the clock to be fully ready for game action, a reality he acknowledged just last week. But it’s still notable that he’s ready to start taking swings in anticipation for potentially returning during the postseason if the Red Sox make a run.
Crochet throws again at Fenway
Left-hander Garrett Crochet took another small step toward a late-season return Tuesday, throwing a two-inning “up-and-down” bullpen (that includes a break simulating a between-inning breather) at Fenway Park. That session came four days after a one-inning high-intensity bullpen on the same mound.
“That went well,” said Tracy. “Everything went well.”
The next step for Crochet might be facing hitters in a live batting practice/simulated game setting but it’s very unlikely he’ll be ready to pitch in a rehab game before Triple-A Worcester’s season ends Sunday. A more likely scenario involves him getting into a simulated game or two and then making a relief appearance late in next week’s final homestand of the year.
“We’ll wait and see on the next steps,” Tracy said. “That was the most volume he’s had, so we’ll see how he feels and go from there.”
Guerrero close to return, Kelly has setback
Right-hander Tyron Guerrero, out since September 1 with shoulder inflammation, is with the Red Sox in Arlington and is expected to be activated before Wednesday’s game. Lefty Raymond Burgos and righty Wyatt Olds are the two leading candidates to be sent down as Guerrero takes a roster spot.
“We’ll see how everything goes with that today,” Tracy said.
The return of Guerrero will give the Red Sox another high-octane option at the end of a bullpen that also includes lefty Erik Miller, Whitlock and Chapman (and won’t have Slaten for the rest of the year).
One reliever who won’t contribute the rest of the way is righty Zack Kelly, who has been out since early July with a stress reaction in the olecranon (bone at the tip of the elbow). Kelly had been throwing live BP sessions in Fort Myers and was close to a rehab outing but had a setback last week and will undergo updated imaging this week.
Rafaela progressing
Center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela (right quad strain) has said his goal is to rejoin the Red Sox for this weekend’s series against the Rays and that is still in play. He’s back in Boston and going through strength tests on his leg while ramping up his running program.
“Started to increase running volume today,” Tracy said. “Nothing new to report there. He’ll continue to do that over the next 2-3 days and we’ll see where he’s at.”
The Red Sox could be careful with Rafaela and welcome him back early next week when the Guardians are at Fenway Park.
Houck, Oviedo on track for rehab outings
Right-hander Tanner Houck is pitching for the WooSox at Polar Park on Tuesday as planned. His outing was planned as a shorter relief outing (he entered in the seventh, following six strong innings for starter Jedixson Paez) and he’s expected to make another appearance over the weekend in a longer stint on the mound.
Right-hander Johan Oviedo is still on track to make a rehab start in Worcester on Thursday.

item.title: [mlb.com] Reliever Slaten (elbow) expected to miss the rest of the season
item.dc:creator: Perla Paredes
item.description: ARLINGTON -- Right-handed reliever Justin Slaten’s season is over, Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy announced ahead of Boston’s three-game series opener against the Rangers at Globe Life Field on Tuesday night. According to Tracy, Slaten met with Dr. Keith Meister, an orthopedist in the Dallas area, and an evaluation revealed “degenerative changes in his flexor mass” in his right elbow. “Probably just means a chronic thing over time, but I’m speculating there,” Tracy said. “I just know that th
item.content:encoded:
ARLINGTON -- Right-handed reliever Justin Slaten’s season is over, Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy announced ahead of Boston’s three-game series opener against the Rangers at Globe Life Field on Tuesday night.
According to Tracy, Slaten met with Dr. Keith Meister, an orthopedist in the Dallas area, and an evaluation revealed “degenerative changes in his flexor mass” in his right elbow.
“Probably just means a chronic thing over time, but I’m speculating there,” Tracy said. “I just know that the conservative course of action is [a platelet-rich plasma injection]. He’s going to rehab and go from there, but because of that, it’s going to probably cost him the season.”
“As we sit here right now, we were operating and moving forward, planning on having to operate without him,” Tracy said. “This maybe adds some finality to the fact that, ‘OK, now the chances of getting him back are slim.’”
The 29-year-old Slaten posted a 4.60 ERA with 39 strikeouts across 31 1/3 innings over 36 appearances for Boston.
“It’s a big loss,” Tracy said. “At least now the finality of knowing we can’t have him back. But you guys have seen the way he can come in and pitch in those big-moment cleanup innings, to get you out of the sixth, seventh inning. We’ve seen him do that, so he’s an important arm. But we have to deal with it and move on.”
Slaten and Garrett Whitlock served as the Sox’s top right-handed setup men when both went down last month. Whitlock returned from the IL on Aug. 29.
When Slaten and Whitlock first went down, Tracy believed he had enough arms to navigate the bullpen. That depth, however, continues to be tested.
Right-hander Tyron Guerrero, who landed on the IL on Sept. 1 with right shoulder inflammation, was expected to be activated Wednesday but experienced muscle cramping in his lower back Tuesday, delaying his return. According to Tracy, the team does not know when Guerrero will be activated.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox begin a series on Tuesday night with the Texas Rangers with just 13 regular-season games remaining.
Ahead of the matchup, Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy spoke to the media and gave several updates on some of the players currently injured and on the IL.
One of those players is star outfielder Ceddanne Rafaela, who has been sidelined with a right quadriceps strain since early September.
Red Sox Announce Rafaela Update
There wasn’t any major development in Rafaela’s overall status, but Tracy noted that he began doing increased running volume on Tuesday. He didn’t have anything further to report on a potential timeline, but the injury doesn’t seem overly serious at this point, and Rafaela likely won’t need a crazy ramp-up once he is able to return to the field.
“Rafa started doing increased running volume today, so nothing new to report there. He’ll continue to do that over the next two, three days and we’ll see where he’s at,” Tracy said pregame.
Chad Tracy provides some #RedSox injury updates ⬇️
– Crochet threw today, everything went well
– Guerrero eligible tomorrow
– Rafaela started to increase running volume today, nothing new to report
– Houck is throwing tonight
– Slaten has “some degenerative changes in the flexor… pic.twitter.com/M04YHBmZCP
— NESN (@NESN) September 15, 2026
Rafaela’s 2026 Season
It’s been a tremendous season for Rafaela in his fourth year with the Red Sox.
The Red Sox named Rafaela an All-Star for the first time in his career, and the 25-year-old has hit .282 across 135 games and 535 at-bats. He has recorded 67 runs, 151 hits, 16 home runs, and 70 RBIs while slugging .443 with a .760 OPS.
Looking at the Red Sox
Boston enters Tuesday with an 82-68 overall record, which, as long as they don’t have a late-season collapse, should put them in line to be the second Wild Card team in the American League playoff picture.
There remains a chance they jump the New York Yankees, but they’re 5.0 games behind them for second place in the AL East and the top Wild Card spot. They’re also 8.5 games behind the Tampa Bay Rays for first place in the division and the No. 1 overall seed in the AL.

item.title: [The Boston Globe] Red Sox reliever Justin Slaten to miss rest of season with ‘degenerative’ arm issue - The Boston Globe
item.dc:creator: Tim Healey
item.description: ARLINGTON, Texas — Reliever Justin Slaten’s season is all but over after the discovery of a “degenerative” arm issue, Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy said Tuesday before a 4-2 loss to the Rangers. Before the series opener against the Rangers, Slaten went with team medical staff to visit Keith Meister, a highly regarded orthopedic and sports medicine surgeon based in Arlington. item.content:encoded:
ARLINGTON, Texas — Reliever Justin Slaten’s season is all but over after the discovery of a “degenerative” arm issue, Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy said Tuesday before a 4-2 loss to the Rangers.
Before the series opener against the Rangers, Slaten went with team medical staff to visit Keith Meister, a highly regarded orthopedic and sports medicine surgeon based in Arlington.
Meister diagnosed the reliever, who had been out with what the club called right elbow inflammation, with a more serious problem.
“There’s some degenerative changes in the flexor mass,” Tracy said. “So that’s substantially different news.”
The flexor is in the forearm and connects to the elbow. Slaten will receive an injection of platelet-rich plasma, which is supposed to stimulate healing. Tracy called it “the conservative course of action.”
Already, with Slaten’s pain lingering well beyond what the Red Sox figured would be a brief shutdown period when he went on the injured list on Aug. 16, he was trending toward not having time to return this season.
“This maybe adds some finality to the fact,” Tracy said. “We were already operating that way, but you still held out hope. ‘Hey, if it can turn the corner and [with] what he’s able to do out of that bullpen. . . . So yeah, it’s a big loss — at least now, the finality of knowing we can’t have it back.”
For Slaten, who turned 29 on Tuesday, it is another in a string of injuries that have limited his impact. Since reaching the majors in 2024, he has missed time because of elbow, shoulder, and oblique issues.
This year, the righthander had a 4.60 ERA overall and a 2.84 ERA in the two months before getting hurt.
The Red Sox’ top setup options for lefthanded closer Aroldis Chapman remain righthander Garrett Whitlock, lefthander Erik Miller, and righthander Tyron Guerrero. They expect Guerrero back from the IL as soon as Wednesday.
“[Slaten is] an important arm,” Tracy said, “but we have to deal with it and move on.”
Crochet builds up workload
Back at Fenway Park, Garrett Crochet on endured his heaviest workload yet in his bid to return for the playoffs, a 30-pitch bullpen session across two simulated innings.
“Everything went well,” Tracy said. “That was the most volume he’s had, so we’ll see over the next couple of days how he feels and go from there.”
Among other rehabbing pitchers: Tanner Houck made his third rehab appearance and first for Triple-A Worcester, striking out three of four batters (and walking the other). He threw 22 pitches but only 11 strikes.
The Sox’ plan calls for Houck to pitch for Worcester again late this week, throwing 50 or more pitches in a much longer relief appearance. For playoff purposes, they are keeping their options open, experimenting with Houck in short and long relief.
Progress for Mead
Seven weeks after fracturing his left wrist in his first game with the Red Sox, Curtis Mead is starting a hitting progression.
The infielder is due to begin “tee work” with an “underloaded,” lighter-than-normal bat on Wednesday, Tracy said. An ability to swing comfortably has held back Mead, who for weeks has been throwing/playing catch (including recently actually catching the ball thrown back to him).
Also in a race against the calendar, Mead appears unlikely to return this year unless the Red Sox play deep into the postseason
The running man
Ceddanne Rafaela (right quad strain) has “started to increase running volume” and will continue to do so the next several days, Tracy said. The center fielder has said he hopes to return this weekend when the Red Sox visit the Rays . . . Tracy and his staff gathered for a group dinner Monday, their first time doing so since Kansas City in mid-May. “So to be able to get all of us together and have a meal, it was a nice off day,” he said. Who paid? “The Red Sox.”
Tim Healey can be reached at timothy.healey@globe.com. Follow him @timbhealey.

item.title: [elplaneta.com] Inning inmaculado: la histórica gesta de Payton Tolle en Fenway Park
item.dc:creator: Marcos Grunfeld
item.description: Los Red Sox tuvieron que retrasar dos veces el inicio del juego del domingo debido a la lluvia que azotó Boston en el cierre de la semana. item.content:encoded:
Los Red Sox tuvieron que retrasar dos veces el inicio del juego del domingo debido a la lluvia que azotó Boston en el cierre de la semana. Fue imposible jugar antes de las 4:55 de la tarde, casi cuatro horas después de lo inicialmente estipulado porque iba a ser un domingo normal con el primer pitcheo lanzándose a la 1:35 de la tarde.
En la medida que se acercaban las 3:00 p.m iba despejándose la duda de que tampoco a esa hora iba a iniciar el duelo entre los patirojos y los Reales de Kansas City. En todo caso, el pitcher Payton Tolle se acercó a su manager Chad Tracy, le hizo un saludo militar y le dijo que estaría listo a la hora que el partido comenzara.
El zurdo no estaba mintiendo. A las 4:55 p.m tiró una recta de 95 millas en strike. Ocho envíos después consiguió una hazaña que solo ocho miembros del club habían conseguido. El monticulista tiró ocho rectas y un sinker para ponchar a sus tres primeros rivales con nueve strikes en fila y convertirse en el octavo miembro de la franquicia en lograr un inning inmaculado.
Es el segundo que lo consigue en el primer inning uniéndose al legendario Pedro Martínez.
“Fue divertido”, celebró Tolle después de la victoria de 4 a 1. “Fue chévere. Creo que después del tercer strike me vino la idea a la cabeza. Pero eso no debería pasar. Creo que debería ser mejor y no andar pensando en esas cosas, pero así sucedió”.
La transmisión del equipo captó el momento previo al último envío antes de la hazaña. Tolle miró a su dugout y sonrió. Dio cuenta que estaba al tanto de lo estaba por suceder en conchupancia con su coach de pitcheo Andrew Bailey.
“Estaba definitivamente pensando en eso”, contó. “Lo tenía en mente. Creo que miré a “Bales” y estaba sonriendo también. Fue divertido”.
Solo ocho monticulistas de los Red Sox habían conseguido esa gesta. El último había sido Chris Sale en mayo de 2021.
“Fue impresionante”, agregó el primera base Willson Contreras, quien regresó a la acción después de casi dos semanas lesionado. “Estuvo atacando la zona de strike. No estaba permitiendo mucha gente en base. Creo que es la primera vez que soy parte de algo así”.
Payton Tolle siguió brillando después de la hazaña y terminó con seis innings completos, sin permitir carreras, un bateador golpeado, cuatro hits y siete ponches.
Y si les quedó alguna duda sobre el saludo militar, tal parece es una broma que se gasta con Tracy todos los días.
“Tiene haciéndolo desde que llegué acá”, bromeó Tracy. “No le pedí que lo hiciera. Solo lo hace. No necesito que lo haga, pero es Tolle y eso es lo que hace”.

item.title: [BoSox Injection] Masataka Yoshida’s potential return creates another complicated Red Sox roster decision
item.dc:creator: Stephen Parello
item.description: The Boston Red Sox never fully resolved their outfield-designated hitter logjam, and once again it may create a roster conundrum. For much of the season, things had worked themselves out one way or another. Spending most of the season without Roman Anthony certainly wasn't ideal, but it did make for a cleaner lineup card. His return, of course, has been music to our ears, and it saved the Red Sox from another tough roster decision due to the injuries to Masataka Yoshida and Ceddanne Rafaela. The
item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox never fully resolved their outfield-designated hitter logjam, and once again it may create a roster conundrum. For much of the season, things had worked themselves out one way or another.
Spending most of the season without Roman Anthony certainly wasn't ideal, but it did make for a cleaner lineup card. His return, of course, has been music to our ears, and it saved the Red Sox from another tough roster decision due to the injuries to Masataka Yoshida and Ceddanne Rafaela.
There's a point where push might come to shove, though, and Boston is forced to make a tough choice. Chad Tracy won't rule out Yoshida returning in time for the playoffs, which would lead to some interesting decisions.
"He's [Yoshida] not on the 60-day (injured list). It's just a matter of how does he heal over the next handful of weeks," the interim skipper said.
If the 33-year-old can return in time for October, it could put the likes of Mickey Gasper or Nick Sogard in the crosshairs. At which point, the Red Sox will have to make a choice and leave someone unhappy.
Masataka Yoshida shouldn't cost Mickey Gasper or Nick Sogard a spot on the Red Sox playoff roster
Just because Yoshida can come back (and that's still up in the air) doesn't mean he should. The NPB veteran has done what he's always done since coming stateside, hit for some average and get on base, but has provided very little in the power department.
Through 87 games, he's hit .274/.347/.399 with five homers, which is nothing to sneeze at, but doesn't really scratch the Red Sox's power itch. On top of that, despite what we saw in the World Baseball Classic, he has little defensive value and will be a nonfactor in the outfield coming off a serious hamstring strain.
Comparatively, Gasper's hot bat better fits what Boston needs. While he might simply be riding the wave rather than emerging as a true offensive force, the switch-hitter has brought the pop with eight dingers in just 187 plate appearances and a .500 slugging percentage, all while providing similar contact and on-base numbers to Yoshida.
Furthermore, he has some value in the field with the ability to fill in behind the plate if needed, as well as play first base. That alone gives him an edge over the DH-only Yoshida.
As for Sogard, his offensive profile is similar to Yoshida's, but his positional versatility is far superior. Depending on Curtis Mead's recovery, Sogard is a valuable insurance policy at second base that should have him over Yoshida in the October pecking order, too.
Craig Breslow's failure to move Jarren Duran before he became a radioactive asset is the real key here. Not only does it represent a missed opportunity for the Red Sox, but it is also the main barrier for Yoshida, given that Boston can't really afford to carry a DH-only player. With that, the choice should be clear. Even if Yoshida is healthy, he needs to sit this October out.

item.title: [The Boston Globe] Deep down, Garrett Whitlock doesn’t think his career as a starting pitcher is over - The Boston Globe
item.dc:creator: Tim Healey
item.description: Now is not the time, of course, what with the Red Sox in a playoff push and all. But deep down inside, in a maybe-one-day-eventually sort of way, Garrett Whitlock harbors aspirations to try again to be a starting pitcher, to return to the rotation. Consider it a curiosity. “I definitely know my body better and know everything better now, and so it’s definitely something I’d be open to. Will I?” Whitlock said. “I’m not going to walk into [chief baseball officer Craig Breslow’s] office and be like
item.content:encoded:
Now is not the time, of course, what with the Red Sox in a playoff push and all.
But deep down inside, in a maybe-one-day-eventually sort of way, Garrett Whitlock harbors aspirations to try again to be a starting pitcher, to return to the rotation.
Consider it a curiosity.
“I definitely know my body better and know everything better now, and so it’s definitely something I’d be open to. Will I?” Whitlock said. “I’m not going to walk into [chief baseball officer Craig Breslow’s] office and be like, ‘Hey, I’m starting.’ So it’s one of those things where the team would have to be on board with it and just talk through everything and go through it. But it’s something I’d always be open to.”
Whitlock is intrigued enough to have picked the brain in recent months of Griffin Jax, the righthander whom the Rays converted from reliever to starter this season.
Jax, 31, had an 8.00 ERA in 11 relief appearances, moved to the rotation in April, slowly built up his pitch count, and has a 3.59 ERA in 20 starts.
Whitlock and Jax became buddies when they played together for Team USA during the World Baseball Classic in March. They’ve texted about what amounts to an experiment for Jax.
Jax’s take, per Whitlock: Everything he learned in his years as a reliever, several as a high-end reliever, made him a better pitcher, regardless of role. Tweaks to his repertoire, knowing how to attack hitters, and ensuring his body recovers between outings — it all applies to being a starter.
Whitlock has had similar conversations with the Cubs’ Clay Holmes, another Team USA teammate. He made the switch last year.
“We all joke that we’re all failed starters,” Whitlock said of his bullpen brethren.
Take it from the Royals’ Seth Lugo, who beat the Red Sox on Friday.
He and Whitlock have had very similar career arcs: They reached the majors in their mid-20s as non-elite prospects, bounced between the bullpen and rotation based on team need and their performance, and accepted their club wanting them in a relief role. They were excellent at it.
All along, Lugo, a consummate pro and good employee in his years as a Mets reliever, said he wanted to give starting another go — someday. Now, he is in his fourth season and third contract since getting the chance — once he became a free agent — and turning it into a successful and lucrative second act.
“It’s not as daunting as it seems,” Lugo said at Fenway Park over the weekend. “What happens is you first get to the big leagues and you try to be someone that you’re not, just from other influences, other recommendations. But you [learn] how to get guys out [as a reliever].
“Once you make the switch back, you have the confidence. The problems you had earlier in your career, [which] sent you to the ’pen in the first place — you’re aware why those mistakes happened.”
Lugo, like Whitlock, was a late-innings arm. He faced the other team’s best hitters in some of the most important moments of the game.
“Once you have success pitching the seventh, eighth, ninth inning, the first six innings become a lot easier,” he said. “As a reliever, when you’re going into a game, you’re a lot more stressed out than you are as a starter. So you start to recognize what you’re good at, how you can get out of those situations.”
Whitlock, who possesses a 1.81 ERA in 51 relief appearances this year, last made more than a handful of starts in 2023. Since then, he ditched the four-seam fastball to lean even more on his sinker, went with a slider instead of a sweeper, and changed his changeup, which has become highly effective.
In discussing the possibility, Whitlock is a realist: The Sox’ rotation seems full for the foreseeable future.
His contract includes team options for 2027 ($8.25 million) and 2028 ($10.5 million). Those are good deals for an elite reliever — and a really good deal for even a serviceable starter.
“I doubt Boston will do it. We’re pretty good on starting depth,” Whitlock said. “If I become a free agent and a team approaches me about it, I’m open to it and see how it goes.”
Perez on Abreu
Royals icon and Venezuela captain Salvador Perez, witness to Wilyer Abreu’s WBC star turn, is a big fan — and a big believer of Abreu on a big stage. “He’s going to be the MVP if Boston makes it to the World Series,” Perez said. “He’s built for a moment like that.” … Early returns on Adley Rutschman’s cortisone shot last week, intended to alleviate pain in his right elbow, are solid. Against Kansas City, he went 3 for 10 with a double, as many walks as strikeouts (two) — and played three games in a row for the first time since getting hurt. “It definitely helped a lot,” interim manager Chad Tracy said. “You can tell his body language and stuff too, he looks and feels pretty good.” … Garrett Crochet’s bullpen session Tuesday is scheduled for 30 pitches across two simulated innings, a step up from previous shorter sessions.
Tim Healey can be reached at timothy.healey@globe.com. Follow him @timbhealey.

item.title: [The Boston Globe] Old teammate Kurt Suzuki has only positive words for Craig Breslow and Andrew Bailey, and other Red Sox thoughts - The Boston Globe
item.dc:creator: Peter Abraham
item.description: Andrew Bailey, Craig Breslow, and Kurt Suzuki were teammates with the Oakland Athletics from 2009-11. Now Bailey is the Red Sox pitching coach, Breslow is chief baseball officer, and Suzuki is managing the Angels. Suzuki, a former catcher, knows the Red Sox pitching coach and chief baseball officer well. Bailey was a two-time All-Star closer with the Athletics, and Breslow made 202 appearances as a setup man during that time. “I thought Bres would cure cancer when he was finished with baseball,”
item.content:encoded:
Andrew Bailey, Craig Breslow, and Kurt Suzuki were teammates with the Oakland Athletics from 2009-11. Now Bailey is the Red Sox pitching coach, Breslow is chief baseball officer, and Suzuki is managing the Angels.
Suzuki, a former catcher, knows the Red Sox pitching coach and chief baseball officer well. Bailey was a two-time All-Star closer with the Athletics, and Breslow made 202 appearances as a setup man during that time.
“I thought Bres would cure cancer when he was finished with baseball,” said Suzuki, referencing the lefthander graduating from Yale with a degree in molecular biophysics and biochemistry. “But I can see why he stayed in baseball. He was always ahead of the times the way he thought about the game.
“When I caught him, I called him ‘Everyday Bres.’ He was always ready to pitch every day, never complained, and always got people out. He was a good person to be around.”
Suzuki is not surprised to see his former teammates still involved in the game.
“I think we all love the game. We all had an interest to stay in the game beyond our playing time,” he said. “Bres pitched in the big leagues for a long time and gained a lot of information. I don’t know if I would have predicted he’d be running a team, but I’m not surprised.
“The same with [Bailey]. You knew he would have a bright future in the game if that was what he wanted. He’s one of the best pitching coaches around.”
A few other observations on the Red Sox:
▪ It seems funny to think about now, but Aroldis Chapman came to spring training in 2025 with no guarantee he would be the closer.
The lefthander was competing with Liam Hendriks, who was returning from Tommy John surgery. Breslow said at the time Justin Slaten also would receive consideration.
Chapman had 14 saves for the Pirates in 2024, but nine of them came in September for a last-place team.
Hendriks never had a save for the Sox. Slaten had one in March and two in April that season, and none since.
Chapman has converted 65 of 69 save opportunities for the Sox and taken steps that could lead to the Hall of Fame.
▪ No Red Sox infielder has won a Gold Glove since Ian Kinsler in 2018, and he joined the team at the trade deadline that season and started only 35 games at second base. For a full season, you have to go back to Pedroia in 2014.
Caleb Durbin is set to break that drought.
The third baseman has 11 defensive runs saved, the most in the American League by a wide margin. Tampa Bay’s Junior Caminero, with three, is a distant second. Durbin also leads in other metrics, including outs above average.
▪ As the season winds down, Wilyer Abreu is first in doubles, second in runs and home runs, fourth in RBIs, and fifth in OPS among AL outfielders.
The right fielder believes playing in the World Baseball Classic contributed significantly to that success.
“I worked a lot in the offseason to be prepared for the WBC,” Abreu said. “So when the season started, I was ready to go. That helped me a lot.”
Abreu also benefited from being around Venezuela hitting coach Miguel Cabrera and assistant manager Victor Martinez.
“I talked a lot to them about my approach and how to attack pitchers on what they throw,” he said. “Miggy was such a smart hitter, and he really helped me.”
▪ Fred Lynn was at Fenway Park for the Angels series this past week. He follows the Sox closely and often arrives at the park early to watch batting practice.
Most of the players had no idea who the 74-year-old guy with the good tan was, but Roman Anthony did and had a conversation on the field with Lynn on Tuesday.
“He was somebody I’d wanted to meet for a while, obviously. A legend,” Anthony said. “Somebody said he was out there, so I immediately wanted to say hello to him and his wife, and they were great.
“He shared some of his experiences here, his experiences when he left here. It was great to hear it.”
No. 19 talking to No. 19 was interesting to watch from a distance. Anthony received a lot of attention when he was called up last year, but nothing like the mania for Lynn and Jim Rice in 1975.
Anthony has looked up the statistics. He gets it.
“I got familiar with him when I got 19 when I first came up last year,” he said. “He was pretty excited about it and sent some love. Obviously, he was an unbelievable player, an unbelievable Red Sox. But a great human, too. It was awesome to interact with him.”
▪ The Sox traded for Curtis Mead on July 26. He started at second base against the Athletics in Sacramento the next day, and broke his left wrist when he was hit by a pitch in his second plate appearance.
Red Sox second basemen have since hit .245 with a .718 OPS and 21 RBIs. It’s not great, but nine American League teams have a lower OPS from their second basemen in that span, and 10 have a lower wRC+.
As for Mead, he is playing catch but isn’t hitting yet. The Sox haven’t ruled him out for the rest of the season, but interim manager Chad Tracy has acknowledged it’s unlikely Mead will return until 2027.
Connelly Early, who was traded for Mead, has yet to pitch for the Nationals because of an elbow injury. He is scheduled to make a rehab start for Double-A Harrisburg on Sunday. The Nationals hope he’ll be able to get into a major league game before the season ends.
▪ Baseball lost a legend last week when Joe McDonald passed away at the age of 97.
McDonald started in baseball in the 1940s working with the ticket takers at Ebbets Field. He joined the Mets in 1962 and became their general manager from 1975-80.
He later became GM of the Cardinals (1982-84) and Tigers (1991-92) before scouting for the Angels and Rockies. He finished his career scouting for the Red Sox from 2004-19.
“Joe was a joy to work with and always very generous in sharing his experience and expertise. He loved the game, was willing to go scout a player anywhere at any time, and just wanted to contribute,” said former Sox GM and current Fenway Sports Group senior adviser Theo Epstein, who hired McDonald. “Having two great former GMs like Joe and Bill Lajoie around was incredibly valuable to me. He will be missed.”
Peter Abraham can be reached at peter.abraham@globe.com. Follow him on Bluesky at peteabeglobe.bsky.social.

item.title: [bosoxinjection.com] Cam Schlittler-Dylan Cease Cy Young race has an important Red Sox wrinkle everyone is forgetting

item.content:encoded:
The American League East has always been the sport's most star-driven division, even when the standings don't always show it. The New York Yankees-Boston Red Sox rivalry alone has produced decades of this, but it's not just those two anymore.
The Toronto Blue Jays have peaked into a real contender, the Tampa Bay Rays are leading this year's race and continue to develop, and the Baltimore Orioles are always one prospect wave away from popping off again. With that much noise in one division, it's easy to lose track of just how much individual talent is walking around it.
Case in point: with Tarik Skubal now pitching for the Los Angeles Dodgers, this year's AL Cy Young race is shaping up to be a battle between two AL East arms, Cam Schlittler and Dylan Cease. That trophy is staying in this division no matter what. But for Red Sox fans, it's worth saying the obvious: if Garrett Crochet had stayed healthy all year, he'd be right in that conversation too, not watching it from the outside looking in.
A healthy Garrett Crochet would've made the 2026 AL Cy Young Award race more interesting
It's easy to forget just how dominant Crochet was in 2025. He went 18-5 with a 2.59 ERA across a league-leading 205.1 innings, struck out a league-best 255 batters, and finished as the AL Cy Young runner-up behind Skubal himself. Take a quick glance at his Baseball Savant page from that season and it reads like a cheat code, elite percentile marks across nearly every meaningful category a pitcher can be graded on. That's the version of Crochet the division rivals were supposed to get again in 2026.
Instead, he was clearly not right from the start, posting an ugly-looking 6.30 ERA across his first six starts before landing on the injured list on April 29 with a shoulder issue that turned into a lat problem after a setback in May. The strikeouts were still there (37 in just 30 innings), but the results were far from pretty, and Boston has been without its ace for basically the entire season since.
Here's where it gets exciting again, though. Crochet threw a bullpen session at Fenway this week, his second since resuming throwing, and interim manager Chad Tracy has been candid that a return this season likely means relief work, not a return to the rotation. Crochet has relief experience already from earlier in his career, and has shown flashes of pure domincance. In 72 bullpen appearances, he logged 73 innings with 85 punchies and 2.71 ERA. In his four postseason relief outings, he has a 0.00 ERA and has struck out 6 of the 14 batters he faced.
He's also made it clear he has zero ego about the role. With Boston fighting to hold onto that second Wild Card spot, a healthy Crochet coming out of the bullpen in high-leverage October moments would be about as fun a development as this fanbase could ask for down the stretch.

item.content:encoded:
Willson Contreras is back with the Red Sox, activated Sunday from the injured list for their finale against the Royals. He collected two hits and a walk in the 4-1 win.
The Red Sox didn’t need to think hard about how to open a spot on the active roster: infielder Anthony Seigler went on the injured list with a right wrist issue.
“We talked a lot about as guys were getting healthy, the conversation was like, ‘What are you going to do?’” interim manager Chad Tracy said. “Stuff’s going to happen, which it always does.”
Contreras missed a dozen games because of a left hamstring strain.
After playing through the leg problem for about a month, Contreras asked the front office to let him more thoroughly rest, figuring a September timeout would serve him well down the stretch and into the playoffs.
On his first day back, he tested it plenty — hustling to first base and advancing to second on an error, moving from first to third on a single.
“I ran a lot today on the field, and my hammy feels pretty good,” Contreras said. “I won’t lie: If I wasn’t feeling really good in [Double-A] Portland, I wasn’t going to play tonight.”
Tracy said: “The point of [going on the IL] was to get [the hamstring] to a point where he felt confident in it, where he can go out and play and not have to worry. And at least like to think we’ve got to that point, which is good.”
In a two-game tuneup with Double-A Portland, Contreras went 2 for 7 with three strikeouts and no walks.
His appearance Saturday yielded a strange episode in the fourth inning. After a ball moved the count to 1-and-1, he called timeout, seemingly to get pine tar. Plate umpire Daniel Bytheway called him back to the plate.
Contreras then all but stopped participating in the plate appearance, leaving the bat on his shoulders for the next four pitches. He struck out looking.
On his way back to the dugout, drawing boos from the Portland crowd, Contreras tossed his bat back toward the plate.
“I didn’t even know until somebody showed it to me this [Sunday] morning,” Tracy said before the game. “I haven’t even seen him and asked him that yet. I think that’s something to do with pine tar.”
Contreras said later Sunday: “I don’t know. You can go ask the umpire. His name is Gary. Thank you.”
The Red Sox didn’t have a diagnosis on Seigler, who hurt himself on a seemingly random swing Saturday, but intended to send him for tests in the coming days.
As the rotation turns
The Red Sox will keep their starting pitchers in line against the Rangers: Patrick Sandoval on Tuesday, Jake Bennett on Wednesday, Sonny Gray on Thursday. Brayan Bello is bumped back to the bullpen following a one-start cameo.
Rehab roundup
The Red Sox will bring Tyron Guerrero (right shoulder inflammation) to Texas and activate him during the Rangers series. They haven’t decided which day. He is eligible to return Wednesday.
Ceddanne Rafaela (right quad strain) told NESN he is planning to return for the Rays series next weekend.
“We’ll call that a goal. It’s not a guarantee,” Tracy said. “It really is dependent on strength numbers in the quad and making sure that’s appropriate, and then he gets through all the sprint volume stuff first, and then we’ll see where he’s at.”
The Sox will leave it up to Rafaela, Tracy added, whether he wants to go on a rehab assignment before returning. Triple-A Worcester is the last affiliate still in season.
Justin Slaten (right elbow inflammation) still has not resumed throwing.
Guest of honor
Beverly native Beckett Connolly, a 10-year-old liver cancer survivor and transplant recipient, threw out a ceremonial first pitch — to hefty applause from the Fenway Park crowd.
Tim Healey can be reached at timothy.healey@globe.com. Follow him @timbhealey.
